WF-TRANSITION.todayObjective: Reflect on evidence from the guided Role Path and choose the team's next workflow priorities, using relevant existing topics or a custom huddle.
WF-TRANSITION.whyItMatters: Teams sustain change when they use evidence from practice to set their next learning priorities rather than continuing a fixed path by default.
WF-TRANSITION.desiredOutcome: Sustain team-owned workflow improvement beyond the guided path, choosing relevant huddles and adapting priorities as shared experience reveals useful habits, friction, and changing needs.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about three minutes reconnecting to why the Huddle Motion matters to the work.
2. Recognize the shift from guided Weeks 1-8 to team-owned learning, not the end of the motion.

3. Preview the shared transition: reflect on experience, choose the next focus, and close with participant feedback. These are coordinated session components, not four alternative practices to complete.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about ten minutes comparing experiences using examples the group may discuss.
2. Explain what changed in the workflow or why a practice did not help yet; no success story is required.
3. Identify a habit worth repeating and a friction point or support need.
4. Use these observations to inform the next-focus discussion, without ranking participants.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: AI in Action: choose the next team focus
activities.description: Choose a next work priority and an existing or custom huddle starting point, using tools and content permitted for the team.
activities.expectedOutput: An agreed next priority, a suitable huddle or draft starting point, and an owner; optional backlog ideas remain separate.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the ten-minute AI-in-Action segment to connect the reflection to work where a change would be useful.
2. Choose the priority to try first; keep up to two other ideas as an optional backlog rather than simultaneous commitments.

3. In All Topics, compare relevant outcomes and activities, filtering by Segment, Role, Focus Area, and tools permitted for the team and project. Select one Featured practice for the next ordinary huddle; Extended practices remain optional.
4. If no topic fits, use Huddle in a Box to outline a draft for later review, not to create or publish a finished huddle in this session.
5. Confirm an owner and a practical next step. Without app access, record the priority and locate the content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear next-focus commitment and a participant-owned feedback opportunity, with any unfinished survey completed after the huddle.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Use the final five minutes to restate the useful habit, friction point, and chosen next focus.
2. Confirm who will take the next step and when the team will revisit what it learned.
3. Open the Team Member Impact Survey and let participants complete their own responses. If time or access is insufficient, finish after the huddle rather than extending the live session.
4. Continue the team-owned motion; this transition is not a final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided activation to team-owned practice. The team has completed the eight-week activation journey. Use this huddle to recognize what changed, address friction, and choose what to focus on next.
keyTalkingPoints: This is the same participant experience for every role. Overview: 3 minutes - reconnect to the motion and the transition to team ownership. Share Your Experience: 10 minutes - reflect on useful changes, friction, and support needs. AI-in-Action: 10 minutes - choose the next team priority and a relevant existing or custom huddle starting point. Closing & Next Steps: 5 minutes - confirm the owner and next action, then allow participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey.
discussionQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent?
Which two or three team priorities would be most useful next?
suggestedTransitions: Use the coordinated Transition agenda: Overview, Share Your Experience, AI-in-Action, and Closing & Next Steps. Reflect on real work, agree the next focus and owner, and use the final five minutes for participant-owned survey completion. Review All Topics or a custom-huddle idea only if time and access permit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close the guided path by naming one useful habit, one unresolved friction point, and two or three priorities for team-owned huddles. Assign a follow-up owner for each priority. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately; if access is blocked, record the blocker for follow-up.
preparationChecklist: Before joining, bring one concrete example where AI changed your work, one friction point or challenge, and one idea for what comes next. Keep examples appropriate to share. No separate role-specific Week 9 preparation is needed.
facilitatorQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent, and what support or practice would help?
Which two or three priorities are most useful now?
Which All Topics huddle or custom huddle could help with each priority?
listenFor: Concrete examples of work changed, one useful habit to keep, and a specific friction point. Keep reflection conversational, not a scorecard. priorities grounded in team work and an owner or next step. Remind the group to share only information it is authorized to discuss.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If examples are vague, compare one task before and after and keep tool discussion anchored to the work. If the app, search, download or survey is inaccessible, capture the useful habit, friction point, next priority and follow-up owner manually; do not require Create your own huddle or Huddle in a Box to complete the conversation. A sanitized or clearly labeled synthetic task can demonstrate the reflection method, but is not personal impact evidence or a substitute survey response. Record the access gap and use the approved link/process later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which habit should the team keep, what evidence supports it, and what friction remains? Which two or three priorities should shape the next huddles?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next team-owned huddle, test one chosen habit on real work and decide what to keep, revise or stop. Agree the next topic and owner. Use the Frontier Accelerator topic library or Huddle in a Box if useful; otherwise plan manually. Use approved tools and permitted inputs only. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately, or record an access blocker.
bringBackEvidence: At the next huddle, share one brief, anonymized observation: what changed, what remains uncertain, and what to adjust next. Keep restricted details in approved systems. If untested, share the blocker and next check. Survey completion is not evidence of workflow benefit.

WF-COACH.roleTopicDescription: Prepare and conduct an evidence-led coaching conversation with a subordinate leader, manager, seller, or accountable owner focused on judgment and the next decision.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A decision is stalled, an assumption is weak, or the same execution pattern is recurring without a clear owner-led correction. Focus on one decision and the evidence needed to make it.
keyTalkingPoints: Leadership decision: Choose the decisive coaching question, decision criteria, owner commitment, and follow-up evidence.
Boundary: Only direct or assigned managers provide formal performance coaching; other leaders coach business decisions or subordinate leaders without assuming direct people-management authority.
discussionQuestions: Which assumption can a coaching question test?
Is this business-decision coaching or formal manager-only performance coaching?
What owner commitment and follow-up evidence are needed?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Rehearse the coaching conversation and challenge the reasoning'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the selected evidence or rehearsal to one human-reviewed decision, its authority limit, accountable execution owner and next check. Keep individual-contributor and receiving-owner decisions with those owners. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Retrieve authorized business evidence for the coaching decision', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Leadership coaching tests decision quality without assuming direct people-management authority. Formal performance coaching belongs only to direct or assigned managers. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one permitted stalled business decision, the unresolved assumption and approved evidence. Identify the actual decision authority and next owner. Exclude employee/HR data and AI-generated individual performance judgments.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision criterion should the owner explain rather than defend a score? Which coaching question tests the reasoning? How would another leader stay within assigned management authority while agreeing follow-up evidence?
listenFor: Activity reporting without a decision, local shadow data, mixed metric definitions, assumed authority, AI-generated employee evaluation, or leader takeover of field execution. Only direct or assigned managers provide formal performance coaching; other leaders coach business decisions or subordinate leaders without assuming direct people-management authority.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one de-identified decision-coaching plan: criterion, evidence gap, reasoning question, assigned coaching authority and follow-up evidence. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Rehearse with a peer; if alone, write both sides and mark the exchange untested, not a validated customer or coaching response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which question exposed weak reasoning, and where does your coaching authority stop?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Choose one Featured practice that fits the question and your authorized access and evidence; otherwise review the same question manually. Before the next huddle, rehearse a decision-quality question and seek the appropriate owner next-check agreement without employee scoring or unassigned performance coaching. Keep approvals, people decisions, record changes and messages human-owned. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized example and name the gap rather than infer status.
bringBackEvidence: Share a de-identified question refined and whether it improved reasoning; no employee evaluation or coaching plan is required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on preventing late commercial involvement by making the CE trigger and requested decision explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Use when pricing, agreement route, concessions, funding dependency, renewal, procurement, partner transaction, or approval complexity requires CE judgment.
Current execution: Use the current opportunity, agreement record, approved guidance, and direct request from DAE/opportunity owner.
Fallback: Use a structured engagement brief and named CE acknowledgment if no intake workflow exists.
System of record: MSX for opportunity context; authoritative agreement/licensing and approval sources for commercial facts.
Optional AI boundary: Cowork or Deal Agent may assemble supplied context where available. The CE validates every fact and makes the engagement decision.
discussionQuestions: What commercial decision requires engagement now?
What minimum context lets the owner act?
What would become unsafe if terms were shared before review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test whether CE engagement is required'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect one decision-changing evidence gap in the selected artifact, then compare a peer's approach and name the accountable next action. Drafts do not prove acceptance, approval or a completed system update. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Agree the working boundary', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Early CE engagement follows an actual commercial decision and transaction route, not a general request for help. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one material commercial question, approved opportunity/agreement context, the desired decision and the current engagement owner. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.
facilitatorQuestions: What trigger makes CE engagement necessary on this deal? What is the exact commercial decision and working boundary? How does a peer establish CE acknowledgment without taking over seller execution?
listenFor: Work starting without the stated trigger, partner involvement treated as universal, an unaccepted owner presented as coverage, AI output presented as system evidence, or SME&C Commercial Executive absorbing a decision outside this role boundary.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one CE engagement brief: triggering fact, exact commercial decision, working boundary and acknowledgment needed. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What needs CE involvement, and what can the account owner resolve without it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, clarify a commercial question and ask CE and the customer-path owner whether engagement is needed; evidenced no-engage is valid. Use Microsoft 365 Copilot only for permitted drafting or analysis; otherwise review manually. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. Funding, terms, eligibility and approvals remain with authorized owners. If inputs are unavailable, use a sanitized example and name the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized engagement question clarified and whether it avoided a late surprise or unnecessary handoff. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks
activities.description: Make the chosen workflow visible end to end, then locate the specific steps where time, confidence, or quality is lost.
activities.prompt: I run this recurring workflow: the workflow already described, including its trigger, cadence, and consumers. Here is a recent example of it going badly: the recent example already described. Break the workflow into its actual steps. For each step, identify what input it needs, what decision it requires, and who owns it. Then tell me which two or three steps most likely cost time or quality, and why you think so. Ask me for anything you need rather than assuming it. Do not propose tools yet. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A step-by-step map of the chosen workflow with the two or three highest-friction steps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The person who owns the workflow confirms the step map matches how the work is really done, not how it is supposed to be done.
activities.requiredContext: A recurring workflow you personally run; a recent concrete example; who owns each step; what inputs the workflow depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Describe the workflow and one recent example.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Correct the step map where the model got your work wrong; that correction is where the learning is.
5. Agree as a group which step leaks the most.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most workflow friction is invisible to the person living with it, because they have already adapted to it.

activities.name: Design one bounded experiment you can finish this week
activities.description: Turn the real end-to-end bottleneck into a one-week test tied to an outcome, with explicit permissions, human review, leading evidence, and a capability or improvement worth learning about.
activities.prompt: Here is the business outcome and end-to-end workflow I want to improve: the supplied outcome and workflow map. Here is the bottleneck: the supplied step and why it loses time, quality, confidence, or customer value. Design a one-week experiment. Specify the exact input, action, output, permissions, reviewer, stop condition, human accountability, downstream effect to watch, and leading evidence across time, quality, risk, customer value, or capability added. Keep it small enough to run in under an hour total. Suggest a best-fit tool only after the test is clear. If the scope is too large, narrow it rather than proposing a bigger plan. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A bounded experiment card with outcome, input, action, output, permissions, reviewer, stop condition, downstream effect, and leading evidence of efficiency, quality, risk reduction, customer value, or capability added.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide whether the experiment is genuinely small enough to finish, and you own the judgment about what output is safe to use in real work.
activities.requiredContext: The business outcome; end-to-end workflow map; selected bottleneck; accessible data and systems; required permissions or approvals; downstream users; and an available human reviewer.
activitySteps: 1. Take the step your group identified.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut the experiment down until it fits in an hour.
4. Name your reviewer and your stop condition out loud.
5. Put it in your calendar before you leave the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A fast task is not transformation if it moves the bottleneck downstream. A bounded test should improve the whole workflow or prove a capability the team could not reasonably use before.

activities.name: Review the experiment evidence and decide what to do next
activities.description: Compare the observed result of the bounded workflow experiment with its intended outcome and leading evidence, then record whether to stop, adjust, or continue.
activities.prompt: Use only the experiment plan and observed evidence I provide. Do not assume access to files, systems, or results that I have not supplied. Compare the observed outcome with the intended outcome and leading evidence. Separate observed facts, missing evidence, and interpretation. Identify any unexpected downstream effect or risk. Recommend whether to stop, adjust, or continue the experiment, explain the evidence behind that recommendation, and state one next action and owner. Do not claim the experiment succeeded if the evidence is incomplete. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A short experiment learning record separating observed evidence from interpretation, with a human decision to stop, adjust, or continue and a named next action and owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The workflow owner verifies that the evidence is real and relevant, then makes the stop/adjust/continue decision. Copilot's recommendation is not an approval or a result.
activities.requiredContext: The business outcome, bounded experiment plan, observed output or measurements, known downstream effects, and the human reviewer or workflow owner.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the bounded experiment plan and the evidence actually observed.
2. Run the prompt using only that supplied information.
3. Correct any unsupported inference and mark evidence that is missing.
4. The workflow owner decides whether to stop, adjust, or continue.
5. Record the decision, next action, owner, and evidence to bring back.
activities.whyThisMatters: Designing a test is not enough; the team needs to learn from the evidence and decide what changes in the workflow.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use as a substitute for a specialized agent when the work requires a specific system or workflow, for a multi-step task you would rather hand off and review, which is Cowork, or for work that should keep running on a schedule, which is Scout.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle has no pre-written workflow. Start with a business outcome, choose work people actually run, map the flow end to end, and simplify it before proposing AI. The goal is a better workflow and a useful learning loop, not a tool demonstration.
keyTalkingPoints: The workflow must be recurring and tied to a business or customer outcome.
Someone in the room must own it.
Map the whole flow, including inputs, decisions, handoffs, permissions, approvals, output, and downstream users.
Improve obvious process friction before adding AI.
A specific recent example beats a general description.
discussionQuestions: What outcome are we trying to improve?
What workflow most influences it, and who experiences the result?
Where does the end-to-end flow lose time, quality, confidence, or customer value?
What is impractical today that AI might make possible?
Where must a person review, approve, or intervene?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the outcome to the end-to-end flow, from the flow to its real bottleneck, and from that bottleneck to one bounded experiment with an owner, reviewer, stop condition, and leading evidence. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Workflow improvement starts with the outcome and follows the whole flow, including downstream effects. A bounded test preserves permissions, a human checkpoint and honest benefit or failure evidence. Treat the next use as a small test of better work; share the benefit or correction, not just the draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one recurring workflow you personally run and one recent example of it, including what made that run harder than it needed to be.
facilitatorQuestions: Where does the end-to-end workflow lose time, quality, confidence, or customer value?
Would improving one step move the bottleneck downstream?
What should be simplified before AI is added?
What could the team accomplish that is impractical today?
What permissions, monitoring, approval, or human intervention does the test require?
What would a one-week experiment look like?
Where did a peer's one-step AI improvement move the bottleneck downstream?
listenFor: Tool adoption presented as the outcome, a single-task speedup that moves the queue downstream, inaccessible inputs, missing permissions or approvals, an output nobody would notice if it were wrong, and experiments too broad to finish in a week. Also note capability-add opportunities that improve decisions, anticipate risk, or explore more options rather than only saving time.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one end-to-end workflow map and experiment card: trigger, inputs, decisions, handoffs, bottleneck, bounded test, permissions, reviewer and stop condition. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn about the whole workflow? Name one friction to remove, one new capability AI might add, one downstream risk, and the judgment that must stay human.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, choose the smallest workflow test you can own before the next huddle. State the outcome, permitted input, action, human checkpoint and stop condition; collect a small benefit or harm observation without automating approvals or outreach. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized observation: time or rework changed, a quality issue caught, a capability explored, or no benefit. Say what a person corrected and what the team should try next. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

activities.name: Work out whether your territory actually covers your number
activities.description: Do the arithmetic between what your territory can realistically produce and what you have been asked to deliver, and quantify the gap.
activities.prompt: Help me test whether my territory covers my number. Here is what I have: the supplied quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rate your team actually achieves at each stage. Using the conversion rates I supplied rather than any assumed benchmark, work out what the existing pipeline could realistically produce, and show the arithmetic so I can check it. Keep the renewal base separate from new business in your working rather than netting them together, because how renewals count toward quota depends on how my plan is structured. Then tell me how much new pipeline would be needed to close the remaining gap, and by when it would have to exist in order to close within the year. Derive a latest pipeline-creation date only from the sales-cycle durations or milestone timing I supply. If that timing basis is missing, show the required question instead of inventing a date. Do not double-count pipeline and renewal amounts that overlap. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. activities.requiredContext: Your quota for the year; current pipeline by stage with values; your renewal base; the conversion rates your team actually achieves at each stage; how renewals are treated in your own compensation plan. activities.name: Find where the growth is most likely to come from
activities.description: Identify which accounts in your territory have the strongest evidence for growth, so coverage planning is based on signal rather than familiarity.
activities.prompt: Across my assigned accounts, help me find where new pipeline is most likely to come from. Consider consumption trending against commitment, workloads the customer owns but has not deployed, renewal timing, recent engagement levels, and any account where activity has increased without a corresponding opportunity. Rank by strength of evidence rather than account size, and tell me what the evidence actually is in each case. Flag accounts where I have no basis for a judgment either way. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Accounts ranked by evidenced growth potential with the evidence named, accounts lacking any basis flagged, and the top three matched to a specific play.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides which evidenced opportunity is realistic given their capacity. A ranked list that exceeds the hours in the year is not a plan, and the seller owns that trade-off.
activities.requiredContext: Your assigned account list; consumption and renewal data; your coverage gap from the previous practice.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your assigned accounts.
2. Compare the ranking against your own instinct, and take seriously anywhere they disagree.
3. Note the accounts flagged as having no basis for judgment. Those need research, not a forecast.
4. Pick the top three and name the specific play for each.
5. Check the total against the coverage gap you calculated. If it does not close, say so now.
activities.whyThisMatters: Territory planning defaults to the accounts you already know. The growth is often in the ones you have not looked at, and the evidence for that is usually already sitting in the data.

activities.name: Build the support ask you can defend
activities.description: Turn the coverage gap into a specific, evidenced request for the help you need, rather than a general statement that the number is hard.
activities.prompt: I have a coverage gap and I need to ask for support. Here is what I have: the supplied gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what support you have already tried to get and what came back, and the specific resource or investment you think you need. Using only what I have supplied, help me turn this into a request a manager could act on: state the ask precisely, tie it to the specific accounts and evidence, show what has already been attempted, and set out what changes if it is not provided. Flag any part of the ask my evidence does not support, and do not invent a consequence I have not described. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A support request naming the specific ask, the accounts and evidence behind it, what has already been attempted, and the consequence of not getting it, with unevidenced elements flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what consequence to state. Overstating what happens without support costs credibility in the next review, and the seller is the one who will be there for it.
activities.requiredContext: Your coverage gap; your ranked growth opportunities; what support you have already tried to secure and the response; the specific resource, specialist or investment you need.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what you have already tried, and the specific support you need.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Cut anything you cannot evidence. An unevidenced ask weakens the parts that are real.
4. Check the consequence it states is one you would defend in a review.
5. Take it to your territory review or your manager rather than waiting to be asked.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support goes to the people who ask for something specific and evidenced. A general statement that the territory is difficult competes with everyone else saying the same thing.

activities.name: Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong
activities.description: Find the single assumption your territory plan most depends on, and work out what happens if it does not hold.
activities.prompt: Here is my territory plan and coverage calculation: the supplied plan. Identify the single assumption it most depends on, whether that is a renewal landing, one large opportunity closing, a conversion rate holding, or a consumption ramp continuing. Then tell me what happens to my coverage if that assumption fails, how early I would know, and what I could do now to reduce the dependency. Be direct about how concentrated the risk is. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: The plan's most load-bearing assumption named, the coverage impact if it fails, the earliest warning signal, and a contingency to reduce the dependency.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides how much concentration is acceptable. Some territories are genuinely dependent on one renewal, and the judgment is whether that is a risk to manage or a plan to change.
activities.requiredContext: Your territory plan and coverage calculation; the largest single opportunities and renewals within it; the conversion assumptions you used.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your plan and coverage calculation.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much rests on one deal or one renewal.
4. Work out the earliest signal that the assumption is failing, and schedule a check.
5. Decide now what the contingency is, while there is still time to build one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most territory plans fail on one assumption, not many. Knowing which one, and how early it would show, is the difference between adjusting in month three and explaining in month nine.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. This session tests that claim against arithmetic, while there is still time to do something about the answer.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current fiscal planning and territory-review requirements for your organization. Test the plan against governed quota, pipeline and renewal evidence, preserving dates and metric definitions. Separate actuals, forecasts and assumptions, and name the dependency or support request that changes the plan.
discussionQuestions: Do you know, arithmetically, whether your pipeline covers your number?
What single deal or renewal is your year most dependent on?
What support would actually change your position, and have you asked for it specifically?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out whether your territory actually covers your number'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coverage gap to the specific, evidenced support request each person will make. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Territory planning makes coverage arithmetic and assumptions inspectable. An evidenced support ask informs the manager; it does not authorize staffing or assign capacity. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring your governed quota, current pipeline by stage and renewal base with scope, source and as-of date. Distinguish actuals, forecasts and assumptions, and bring one dependency or support request that could change the plan.
facilitatorQuestions: What is your uncovered gap, and by when would new pipeline have to exist to close it?
Where is the growth evidence strongest, and does it match where you spend your time?
What is the one assumption your plan cannot survive without?
Which conversion or capacity assumption would a colleague challenge before accepting the coverage plan?
listenFor: Optimistic conversion rates used to make a plan look covered, growth ranked by familiarity rather than evidence, concentration risk nobody has named, and support asks phrased as a general complaint about difficulty.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one territory coverage calculation: supplied target/baseline, explicit conversion assumption, concentration/capacity risk and evidenced support question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the arithmetic tell you that your instinct had not, and what changes because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, check a material coverage assumption and take an evidenced support recommendation to the manager or territory review, respecting staffing and capacity authority. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized manual scenario and report the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized coverage assumption checked and whether it sharpened the ask or changed the plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year
activities.description: Separate the deals that can still be fully executed and processed before the period ends from the ones that are already next year's.
activities.prompt: For my patch, or a named account or TPID, list the opportunities with a close date in the current fiscal period. For each, tell me what the record shows about its approval state, what is still outstanding, whether it has been signed, and whether anything indicates it will arrive for processing after a cutoff explicitly confirmed in the guidance I supply. Tell me first which of these you can actually see. Do not tell me whether it will book, because the rule that decides that is set by my own segment's bookings policy and you do not have it. Tell me what still has to happen for each deal to be capable of booking in the period. If no cutoff or bookings rule is supplied, mark the timing question unknown and route it to Deal Desk/operations; do not invent a guaranteed processing date. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Each in-period opportunity with its approval state, what is still outstanding, its signature position, any indication it will miss the processing cutoff, and what still has to happen for it to be capable of booking.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the bookings rule locally and decides what is genuinely closeable. An approval state in the record is a snapshot, and only the person in the deal knows whether the customer will actually sign in time or is simply being polite about the date.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; the opportunities you expect to close in the period; their current approval state; what each is waiting on; your Deal Desk or operations contact for the bookings rule that applies to your segment.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your own patch or one account, and the deals you believe are landing this period.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Confirm the bookings rule that applies to your own segment with Deal Desk or operations rather than assuming it. What has to be true for a deal to book in a period, and by when, is set locally.
4. Separate deals waiting on Microsoft approvals from deals waiting on the customer. Confirm who can act on each and check verified processing runway rather than only the signature date.
5. Decide which deals you are deliberately leaving in the new year, and say so out loud rather than carrying them as hope.

activities.name: Find the renewals whose expiration timing will cost you the booking
activities.description: Identify renewals whose expiration date sits at the period boundary, where how they are handled decides whether they land in this year or the next.
activities.prompt: For my patch, or a named account or TPID, list the renewals with expiration dates at or near the end of the current fiscal period. For each, tell me the actual expiration date, whether it has been committed as on-time, what is still outstanding to complete it, and what the record shows about customer engagement on it. Flag any renewal where the expiration falls on the final day of the period, so I can confirm any booking/billing-calendar difference with the authoritative operations owner. Tell me what you cannot see rather than assuming it is fine. State a calendar rule only where the current guidance I supply confirms it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewals at the period boundary with their actual expiration dates, commitment status, outstanding work and customer engagement, with last-day expirations flagged for deliberate handling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the processing runway with the person who owns it. Renewal processing has a real lead time and the deadline that matters is when the work has to arrive, not when the agreement expires.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; renewals with expiration dates near the period end; their commitment status; your renewals or operations contact.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your patch or one account with renewals near the period boundary.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Flag last-day expirations for an operations check; do not assume a different treatment without current authoritative guidance.
4. Confirm the processing runway with your renewals or operations contact rather than assuming it.
5. Commit the ones that are genuinely on-time and stop describing the others as on-time.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal at the period boundary is the easiest booking to lose and the hardest to explain, because nothing about it looked at risk until it was.

activities.name: Prioritize record corrections against verified fiscal deadlines
activities.description: Find apparent record discrepancies and distinguish corrections with a confirmed fiscal deadline from year-round hygiene or timing that still needs verification.
activities.prompt: For [patch / account / TPID], inspect the authorized records and agreement evidence available or supplied for apparent discrepancies in agreement, licensing, enrollment, amounts, forecast dates and commitments. State what the record shows, what the authoritative evidence shows and what remains uncertain. Using current correction-window guidance I supply, separate items with a confirmed fiscal-close deadline, year-round hygiene and items whose deadline is unverified. Cite the rule behind a deadline; do not assume a field becomes uneditable at year end. Identify which owner must verify or correct each item. Do not change any record. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidence-backed correction list with confirmed fiscal deadlines, year-round hygiene and unverified timing separated; each discrepancy has an accountable verification/correction owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller verifies the correct position against the agreement before changing anything. A confidently inferred correction is still a guess, and a wrong correction made in the last week of the year is materially harder to undo than a wrong original.
activities.requiredContext: Authorized account/patch and identifiers; authoritative agreement/licensing evidence; current correction-window guidance if available; operations or Deal Desk contacts. Missing guidance leaves the deadline unverified.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one authorized account/patch and the executed agreement or other authoritative evidence.
2. Confirm current correction-window guidance with operations or Deal Desk.
3. Run the prompt and verify each apparent discrepancy and deadline.
4. Prioritize confirmed deadline-sensitive items by consequence and remaining runway; leave unverified deadlines as questions.
5. The authorized owner approves and makes exact corrections through the usual process, or routes them to the team that can act.
activities.whyThisMatters: Verified correction windows let the seller prioritize material discrepancies without treating an assumed fiscal cutoff as policy.

activities.name: Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented
activities.description: Sort your year-end pressure into work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar and work that belongs on the customer's own timeline.
activities.prompt: Here is everything I am treating as urgent because of year end: the supplied list, and for each say what i believe the deadline is and where that deadline comes from. Sort it into two groups. The first is work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar, meaning it must happen before the period closes because a system, an approval chain or a booking rule requires it. The second is work I am pulling forward into this month even though the real driver is the customer's own decision, contract or delivery timeline. For anything in the second group, tell me what it would cost to force it early. Where I have not said where a deadline comes from, ask me rather than assuming there is one. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Your year-end work sorted into genuinely fiscal-dated and customer-dated, the cost of forcing each item that is being pulled forward, and an owner and date for the items that are genuinely fixed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to force. Some work is worth pulling forward even at a cost, and that is a judgment about the customer relationship and the number, not one a model can make.
activities.requiredContext: Your own list of what you are treating as year-end urgent; where you believe each deadline comes from; the customer decision or contract timing behind each item.
activitySteps: 1. Write down everything you are treating as urgent because of year end, and where you think each deadline comes from.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about the ones where the only deadline is that it is June.
4. For anything you are pulling forward, decide whether the cost of forcing it is worth it. Often it is; the point is to decide rather than to drift.
5. Take the genuinely fiscal-dated items and make sure each one has an owner and a date that is earlier than the cutoff.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of what feels like a June deadline is a deal on its own clock being pulled forward. Doing that deliberately is fine. Doing it because the month feels urgent is how good deals get discounted and customers get pushed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Year end generates a lot of urgency and only some of it is real. This session separates the part that is genuinely fixed by the calendar from the part that only feels that way, and acts on the first while there is still room.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current local systems-close calendar and authoritative booking, billing and approval guidance; historical dates do not establish current deadlines. Work backward from the applicable cutoff and allow the confirmed processing runway. Verify period-end renewal handling with the responsible owner. Check any ECIF or milestone calendar for its region and motion rather than treating it as a worldwide rule.
discussionQuestions: Which of the things you are rushing right now would still be urgent if it were March?
What did you find out too late at the last year end?
Which deal did you pull forward last year, and what did it cost to do it?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use the chosen result to identify one evidenced close-period action or deliberate carry-forward decision; do not require both a full deal review and record repair live. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Fiscal close depends on verified cutoffs, customer reality and authorized record ownership. Calendar pressure cannot justify forced period timing or unsupported commitments. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring your own patch or one account, the deals and renewals you expect to land in this period, and a written list of everything you are currently treating as year-end urgent.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your in-period deals is waiting on Microsoft, and which is waiting on the customer?
What could you correct today that stops being correctable after close?
Which of your urgent items has a deadline you could actually point to?
How does a peer distinguish a real processing deadline from urgency inferred only from the fiscal calendar?
listenFor: Signature dates being treated as booking dates with no processing runway, renewals at the period boundary assumed to be fine, corrections being deferred to the week when every queue is longest, and deadlines whose only source is that it is June.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one fiscal-close workback: processing deadline requiring current confirmation, customer/Microsoft dependency, correctable record and carry-forward rationale. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your year-end deadlines turned out to have no source other than the month it is?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, verify the applicable close cutoff and inspect a record or timing assumption at risk. Make an authorized correction or route it, and have the accountable person review any proposed customer timing message. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized manual scenario and report the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized cutoff or timing assumption checked and whether it prevented a rushed correction or unsupported year-end commitment. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

AE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Explore how peer-led huddles connect business outcomes, recurring workflows, and responsible AI experimentation, including what to try and share between sessions.
AE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.
AE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Participate confidently in the motion, starting with a meaningful workflow and testing improvements in real work while retaining human judgment and learning from evidence.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. activities.name: Prioritize account action for this week
activities.description: Use Sales Agent and available sales context to rank accounts and name one next action for each.
activities.prompt: For [account scope], propose the ten accounts most deserving attention this week, or fewer if evidence is insufficient. For each show the priority driver, active opportunity stage, available renewal or whitespace signal, partner context and one seller action. Identify the dated source signal and missing context. Do not equate whitespace with customer demand; distinguish customer-confirmed need from a hypothesis. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A proposed weekly account ranking with dated priority evidence, available stage/renewal/whitespace/partner context, missing inputs and one seller action per account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which account genuinely deserves attention this week. A ranking built from recorded signal cannot see a relationship about to open or close, and cannot know what is realistic in the days actually available.
activities.requiredContext: Your account list; access to opportunity, renewal and whitespace signals; partner coverage for those accounts.
activities.whyThisMatters: Prioritization is a decision about what will not get attention.

activities.name: Build or assess the account plan with approval gates
activities.description: Assess the current account plan and propose evidence-backed additions for AE review; any record change follows a separate, explicit approval gate.
activities.prompt: For [Account] / [TPID], assess the current account plan and supporting evidence I supply. Propose additive updates to priorities, stakeholders, opportunities and next actions, explaining the source behind each. Identify missing or conflicting evidence. Research a gap only in sources I am authorized to access and share and that this tool can actually reach; otherwise ask for a permitted extract or leave it open. Keep changes as drafts. Do not write to MSX, notify anyone or make a commitment unless I separately approve the exact content and action and an authorized tool is available; otherwise give me the accepted changes to apply through my usual process. Use only customer and commercial data I am authorized to access and disclose through this tool. Name unavailable sources instead of assuming access; the separate exact-action approval gates above remain required.
activities.expectedOutput: Account-plan assessment with proposed updates, evidence gaps, and explicit approval/rejection decisions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE approves or rejects each proposed change and confirms nothing is written or committed without review.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its TPID; the current account plan and approved supporting evidence; your authority to approve or reject an MSX write. A write requires an authorized tool or your usual manual process; no installed account-plan skill is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout; this practice does not require an installed account-plan skill.
2. Replace [Account] and [TPID] in the prompt with your details.
3. Supply the current account plan and approved evidence, then run the prompt.
4. Review the assessment, evidence gaps and proposed additions against your own knowledge.

5. Approve or reject each proposed change. If an authorized MSX write tool is available, approve its exact changes before execution; otherwise apply accepted changes yourself through the approved process.
6. Confirm no write or commitment occurred without your approval.
activities.whyThisMatters: Account planning becomes usable when it creates next actions, not just more content.

activities.name: Pressure-test the account priority list
activities.description: Challenge whether your account priorities are driven by evidence or by habit and familiarity.
activities.prompt: Review my account priority list. For each of the top accounts, state the evidence behind the priority and whether it reflects a current signal or a standing assumption. Identify the account most likely to be wrongly prioritized, the account most likely to be wrongly ignored, and what would confirm either. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A priority challenge showing evidence per account, plus the most likely over-prioritized and under-prioritized account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which account is genuinely mis-prioritized. A model sees only the signals that were recorded, and the account most often wrongly ignored is the one whose activity happens off-system.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized account list; the source signal behind each priority; the accounts you have not touched recently.
activities.whyThisMatters: Challenge familiar account priorities before they consume a week that a better-supported account needed.

activities.name: Create the account follow-through plan
activities.description: Convert the account priorities into named next actions and the rhythm that keeps them from decaying into a list.
activities.prompt: Turn the account priority list into a follow-through plan. For each top account, define the next action, the owner, the date, the signal you will check to know it worked, and the point at which you would drop the account down the list. Set a weekly rhythm for reviewing it. Work from the material I have supplied rather than looking it up, and where a piece of it is missing, name the gap instead of filling it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: An account follow-through plan with next actions, owners, dates, verification signals, and a weekly review rhythm.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE sets the point at which an account drops down the list. That threshold is a judgment about where the AE own time is best spent, and no analysis can make it for them.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized account list; the next action for each top account; your weekly planning rhythm.
activities.whyThisMatters: A weekly account plan needs both an accepted next action and a reason to stop prioritizing it when the signal fades.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Account planning fails when it becomes an inventory. Focus on a short operating plan that helps you decide where attention goes this week.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritization requires saying no. AI can assemble customer, pipeline, renewal, whitespace, partner, and investment signals. You decide which account deserves action and why.
discussionQuestions: Which accounts get your attention by habit rather than evidence? Where is the account plan missing a decision? What signal would change your priority list?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prioritize account action for this week'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from account list discussion to one AE selecting a top account and naming the next action. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the account priority list', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Prioritization improves when account signals change where you spend attention, not when the list grows. Separate supported priorities from assumptions before choosing the next account action. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one territory or account list and one account where the next action is unclear. For the account-plan practice, also bring its TPID, current account plan and approved supporting evidence to supply to Scout.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account deserves attention that it is not getting? Which account gets attention mostly by habit? What evidence would change your top three?
How does another AE distinguish evidence-led priority from an account that gets attention by habit?
listenFor: Planning as annual documentation, prioritization by revenue alone, unclear next actions, missing role coverage, and customer priorities not connected to pipeline.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-account priority table: dated signal, customer priority, role gap, next action and AE judgment. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, use AI to build or refine one account priority view, then choose one next action you will actually take. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share one priority you checked and whether it clarified the next action. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Schedule account or opportunity checks
activities.description: Run a recurring MSX and interaction-grounded check In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: For [account/opportunity scope], check material changes, missing next steps, stale recorded engagement and new risk. For each item show the dated source signal, what cannot be established and one proposed seller action. First run this once, read-only, against the small named scope I supply. Use only sources I am authorized to access and disclose that are actually available to this tool; ask for a permitted extract or mark unavailable sources as gaps. Report source coverage and as-of dates. Use a previous verified result if supplied; otherwise create a dated baseline and do not claim a change. Do not create a schedule until I have reviewed the first result and explicitly approved the exact scope, sources, cadence, output location and human reviewer. If scheduling or a needed connection is unavailable, return a manual repeat procedure. Draft follow-ups only; do not send, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run opportunity review with actual source coverage, signals and proposed seller actions. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides what the scheduled check should be looking for. A check scoped too broadly reports everything and stops being read, and only the person reading it knows which signals would change what they do.
activities.requiredContext: The scope to watch; the cadence; approved access to the opportunity and account sources the check should read A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Read that first result against opportunities you already know. Every flagged item should name a source signal you can check; discard anything it got wrong.
5. Make one correction you own off the back of that read, so the check has earned its place.
6. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
7. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recurring checks should reduce review burden, not create another inbox.
