Preserve the difficult trade-off instead of hiding it behind technical detail. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming executive conversation, the desired decision, approved technical proof points and the claims that need validation. Confirm access to the named tools and review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: Read your opening line aloud. Would a CFO know what you meant?
Which claim in your narrative rests on a proof point you do not have?
What are you asking the executive to decide, stated in one sentence?
How would another ATS translate your strongest technical claim without losing its caveat?
listenFor: Architecture described rather than translated, value asserted without evidence, narratives that end without an ask, and jargon that survived because nobody in the room questioned it. Also note a narrative aimed at the technical stakeholder while claiming to target the executive.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one executive technical narrative: business decision, technical option, sourced proof, caveat and one-sentence ask. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which technical trade-off became clearer in customer terms, and what proof does the executive still need?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, rewrite one technical narrative for an executive audience, state the single decision you are asking for, and give them the options with their tradeoffs. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized trade-off made clearer and whether a reviewer better understood the executive decision. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on prioritizing AI and Azure workloads by readiness and impact.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a ranked workload view with readiness, impact, evidence, owner, and validation gaps. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Which workload are you spending time on because it is genuinely the priority, and which because it has momentum?
What readiness evidence would change your ranking?
Which workload would you drop if you had to drop one this quarter?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prioritize AI and Azure workloads'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the ranked list to the one workload you will commit technical time to, and what evidence you still need. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the workload readiness evidence', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Workload prioritization balances readiness, impact and dependencies. A high score does not authorize capacity or turn missing readiness evidence into commitment. Treat the next use as a small test of better work; share the benefit or correction, not just the draft.
preparationChecklist: Confirm access to the named tools, bring an approved pasted or exported MSXI or Proactive Insights snapshot with its account scope and as-of date, account context, and candidate workloads. Supply these to Cowork for the first practice; access to MSXI alone does not supply the evidence. Review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: What evidence supports your top-ranked workload, beyond it feeling important?
Which workload is ranked high because of readiness, and which because of upside?
What would have to be true for your ranking to be wrong?
What readiness assumption did a peer discover too late in a previous workload ranking?
listenFor: Rankings driven by the loudest stakeholder, readiness assumed rather than checked, upside estimated with no basis, and dependencies discovered after commitment. Also note a list that ranks everything and therefore prioritizes nothing.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a two-workload comparison: customer impact, evidenced readiness, unconfirmed dependency, ranking rationale and overturning evidence. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What readiness or impact evidence changed the workload order, and what capacity assumption still needs checking?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, compare readiness and impact for the workloads in an upcoming priority decision, then recommend where technical time should go; confirm capacity with its owner before committing it. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized readiness assumption that changed the workload order or supported a hold, and whether it focused technical attention. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Analyze consumption and technical blockers

activities.prompt: Show consumption versus target for the account and surface what the record indicates may be holding it back: open support or delivery issues, workloads deployed but showing little use, and milestones that have not moved. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Consumption gap and blocker view with the owning role identified for each blocker, and the technical action left open for the strategy work that follows.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides what the technical action should be. activities.whyThisMatters: The technical trajectory should respond to the blockers that are actually slowing value.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on developing a technical strategy and decision trajectory.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a technical trajectory with priority bets, proof needs, owners, risks, milestones, and open decisions. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What is the next technical decision this customer has to make, and when?
Which of your technical bets is least supported by evidence?
What would have to be true for the customer to commit to the direction you are recommending?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Analyze consumption and technical blockers'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the technical direction to the next decision it requires, with an owner and the evidence that unblocks it. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate technical and business assumptions', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical strategy advances through sequenced, evidence-backed decisions. A proposed owner or date remains a proposal until the person with authority confirms it. Agree where this fits in recurring work and how a small, safe signal will help the team learn together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one technical strategy decision, approved customer context, known constraints and the next proof or decision needed. Confirm access to the named tools and review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next decision in the trajectory, and who makes it?
Which bet would you abandon first if evidence went against it?
What proof does the customer need before they will commit, and do you have a path to producing it?
How does a peer make the next technical decision visible before it becomes a delivery blocker?
listenFor: A strategy that is a destination without a sequence, bets with no falsification condition, proof needs identified after the customer already asked, and milestones with no owner. Also note technical direction set without the customer's own objectives in the room.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one technical decision path: customer objective, options, next decision, proof gap, decision owner and date. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which assumption affects the technical decision sequence, and what proof or owner confirmation would change it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, clarify the next technical decision, ask its owner to confirm proposed proof and timing, and mark anything unconfirmed as open. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized technical decision or proof gap clarified and whether owner confirmation improved the next step. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.prompt: Help me organize an EBC for the customer. Choose the right session design and propose a coherent timeline and prep plan. For each customer participant, state what they get out of attending in their own terms, covering what they will learn, who they will meet and what will be clearer afterwards, and draft the invitation line that says it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. activities.expectedOutput: EBC plan with session design, participants, evidence, timeline, follow-through, and a stated reason to attend for each customer participant.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides what the briefing is actually asking the executive to decide. A briefing without a decision produces a good session and no movement, and who should be in the room follows from what is being decided. The ATS also decides whether the reason to attend would land with the person it is written for, since a reason that reads well internally can still be the wrong one for the person receiving the invitation.
activities.requiredContext: Customer; executive audience; desired decisions; approved context; the named customer participants and what each of them is measured on.
activities.whyThisMatters: An EBC only works if the decision, people, evidence, and follow-through line up.

activities.name: Build the run-of-show and evidence pack
activities.description: Turn the approved briefing plan into the run-of-show the session is actually delivered from.
activities.prompt: Using the approved EBC plan, build the run-of-show: each segment in order with its time allocation, the person leading it, the evidence or demonstration used, the questions put to the customer, and the decision the session closes on. Then build the preparation list that sits behind it: who needs to be asked for time and by when, what each contributor needs to be briefed on, and the room, catering, travel and equipment items that need an owner and a date. Assume the plan, participants and objectives are already agreed. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Run-of-show with segment order, timing, owners, evidence, customer questions, and the closing decision, plus a preparation list covering contributor briefings and logistics, each with an owner and a date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS confirms every piece of evidence is approved for customer use and that each segment owner has agreed to their part. The ATS also confirms the logistics items have a real owner, since room, catering and equipment tasks are easy to list and easy to leave unassigned.
activities.requiredContext: Approved EBC plan, confirmed participant list, and approved evidence; the session date, venue and format.
activities.whyThisMatters: The plan says why the briefing exists. The run-of-show is what the room is actually delivered from.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on designing an executive briefing experience.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is an EBC plan with desired decisions, participants, evidence, preparation milestones, and follow-through ownership. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What is the one thing the customer should leave the briefing believing?
Who in the room can actually approve the next step?
What is on your briefing preparation list that currently has no owner?
What would make this briefing worth their time rather than ours?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Design the executive briefing experience'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the briefing design to the single decision it is meant to produce and who must be present for that. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate briefing evidence and decisions', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: A briefing earns executive time by advancing a relevant customer decision with the right evidence and contributors. An invitation is not confirmed attendance or a decision guarantee. Make that evidence check part of recurring work; share a safe example of what changed so peers can adapt the habit.
preparationChecklist: Bring one planned executive briefing, its intended customer decision, proposed participants and known preparation dependencies. Confirm access to the named tools and review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: What will the customer do differently after this briefing?
Who in the room can approve that, and are they invited?
Which part of the agenda serves us rather than them?
Which agenda choice did a peer remove to make room for the customer decision?
listenFor: Agendas built around what we want to present, attendee lists without a decision maker, briefings with no ask, and content density that leaves no room for the customer to talk. Also note an experience designed for the meeting rather than for what happens after it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one executive briefing outline: customer decision, required decision-maker role, agenda choice, evidence and follow-through ask. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What makes the briefing worth executive time, and which decision or contributor is still missing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, review an executive briefing around a customer decision, check who can make it and draft the reason to attend; report attendance as requested or confirmed, not guaranteed. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized change to the decision, audience or reason to attend and whether it made the briefing more purposeful; pending attendance is acceptable. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the upcoming strategic technical conversation with the customer or stakeholder. Use the approved narrative and focus on technical outcomes, open decisions, likely objections, evidence, and the technical ask. Pause for my response before coaching me on clarity, listening, evidence, and next step. Do not invent customer facts or commitments. Use only the scenario and material I am authorized to share here. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on adjusting the technical talk track from customer signals.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a signal-adjusted talk track with opening language, questions, objections, responses, and human review flags. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What did the customer say recently that should change how you talk about this?
Where is your current talk track still answering last quarter's objection?
What signal are you choosing to ignore because it is inconvenient?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Adjust the talk track from current signals'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the customer signal to the specific line in your talk track that has to change because of it. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find the weak claims before the customer does', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Talk tracks improve when actual customer signals change a specific message. Keep what the customer said separate from your interpretation and validate new claims. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one current talk track, recent approved customer comments or signals, and the objection or assumption those signals challenge. Confirm access to the named tools and review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: What specifically did the customer say, and what did you infer from it?
Which part of your talk track is now answering a question they stopped asking?
What would you change if you took their last objection at face value?
What change in a customer's wording caused a colleague to change the substance, not just the phrasing?
listenFor: Signals interpreted to confirm what we already planned, talk tracks updated in wording but not in substance, and customer silence read as agreement. Also note adjustments based on one conversation with one person treated as the account's position.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one talk-track revision: quoted synthetic or sanitized signal, separate inference, changed line, caveat and customer validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What customer statement changed the message, and where did you separate the signal from interpretation?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, change one line in your talk track based on something a customer actually said this month. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized customer signal and a paraphrase of the line it changed, plus whether the revised message was clearer or still needs testing. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Build the v-team commitment board
activities.description: Lay the v-team's commitments out as a board the team can see and work from.
activities.prompt: Using the approved account and technical context, lay the v-team's work out as a board rather than a document: one row per commitment, showing the account, the owner, what it is waiting on, the date of the last observed activity and what that activity was, and the agreed next checkpoint. Sort the board by last observed activity, oldest first. Where a commitment has no agreed checkpoint, show it as not agreed rather than filling one in, and label any date you propose as a proposal. Mark a checkpoint as passed only where an agreed date already exists and today is later than it, and do not treat a checkpoint you are proposing as one that was missed. Cover every account I am carrying, not one. Include customer outcome, priority workloads, technical decisions, risks and required roles as supporting detail. Keep my own portfolio view separate from the per-account views I would share, so nothing from one account appears on another account's board. Format each shared view so it can be pasted into whatever that v-team already works in, and where a team has no shared tracker, give me a plain table I can paste into a message. Flag unsupported assumptions. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A v-team commitment board covering your accounts, sorted by last observed activity, oldest first, with an owner and a last-activity date on every row, the agreed next checkpoint where one exists and not agreed where none does, any proposed date labelled as a proposal, passed checkpoints marked, and the shared per-account views kept separate from your own portfolio view.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms each named role has capacity to take the work. Orchestration that assigns without asking produces a plan everyone nods at and nobody starts. The ATS also decides where each board lives and what belongs on a shared view, because accounts carry different teams and different confidentiality boundaries, and a tracker the v-team did not agree to use becomes another thing the ATS maintains alone.
activities.requiredContext: Approved account and technical context across the accounts you carry; role list; decision needs; for each open commitment, the date of the last observed activity on it, what that activity was, and the agreed next-checkpoint date where one exists; today's date; the tool each v-team already uses to track work, where they use one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Twelve commitments written as prose have to be re-read. The same twelve as rows can be sorted.

activities.name: Keep the v-team commitments moving between huddles
activities.description: Set up a recurring check that watches the technical v-team commitments and tells you what has slipped, without you having to go looking. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: Run a read-only check on the technical v-team commitments for the account or opportunity. Each week, look across our meetings, mail and the account record for the commitments made, and tell me which ones have no activity since they were made, which have passed their date, and which have gone quiet on the customer side. Give me the specific chase for each one and who should make it. Use the previous verified result I supply to distinguish new from repeated items. First run this once, read-only, against the small named scope I supply. Use only sources I am authorized to access and disclose that are actually available to this tool; ask for a permitted extract or mark unavailable sources as gaps. Report source coverage and as-of dates. Use a previous verified result if supplied; otherwise create a dated baseline and do not claim a change. Do not create a schedule until I have reviewed the first result and explicitly approved the exact scope, sources, cadence, output location and human reviewer. If scheduling or a needed connection is unavailable, return a manual repeat procedure. Draft follow-ups only; do not send, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run commitment check that reports slipped, stalled and quiet items with a named chase for each. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS decides whether silence actually means a stall, and owns the judgment about which chases are appropriate given the relationships involved.
activities.requiredContext: The v-team commitments and owners from the commitment board; approved access to your own mail, meetings and account record. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Bring the current v-team commitments with owners and dates.
5. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
6. Confirm each flagged commitment is genuinely stalled rather than progressing somewhere you cannot see.
7. Raise slipped items with the owner directly rather than in the group thread.
8. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
9. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical commitments do not fail loudly. They go quiet, and by the time anyone notices the customer has moved on. This is exactly the persistent, between-sessions work that Scout is built for.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on mobilizing the technical v-team around priorities and risks.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a v-team commitment board with owners, dependencies, investment signals, checkpoints, and next actions. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Who on your technical v-team could not state the current priority if asked today?
Which dependency has gone quiet in the last two weeks?
Where does your v-team actually look to see what is outstanding?
What are you carrying yourself that should belong to someone else?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the v-team commitment board'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coordination picture to one specific ask, to one named person, with a date. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Keep the v-team commitments moving between huddles', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: V-team mobilization turns a dependency into a bounded, answerable ask. Confirm accepted ownership and capacity rather than treating the board as agreement. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Confirm access to the named tools, bring the accounts you currently carry with the open commitments on each, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: If I asked each v-team member the current priority, would I get the same answer?
Which dependency is at risk, and does its owner know?
What are you doing yourself that is really someone else's accountability?
How does another ATS confirm a v-team commitment without absorbing another role's accountability?
listenFor: Priorities that live only in the ATS's head, owners assigned in a document but never agreed in a conversation, dependencies tracked without dates, and the ATS absorbing work because delegating it feels slower. Also note v-team meetings that report status without deciding anything.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one v-team commitment row: technical priority, dependency, proposed accountable role, acceptance needed, date and escalation trigger. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which handoff is still assumed rather than accepted, and what owner, request, or date would make it actionable?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, use the existing board for a priority account, or a small manual note, to draft and personally send a reviewed v-team ask with the input and proposed date. Ask the receiving owner to accept the work; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a safe description of a v-team ask and whether it was accepted, clarified or held; note any reduction in handoff ambiguity. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

SSP-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

Do not claim knowledge of their environment we do not have, and do not assert a product feature I have not given you. Do not send anything. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of unanswered asks with elapsed time and a drafted follow-up for each that adds new value rather than repeating.

activities.requiredContext: Access to your sent messages; your current lead and opportunity list; your team's follow-up cadence norms.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Lead and account signals are noisy. Focus on turning them into a focused follow-up plan.
keyTalkingPoints: Qualification is evidence work. Solution relevance, owner, message, consent, and next action must be explicit.
discussionQuestions: Which lead or signal deserves attention first? What evidence makes it real? Who owns the next action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from noisy signals to one prioritized follow-up plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Lead prioritization matters when credible demand leads to appropriate, consent-aware follow-up. Activity or a high AI ranking alone does not establish customer intent. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one lead or account signal, dated qualification evidence and the proposed follow-up owner. Confirm tool access and review the prior commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which lead has the strongest dated evidence of solution relevance, and what is only inferred? Who owns the first follow-up? How does a peer distinguish a buying signal from marketing activity before outreach?
listenFor: Undifferentiated lead lists, vague ownership, weak message fit, and missing consent/context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-lead ranking: dated solution signal, customer relevance, missing context/permission, follow-up owner and next question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which signal warrants a customer action rather than just a new record, and what evidence would disprove the opportunity?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, turn your top-priority lead into an actual first contact this week. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized lead signal and whether the reviewed follow-up clarified interest or avoided a poor contact; no sent message is required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Map who actually decides and who is missing
activities.description: Build the real decision map for this solution play, including the people who can stop it, not only the people who like it.
activities.prompt: Here is my solution-selling plan and the stakeholders I have engaged: the supplied plan and stakeholder list with roles and engagement level. The solution play is the supplied information, the decision type is the supplied value, such as new workload, renewal, or migration, the customer's organizational model is the supplied value, such as centralized IT, business-unit autonomy, or shared services, and their known procurement and technical governance constraints are the supplied information. Build a decision map showing who decides, who influences, who implements, and who can block. For each person, state what they need to believe for this to move forward and what evidence would convince them. Then identify missing roles ONLY where the solution play, decision type, organizational model, or governance constraints I gave you imply that role is required. Do not list generic enterprise buying-committee roles. Do not invent names; describe missing roles by function. If my context is too thin to identify missing roles, say so rather than guessing. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A decision map with what each stakeholder needs to believe, plus a named list of missing roles and the risk each creates.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP validates the stakeholder reality against what the account team actually knows, and owns the plan to reach anyone missing.
activities.requiredContext: Solution-selling plan; stakeholders engaged with roles; the solution play and decision type; the customer's organizational model; known procurement and technical governance constraints; who owns the customer relationship.
activitySteps: 1. List stakeholders engaged so far with role and engagement level.

3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Identify the highest-risk absence.

activities.whyThisMatters: Solution plans usually fail on a person nobody engaged, not on a fact nobody knew.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A solution-selling plan is useful only if it changes pursuit execution. Focus on building a plan that can be worked.
keyTalkingPoints: Plan around customer outcome, solution play, stakeholders, proof needs, demo or workshop sequence, and next decision.
discussionQuestions: Which solution pursuit needs a clearer plan? What proof or stakeholder coverage is missing?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the solution-selling plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Solution-selling plans should expose who decides, what proof matters and where engagement is missing. A stakeholder map is a hypothesis until the account team or customer confirms it. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one solution pursuit, the customer outcome, known stakeholders and the proof or decision gap in its current plan. Confirm tool access and review the prior commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: What next customer decision makes this pursuit worth specialist time? Where does the plan lack a stakeholder, proof path or dated commitment? What planning check from a colleague would expose that gap earlier?
listenFor: Generic solution plans, missing stakeholder coverage, unclear proof path, and no 30-day plan.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one solution-pursuit plan slice: next decision, stakeholder coverage, minimum proof, dependency, owner and dated action. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, check the decision map for a live pursuit and validate a missing stakeholder or proof requirement with the account owner before outreach. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized decision-maker or proof gap checked and whether it improved the pursuit plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Stress-test the assumptions the value claims depend on
activities.description: Expose what each outcome number quietly assumes, and record which assumptions the customer would have to accept.
activities.prompt: Here is our value narrative and the evidence brief behind it: the supplied information. For every outcome claim, produce a row containing: the claim, the assumption it depends on, who has to accept that assumption for the claim to hold, the evidence we currently have, and what happens to the claim if adoption is half as fast as projected. Rank the rows by how much the claim collapses when its assumption fails. Do not add claims that are not in my narrative, and do not supply evidence I have not given you. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: An assumption and risk table ranked by how much each claim depends on an unproven assumption.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP decides which assumptions are defensible with this customer, and owns every outcome figure before it reaches them.
activities.requiredContext: The value narrative; the evidence brief; the customer's financial context; adoption expectations already discussed with them.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value narrative and evidence brief.

5. Bring the assumption table to the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: The value claim you cannot defend is the one the customer will ask about.

activities.name: Prepare the solution-specific customer conversation
activities.description: Build grounded discovery, proof, objection, role contribution, and ask structure.
activities.prompt: Prepare me for the upcoming meeting with the account. Summarize priorities, stakeholders, open risks, competitive mentions, and solution context. Draft five discovery questions, proof points, likely objections with responses, role contributions, primary ask, and fallback ask. Flag uncertainty. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Conversation plan with discovery questions, proof, objections, role contributions, and ask.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides which parts of the prepared structure survive contact with the customer. A conversation plan assumes the customer's priorities are what the record says, and the opening minutes are where that assumption gets tested.
activities.requiredContext: Account; meeting; solution play; current stage; approved sales context.
activities.whyThisMatters: Preparation is where the solution conversation is decided.

activities.name: Find the discovery gap before the meeting, not after
activities.description: Check what you still do not know that would change your recommendation, and build the question that closes it.
activities.prompt: Here is what we currently know about the account for the solution play: the supplied priorities, environment, stakeholders, constraints, prior conversations. Identify what we do not know that would materially change our recommendation, ranked by how much it would change it. For the top three unknowns, write one open question each that could be asked naturally in the upcoming conversation without sounding like a survey. Distinguish what we actually know from what we have assumed. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of decision-changing unknowns and three natural questions to close the top ones.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies which items are genuinely known versus assumed by the account team, and chooses which question is worth the meeting time.
activities.requiredContext: Everything currently known about the account and solution context; prior conversation notes; the recommendation you intend to make.
activitySteps: 1. Assemble what is known about the account.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Separate known from assumed.
4. Choose one question to definitely ask.
5. Add it to the conversation plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: The most expensive assumptions are the ones nobody noticed they were making.

activities.name: Turn the conversation into decisions and commitments
activities.description: Convert meeting notes into what changed, what was agreed, and what the customer actually committed to.
activities.prompt: Here are my notes from the customer conversation: the supplied notes or transcript summary. Produce three separate lists: what we learned that changes our understanding, what was explicitly agreed and by whom, and what remains open. Then draft a short follow-up note to the customer confirming only what was actually agreed. Do not record something as agreed if the notes only show it was discussed. Flag anything ambiguous rather than resolving it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Separated lists of learnings, agreements, and open items, plus a short confirming follow-up note.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP confirms that anything recorded as agreed was actually agreed, and owns the follow-up wording before sending. The record update happens in Sales Agent rather than here, and the confirmation card it shows is the last point at which a misheard agreement is still only a note rather than the record everyone downstream works from.
activities.requiredContext: Meeting notes or transcript summary; who attended; what was asked for; the conversation plan you went in with.
activitySteps: 1. Capture notes immediately after the meeting.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Check the agreed list against your memory.
4. Send the follow-up note.

5. Update the opportunity separately in Sales Agent, which is the agent that writes to MSX. Ask it to add a forecast comment or change the close date, and it will show a confirmation card setting out exactly what it is about to write.
6. Read that card against your notes before you confirm. Nothing is committed until you do.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deals slip on the gap between what was discussed and what was agreed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Preparation is the difference between explaining a solution and advancing a decision.
keyTalkingPoints: Prepare discovery questions, proof points, likely objections, role contributions, and a primary/fallback ask. Rehearse where useful.
discussionQuestions: What decision should this conversation advance? What objection is most likely? What proof will you use?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prepare the solution-specific customer conversation'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from preparation to rehearsal or next customer ask. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find the discovery gap before the meeting, not after', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Solution conversations should resolve the unknown most likely to change the recommendation. Use proof and rehearsal to improve the question, not manufacture customer commitment. Agree where this fits in recurring work and how a small, safe signal will help the team learn together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming solution conversation, the desired customer decision, known objections and approved proof points. Confirm tool access and review the prior commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision and fallback ask should this meeting advance? Which objection would expose a gap in discovery? What did a peer change after rehearsing a similar customer conversation?
listenFor: Meetings framed around content rather than customer decision, objections first discovered live, and unclear ask.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a short customer rehearsal: intended decision, discovery question, likely objection, evidence-qualified reply and fallback ask. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Rehearse with a peer; if alone, write both sides and mark the exchange untested, not a validated customer or coaching response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence would make this customer conversation credible, and what decision or question still belongs to a person?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, find the unknown that would change your recommendation, and ask about it in your next conversation. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized discovery question and what its answer changed, or what remains unknown; note whether the conversation became more focused. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

activities.name: Make each ask specific enough to be accepted
activities.description: Turn a role requirement into an ask a busy colleague can say yes to without a meeting to clarify it.
activities.prompt: From this pursuit orchestration plan the supplied information, write the individual ask for each role involved. Each ask must state: what specifically is needed, why this pursuit needs that role rather than someone else, what the person receives from me to make it easy, the date it is needed by, and how long it should take. Keep each ask under 80 words. Do not represent funding, approvals, or customer commitments as secured if the plan does not show them as secured. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: One short, specific, dated ask per role, ready to send.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies that no ask overstates funding, approval, or customer commitment status, and owns what is promised in return.
activities.requiredContext: The pursuit orchestration plan; the roles required; what you can supply to each; the customer timeline.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the orchestration plan.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.

activities.whyThisMatters: A vague ask gets a polite yes and no calendar time.

activities.name: Catch the checkpoint that quietly slipped
activities.description: Compare the plan against what has actually happened and surface the dependency nobody has mentioned in two weeks.
activities.prompt: Here is the pursuit orchestration plan with its checkpoints and owners the supplied information, and here is what has actually happened since the supplied updates, meeting notes, or status. Identify every checkpoint that has passed without evidence of completion, every dependency that has gone quiet, and every owner who has not confirmed. Rank by impact on the customer timeline. For the top item, draft the one message that would restart it. Do not assume something is complete because it was not mentioned. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled checkpoints and quiet dependencies, plus one message to restart the highest-impact item.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms an item is genuinely stalled rather than simply undocumented before escalating to an owner.
activities.requiredContext: The orchestration plan with checkpoints and owners, written down even if only informally; recent updates, notes, or status; the customer timeline. If checkpoints and owners do not exist yet, create them before running this activity.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Pursuits stall at handoffs. Focus on making every role, partner, funding dependency, and checkpoint explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Name the objective, contributors, asks, owners, dates, dependencies, and escalation points.
discussionQuestions: Which handoff is currently assumed rather than owned? Where could partner or funding support change the path?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Bring funding into the pursuit orchestration plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from orchestration principles to one stalled handoff. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Make each ask specific enough to be accepted', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Cross-role orchestration should unblock the customer decision with the smallest necessary accepted contribution. Funding, partner capacity and technical help are not secured merely by requesting them. Make that evidence check part of recurring work; share a safe example of what changed so peers can adapt the habit.
preparationChecklist: Bring one pursuit handoff, current contributors, partner or funding dependencies and the owner or date still unconfirmed. Confirm tool access and review the prior commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which specialist, technical, partner or funding dependency is stalled? What evidence and acceptance does the next owner need? How does a peer make that handoff executable without representing funding as approved?
listenFor: Unnamed owners, handoffs without dates, partner input treated as optional, and funding status overstated.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one specialist/technical/partner/funding handoff row: contribution needed, proposed owner, evidence, acceptance gap and next date. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which handoff is still assumed rather than accepted, and what owner, request, or date would make it actionable?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take the most consequential stalled handoff and personally send a reviewed, dated ask to its contributor. Do not request work from every role merely to complete the exercise. Ask the receiving owner to accept the work; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized stalled handoff and whether a bounded ask clarified ownership or exposed a gap; no collection of every role request is needed. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.prompt: You are helping a specialist seller sharpen a competitive position. For each differentiator, state which specific decision criterion it addresses, how directly it addresses it, and what proof the customer would need to accept it. Identify any differentiator that does not map to a stated criterion and recommend dropping or reframing it. Flag any criterion we currently have no answer for. Do not add differentiators that are not in my list. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.

activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms the decision criteria are what the customer actually said rather than what the team assumes, and owns the decision to drop a differentiator.
activities.requiredContext: Customer decision criteria and evaluation process; current differentiators and supporting proof; who is on the evaluation team.
activitySteps: 1. Gather the customer's stated decision criteria from meeting notes or MSX.

3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Cut differentiators that do not map to a criterion.
5. Name the gaps you cannot yet answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: A differentiator the customer is not deciding on is noise, however true it is.

activities.prompt: Play the role of a technical evaluator at the customer who currently favors the competitor. I will present our competitive position. After three exchanges, stop the role-play and produce an objection handler table: each objection you raised, my response, the approved proof that supports it, and a note where no approved proof exists. Do not soften the objections and do not supply proof I have not given you. Use only the scenario and material I am authorized to share here. Keep reactions explicitly simulated, not new customer facts; do not make commitments or send communications.
activities.expectedOutput: An objection handler table mapping each objection to a response and the approved proof behind it, with proof gaps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP judges whether the rehearsed language is accurate, appropriate for this customer, and consistent with approved competitive guidance before using it externally.
activities.requiredContext: Competitive position and differentiators; the competitor in play; approved competitive proof sources; known evaluator concerns; customer role you will be speaking to.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the differentiator list from the previous activity and the approved competitive proof.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run a short rehearsal with the agent as the skeptical evaluator.
4. Have it produce the objection handler table.
5. Fill or remove any row where proof is missing.
6. Bring the table to the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: Competitive conversations are lost in the moment, not in the brief.

activities.name: Convert the competitive position into the next customer step
activities.description: Turn the position into a concrete next action in the opportunity rather than a document that stops at the brief.
activities.prompt: Using this competitive position and the customer's decision criteria the supplied information, propose the single next step that would most reduce competitive risk in this opportunity. Give me three options ranked by impact, each with: what it is, who from our side needs to be involved, what the customer gets out of it, and what evidence it would generate for the decision. Then draft the short note I would send to the customer to set it up. Keep the note under 120 words and do not overstate what we have proven. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: One chosen next step with owner and purpose, and a short customer-ready note to set it up.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP owns the choice of next step and the customer-facing wording, and confirms it fits the account team's plan before sending.
activities.requiredContext: Tested differentiators and open gaps; opportunity stage and close plan; who owns the customer relationship.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the tested differentiator list and the open gaps.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Pick one next step.
4. Adjust the draft note in your own voice.
5. Record the next step in the opportunity.
activities.whyThisMatters: A competitive brief that does not change the next customer interaction has not changed the deal.

activities.name: Build a reusable objection and language library from real calls
activities.description: Mine your own customer conversations for the objections and language that keep recurring, and turn them into something the team can reuse.
activities.prompt: Work across my customer meeting transcripts and mail from the last quarter for the solution area. Identify the objections that keep recurring, the language customers actually use to describe the problem we solve, the competitor claims that come up, and the points where conversations stall. Group them by how often they appear. For each recurring objection, show me the customer's own words rather than a paraphrase, and note which conversations it came from so I can go back to the source. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Separate the private source/quote index from any proposed reusable library. In the shareable draft, remove customer names, identifying detail and source links that expose the original conversations; keep provenance in the approved private location for my verification. Do not publish or share either version.
activities.expectedOutput: An objection and customer-language library grouped by frequency, quoted in the customer's own words, traceable back to source conversations.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies the quotes against the source conversation, removes anything customer-identifying before sharing, and decides what is safe to circulate beyond the account team.
activities.requiredContext: Approved access to your own meeting transcripts and mail; the solution area in scope; a quarter or more of conversations.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm you can reach your own meeting transcripts and mail for this solution area.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Check the recurring objections against your own memory of those calls before treating them as a pattern.
5. Keep the customer language the customer actually used rather than rewriting it into product language.
6. Share the library with your solution area only after removing customer-identifying detail.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recurring objections in authorized conversations can improve positioning when quotes are verified and the shared version is sanitized.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Competitive response should be built on customer context and proof, not generic battlecards.
keyTalkingPoints: Use current approved competitive evidence, win/loss context, differentiators, objections, risks, and review flags.
discussionQuestions: Which competitor or alternative is shaping the decision? What proof is strongest and where is it weak?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the competitive differentiation brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from competitor context to one proof-backed response plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test the differentiator against the customer's real decision criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Competitive responses are credible when current approved proof addresses the customer decision criterion. Objection handlers are not permission for unsupported competitor claims. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one competitive pursuit, the customer decision criteria and current approved competitive evidence; label gaps and assumptions. Confirm tool access and review the prior commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which competitive claim changes the customer decision, and which dated source supports it? What would make it inapplicable here? How has a colleague tested differentiation against the customer's actual criteria?
listenFor: Stale battlecard claims, unsupported competitor statements, and differentiators not tied to customer priorities.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one competitive response row: customer criterion, proposed differentiator, dated source or unknown, applicability caveat and validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which customer criterion does approved competitive proof address, and what claim should you qualify or avoid?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, build one objection handler tied to approved proof, and use it in a live conversation. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized objection and whether approved proof answered it, required a caveat or showed a need for discovery. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: State the close plan in the customer's terms
activities.description: Confirm which customer commitments and decision milestones are genuinely agreed; return the shared plan with dependencies and unconfirmed items marked for human closure.
activities.prompt: Rewrite this existing internal close plan for one opportunity the supplied approved plan as a draft shared plan from the customer's point of view. Use their supplied stated outcome, decision process and confirmed-versus-assumed dates. Replace our sales stages with their decision milestones, name what they need from us and what we need from them, and end with their stated outcome. Remove internal language and forecast terms. Flag unconfirmed steps, dates and dependencies for SSP review; do not turn portfolio priorities into a close plan or invent missing customer agreements. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Customer-facing decision plan with customer-confirmed commitment, milestones, dependencies, and any unconfirmed items clearly flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP verifies the customer agreement and whether the person can make the commitment, and separates customer-confirmed milestones from internal forecast language before sharing the plan.
activities.requiredContext: An existing internal close plan for one opportunity, approved for use in this practice; the customer's stated outcome and decision process; confirmed dates versus assumed dates. The portfolio action list from WF-DEAL-01-P-SSP-02 is not a substitute.
activitySteps: 1. Bring an existing, approved internal close plan for one opportunity, not a portfolio prioritization report.
2. Paste it into the prompt and supply the customer's stated outcome, decision process and confirmed-versus-assumed dates, then run it.
3. Remove anything still internal.
4. Confirm which dates and steps the customer has actually agreed to and keep the rest marked unconfirmed.
5. Review and approve the customer-safe draft before sharing it through your usual channel and asking the customer to correct it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A close plan the customer has never seen is a forecast, not a plan.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle focuses on the next decision, not the whole deal.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect milestone readiness, stakeholder gaps, proof, blockers, dependencies, partner/funding needs, and owners.
discussionQuestions: What is the pursuit actually waiting on? What evidence or owner will clear the next decision?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect solution opportunity readiness'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from readiness inspection to a 14- to 30-day action plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Prepare the conversation that clears the next decision', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Opportunity progress means clearing an evidenced customer decision, not just advancing a record. Separate confirmed milestones from assumptions and validate the next conversation with its owner. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one live solution pursuit, its current milestone, decision evidence and next blocker. If selecting the customer-facing close-plan practice, bring an existing approved close plan for one opportunity, the customer decision process and outcome, and confirmed-versus-assumed dates. A portfolio action list is not that plan.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next customer decision, rather than the next internal task? Which evidence gap or missing owner prevents it? What would another specialist change in the next 14 to 30 days without promising a close?
listenFor: Close-date language instead of next decision, unowned blockers, missing proof, and unclear stakeholder gaps.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one solution-readiness card: next decision, proof gap, stakeholder gap, owner and bounded 14-to-30-day action. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal assumption changed when you inspected the evidence, and who owns the next decision or approval?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, draft or rehearse the conversation that could clear the next decision on a stalled opportunity, validate its ask with the owner, and use it when an appropriate meeting is available. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a safe description of the next decision and whether preparing the conversation clarified a blocker; a closed decision is not required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.
