activities.name: Mine the verbatims for what the score hides
activities.description: Read what customers actually wrote rather than the number it rolled up into, and find the theme the score cannot show.
activities.prompt: Show me all recent verbatims for the customer or account identifier and group them by theme. For each theme, tell me how many comments support it, whether it is getting better or worse over time, and whether it points at product, support, delivery or relationship. Quote the customer's own words rather than paraphrasing. Do not infer a theme from a single comment. Keep CX Vitals metrics, survey responses and verbatims internal; do not quote them or expose respondents in any customer-facing draft. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Verbatim themes with supporting comment counts, direction of travel, the function each points at, and the customer's own wording preserved.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which themes are real signal and which are one unhappy individual. A single strong comment is not a pattern. The AE is also accountable for the boundary: verbatims inform the questions you ask, and never appear in anything the customer sees.
activities.requiredContext: One account with verbatim coverage; the themes you already believe are true so you can test them.
activitySteps: 1. Use an account where the score alone has not explained the situation.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Read the actual quotes before reading the themes.
5. Discard any theme resting on a single comment.
6. Use the customer's own vocabulary in your next conversation rather than translating it into internal terms, but never quote a verbatim directly or reveal that you have their survey responses.
activities.whyThisMatters: The number tells you something is wrong. The verbatims tell you what. Only one of those is useful in the next customer conversation.

activities.name: Run a standing satisfaction sweep across your portfolio
activities.description: Sweep every account you own for satisfaction movement, and put the sweep on a cadence you run yourself so decline surfaces before a customer raises it.
activities.prompt: Across my accounts, show me current OSAT with its trend, any account scoring below 3.5, where the most negative recent verbatims sit, and where the support experience measured by ATQ is getting worse. Rank by size of recent movement rather than absolute score. Do not compare my accounts against another seller's portfolio. Use 3.5 only as this exercise's screening threshold; do not infer a policy breach or automatic escalation. Keep CX Vitals metrics, survey responses and verbatims internal; do not quote them or expose respondents in any customer-facing draft. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A portfolio satisfaction sweep ranked by recent movement, with sub-3.5 accounts, negative verbatims and worsening support experience identified, plus a dated record to compare against next time.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which movements are real. A single survey response can move a score on a small account without anything having changed, and the AE owns that judgment rather than the ranking.
activities.requiredContext: Your owned account list with TPIDs; the note or record from your previous sweep if you have one; the review rhythm this should feed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm which of your accounts are TPID-mapped, since only those are covered.
2. Run the prompt in Sales Agent across your portfolio.
3. Compare the result against the note you kept from the last time you ran it. The movement is the finding, not the score.
4. Put a recurring reminder in your own calendar, timed to land before your account review. CX Vitals has no alerting in this version, so nothing will tell you to look.
5. Keep a short record of what you saw so the next sweep has something to compare against.
activities.whyThisMatters: CX Vitals will not tell you when a customer sours; there is no alerting in this version. The sweep is the substitute, and it only works if you run it on a rhythm rather than after someone complains.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most accounts already carry a satisfaction signal the seller has never looked at. Focus on reading it, deciding whether it matches the relationship you think you have, and acting while the conversation is still yours to lead.
keyTalkingPoints: Use available CX Vitals in Sales Agent as internal, read-only evidence for the identified account. Confirm scope with its TPID, verify freshness and distinguish the score from account-team interpretation. Do not copy internal signals into customer-facing material.
discussionQuestions: Which account are you most confident about, and when did you last check that confidence against data?
Where would a satisfaction score and your own read of the relationship disagree?
Who tells you first today when a customer becomes unhappy?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Read what the customer's satisfaction data already says'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the account picture to the single account each person will act on this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Mine the verbatims for what the score hides', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Satisfaction trends prompt investigation and owned intervention, not automatic customer conclusions. Compare the data with relationship evidence before acting. Make that evidence check part of recurring work; share a safe example of what changed so peers can adapt the habit.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account you own with its TPID, confirm Sales Agent access, and write down how you would rate that customer's satisfaction before you look at any data.
facilitatorQuestions: Where did the data disagree with your own read, and which one do you trust?
Which of the causes you found do you actually own, and which belong to support or delivery?
What would have to get worse before you escalate this?
What evidence would a colleague use to challenge both the satisfaction score and the account team's intuition?
listenFor: Sellers treating a score as a diagnosis rather than a symptom, accounts written off as fine without evidence, surprise at what verbatims say, and anyone about to take an internal metric into a customer conversation.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one satisfaction evidence card: customer signal, alternative explanation, source/date, intervention owner and escalation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the data tell you about a customer that you did not already know, and what will you do differently because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, run a CX health summary on the account you are least certain about, and take one action on what you find. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized mismatch between signal and expectation and whether checking it improved the intervention or exposed an uncertain cause. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Find out what you actually inherited
activities.description: Assemble the history, relationships, open work and unresolved risk on an account you are taking on, before you speak to anyone.
activities.prompt: I am taking over the account or account identifier. Build me a picture of what I am inheriting: the customer's stated priorities, the open opportunities and their current stage, active commitments and milestones, recent support or delivery escalations, who the known stakeholders are and who owns each relationship, and anything that looks unresolved or overdue. Tell me plainly where the record is thin or stale, because that is what I most need to know before I meet this customer. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: An inherited-context brief covering priorities, open opportunities, commitments, escalations and stakeholders, with the thin or stale parts of the record explicitly named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what the silence means. An account with no recorded risk is not a healthy account, it is an unwritten one, and the incoming seller must treat an empty field as unknown rather than as good news.
activities.requiredContext: The account you are inheriting or handing over, with its TPID; access to MSX for that account; the name of the outgoing or incoming seller.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account you are inheriting, or one you are handing over.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the record says from what it does not say. The gaps matter more than the summary.
5. Write down the three questions only the outgoing seller can answer.
6. Do not contact the customer yet. The internal handoff comes first.
activities.whyThisMatters: You inherit whatever the last person wrote down, and most of what mattered was never written down. Finding that out before the customer meeting is the difference between a handover and a restart.

activities.name: Run the internal handoff conversation properly
activities.description: Turn the gaps you found into the specific questions for the outgoing seller, and capture the answers where the next person will find them.
activities.prompt: Here is what I found on the account or account identifier and here is what is missing: the supplied gaps. Help me prepare the internal handoff conversation with the outgoing seller. Draft the specific questions I should ask about relationships, unwritten history, sensitivities, commitments made verbally, and anything that would embarrass me in front of this customer. Prioritize the questions whose answers exist only in that person's head. Give me questions to confirm who will notify the customer and how; do not assume that notification is already agreed. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A prioritized outgoing-seller question list. After the human handoff conversation, reviewed answers and the confirmed customer-notification plan are captured through the authorized process.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what is safe to record. Some relationship context is candid and belongs in a conversation rather than a permanent field, and the seller owns that line rather than transcribing everything.
activities.requiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and its gaps; time with the outgoing seller; access to update the account record in MSX.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the inherited-context brief and its evidence gaps.
2. Run the prompt to prepare the outgoing-seller questions.
3. Hold the internal handoff conversation and capture answers, separating customer statements from seller interpretation.
4. Confirm who will introduce the incoming owner to the customer and the notification approach.
5. Review what is appropriate for a permanent record, then update it yourself through the authorized process; discuss sensitive relationship context separately.
activities.whyThisMatters: The handoff conversation is the only chance to collect what was never written down. Held badly, the next transition starts from the same empty record.

activities.name: Prepare the customer conversation that earns the relationship
activities.description: Plan the introduction so the customer hears continuity and a reason to invest in a new relationship, not an administrative notification.
activities.prompt: I am being introduced to the account or account identifier as their new [role]. Help me prepare the first conversation. I want to show I already understand their priorities and open commitments, ask what the record cannot tell me, and give them a reason to invest in this relationship. Draft the opening, the three questions worth their time, and how I acknowledge anything that has gone wrong recently without over-promising. Do not invent history I have not confirmed. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A first-conversation plan with an opening that demonstrates continuity, three questions the record could not answer, and a considered position on any recent problem.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to acknowledge. Raising a known problem you cannot yet fix builds credibility only if you also say what happens next, and the seller judges whether that is ready.
activities.requiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and the handoff answers; the outgoing seller's introduction plan; the customer stakeholders you will meet.
activitySteps: 1. Use the context and the answers from the internal handoff.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Cut anything you cannot personally stand behind. Confidence about details you have not verified is what damages a first meeting.
5. Agree with the outgoing seller how the introduction is made.
6. Hold the introduction and record its actual status and follow-through owner through your usual approved process.
activities.whyThisMatters: The customer did not choose this change and is measuring whether it costs them. The first conversation is where they decide whether to invest in you or wait you out.

activities.name: Pressure-test what you are handing over
activities.description: Look at an account you are handing on and find what only exists in your own head, before it is lost.
activities.prompt: I am handing over the account or account identifier. First, based on what is recorded in MSX, tell me what an incoming seller would and would not understand about this account. Then interview me: ask me up to six questions, one at a time, designed to surface what I know that is not written anywhere, covering informal relationships, the history behind a decision, sensitivities, verbal commitments and who actually influences outcomes. Do not guess my answers. After I have answered, organize what I told you into what belongs in the record and what is better said in conversation. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on what the record fails to convey, plus your own tacit knowledge drawn out through questioning and sorted into what to record and what to say in person.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The outgoing seller decides which commitments must be written down. A verbal commitment that dies with the handover becomes the incoming seller's credibility problem and the customer's evidence that Microsoft does not remember.

activities.whyThisMatters: Every seller who inherited a thin account was handed it by someone who knew more than they recorded. This is where that stops being someone else's problem.

activities.name: Own the ninety days after the introduction
activities.description: Convert what the customer said in the first meeting into commitments with dates, so the transition is judged on follow-through rather than on the meeting.
activities.prompt: Here is what came out of my first conversation with the account or account identifier: the supplied notes. Turn this into a follow-through plan: what I committed to, what the customer asked for, what needs someone else at Microsoft, and what I should have demonstrably delivered before the ninety-day mark. Flag anything I appear to have committed to that I have not confirmed I can deliver. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A ninety-day follow-through plan with commitments, owners, dates, and any unconfirmed promise flagged for resolution.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms every commitment is one they can actually keep. A transition is judged on whether the first promise was kept, and an unkept one costs more than the original change did.
activities.requiredContext: Your notes from the first customer conversation; the commitments you made; the Microsoft roles who would own anything outside your control.
activitySteps: 1. Open your notes from the first customer conversation.
2. Paste those notes into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it.
3. Check every commitment it identifies. Deal with anything you promised without meaning to.
4. Put dates against each item and name owners for anything that is not yours.
5. Put a date on the ninety-day point now, while it still feels urgent.
activities.whyThisMatters: Transitions are not judged by the introduction meeting. They are judged ninety days later, on whether the thing you said you would do happened.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every seller in this room has inherited an account with nothing useful written down, and every seller has handed one over. Focus on the transition you are in the middle of right now, on either side of it.
keyTalkingPoints: Verify current transition timing and completion requirements for the applicable segment and geography with authoritative guidance. Make contacts, the current plan, open commitments and the customer conversation usable to the receiving seller. Record actual acceptance and unresolved gaps; populated fields alone do not prove a completed transition.
discussionQuestions: What is the worst account you have ever inherited, and what specifically was missing?
What do you know about your accounts that exists nowhere in MSX?
When a customer is handed a new seller, what does it actually cost them?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find out what you actually inherited'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from what the record is missing to the one conversation each person needs to have this week, internal or customer-facing. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test what you are handing over', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Account continuity depends on tacit context reaching the next owner with accepted responsibility. Record updates support transition but cannot replace the right conversation. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account you are currently inheriting or handing over. If you have neither, bring the account you would find hardest to hand to someone else.
facilitatorQuestions: What did the record fail to tell you that you needed?
What do you know that would be lost if you handed this account over tomorrow?
What would this customer say if you asked them how the last transition went?
What unwritten commitment has a peer receiver needed to avoid making the customer start over?
listenFor: Transitions treated as administration rather than as a customer experience, records closed before the customer meeting happened, verbal commitments nobody has captured, and sellers assuming an empty risk field means there is no risk.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one transition brief: inherited fact, unwritten commitment, customer continuity risk, outgoing/receiving-role question and proposed next conversation. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you find missing from an account record that you assumed would be there, and what will you write down differently because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, capture permitted tacit account context in its approved record or draft and check with the transition owner what conversation or acceptance is still needed. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized manual scenario and report the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized continuity gap captured and whether it reduced repeated questions or improved transition. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role
activities.description: Check that an opportunity being handed on has the qualification evidence the receiving role needs, before you transfer it rather than after they reject it.
activities.prompt: I am handing over the opportunity to the specialist team. Review what is documented and tell me whether a specialist receiving this could act on it immediately. Specifically: is the customer outcome clear, are the business and technical decision makers identified, is the budget and timing evidenced, are the blockers named with a mitigation, and does the milestone carry an evidence-backed estimate and date, or an explicitly applicable non-monetary measure, rather than a placeholder. Tell me what is missing rather than summarizing what is there. Apply the qualification criteria I supply, not invented universal criteria. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A gap list against the qualification the receiving role needs, covering outcome, decision makers, budget, timing, blockers and milestone completeness.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what is genuinely known versus assumed. Handing over an assumption dressed as a qualified fact is worse than handing over an acknowledged gap, because the receiving role will act on it.
activities.requiredContext: One opportunity being transferred, with its ID; the milestone attached to it; the qualification criteria your team applies.
activitySteps: 1. Choose one opportunity you are about to hand over, or one you recently received.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Treat every gap as work to do before the transfer, not after.
5. Verify the date and applicable value or outcome measure from evidence; flag unknowns rather than entering an artificial non-zero value.
6. If you received this handoff, send the gap list back rather than rebuilding it silently.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most handoffs are rejected or quietly rebuilt because the receiving role cannot act on what arrived. The gap was always visible before the transfer; nobody looked.

activities.name: Write the handoff so the next role does not have to ask
activities.description: Capture the qualification, the customer context and the unwritten detail in the record itself, so the transfer survives without a meeting.
activities.prompt: Help me write the handoff notes for the opportunity moving to the receiving role. Cover what the customer is trying to achieve and in their own words where I have them, what has been agreed and what has not, who influences the decision and how, what I have already tried, and what I would warn the receiving person about. Write it so someone who has never spoken to this customer could pick it up. Flag anything I have written that is my opinion rather than something the customer said. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Handoff notes covering customer outcome, agreed and unagreed items, decision influence, what has been tried, and warnings, with opinion separated from evidence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what belongs in a permanent record. Candid relationship context may be better said than written, and the sender owns that judgment rather than transcribing everything.
activities.requiredContext: Your gap list; what the customer has said in their own words; the receiving role and who specifically will take it.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the gap list you produced in the previous practice.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the customer actually said from your interpretation of it, and label both.
5. Put the notes in the record, not in a chat message. Chat is not where the next person will look.
6. Hold the handoff conversation as well. The notes make the conversation shorter, not unnecessary.
activities.whyThisMatters: The handoff conversation happens once and is forgotten. The record is what the receiving role actually works from, and what the person after them inherits.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role

activities.name: Find the handoffs that stalled in the gap between roles
activities.description: Look across your opportunities and milestones for transfers that were started and never completed, where ownership is ambiguous and nothing is moving.
activities.prompt: Across my opportunities and milestones, find where a transfer between roles looks incomplete or stalled: ownership that changed but where nothing has happened since, milestones sitting at the same stage well past their estimated date, opportunities where the specialist or customer success team was engaged but no activity followed, and anything where I cannot tell from the record who currently owns the next action. Rank by how long each has been static. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled or incomplete transfers with time static, and the ownership ambiguity named for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms actual ownership with the other role directly. A record showing a transfer completed is not evidence that anyone picked it up.
activities.requiredContext: Your opportunities and milestones; the expected transfer windows your team works to; the roles you routinely hand off to.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your own opportunities and milestones.
2. For each result, establish who actually believes they own it. It is often nobody, and sometimes two people.
3. Pick the one that has been static longest and resolve ownership today.
4. Check whether the customer is waiting on any of these. That changes the priority.
5. Record the owner in the system rather than agreeing it verbally.
activities.whyThisMatters: Work does not usually stall inside a role. It stalls in the space between two, where both parties believe the other has it.

activities.name: Rehearse receiving a handoff you were given badly
activities.description: Practice the conversation that recovers a thin handoff without damaging the relationship with the role that sent it.
activities.prompt: I have received a handoff for the opportunity and it is thin. Play the role of the person who sent it. I will ask for what I need. Push back the way a busy colleague would, including being defensive if I imply they did it badly. Afterwards, tell me which of my questions got the most useful information, where I put them on the defensive unnecessarily, and how to ask for the missing context without making it a complaint. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed recovery conversation with coaching on which questions produced information and where the approach created defensiveness.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The receiving role decides how hard to push. The relationship with that colleague outlasts this opportunity, and a handoff recovered at the cost of a working relationship is a poor trade.
activities.requiredContext: A handoff you received that was insufficient; what specifically you still need; your relationship with the sending role.
activitySteps: 1. Use a real handoff you received that was not enough.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the role-play.
4. Notice where you made it about the process rather than the customer.
5. Rewrite your opening so it leads with what the customer needs.
6. Have the real conversation.
activities.whyThisMatters: Nobody sends a bad handoff deliberately. Getting what you need without making it an accusation is the skill that keeps the next one better.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Write the handoff so the next role does not have to ask

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A handoff stalls when the sender considers it complete but the receiver cannot act. Focus on one live transfer: the decision, usable evidence and acceptance still needed.
keyTalkingPoints: Confirm the applicable current handoff requirements and timing with the accountable owners. A handoff is complete only when the receiving role can act and acceptance is recorded. Include the customer outcome, usable evidence, open decisions and next checkpoint; do not substitute an ownership-field change for acceptance.
discussionQuestions: What is the least useful handoff you have ever received, and what was missing?
When you hand something over, what do you assume the other person already knows?
How would you know today if a handoff you sent had gone nowhere?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the gap analysis to the one handoff each person will prepare, repair or chase this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Rehearse receiving a handoff you were given badly', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Handoffs succeed when the receiver can use qualification evidence and accepts the next action. Completeness reduces ambiguity, not legitimate questions or conversation. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one opportunity or milestone you are currently handing over or have recently received. If you have neither, bring the one that went worst.
facilitatorQuestions: Could the receiving role act on what you sent, without asking you anything?
Where in your own list has a transfer stalled with nobody owning it?
What do you know about this opportunity that is written nowhere?
What missing field has a peer receiver needed before they could accept a handoff?
listenFor: Handoffs described as notifications, ownership that changed without anyone accepting it, milestones carrying placeholder values or dates, and sellers rebuilding a thin handoff silently rather than sending it back.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or approved context is unavailable, use a sanitized supplied example or a clearly labeled synthetic case. On paper, complete one handoff acceptance check: required context, milestone evidence, proposed receiver, missing field and draft return reason. Mark evidence, assumptions and unknowns. Treat the receiver and acceptance state as proposed until confirmed; record the access gap and who must validate the handoff before use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you assume the receiving role already knew, and what will you write down next time instead of assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, review a handoff with the other role, clarify the consequential missing input and seek explicit acceptance of the next action; follow-up questions remain welcome. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized missing input clarified and whether the receiver could act or identified a remaining gap. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Establish what the customer committed to and what they have actually deployed
activities.description: Set the honest baseline for a consumption plan by separating what was committed, what is deployed, and what is only forecast.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, give me the consumption picture: what the customer has committed to, what is currently deployed and consuming, what is planned but not yet started, and the gap between commitment and current run rate. For each workload, tell me whether the number is measured or projected. Where the data does not support a claim, say so rather than filling the gap. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A consumption baseline separating committed, deployed, planned and forecast, with the gap quantified and measured figures distinguished from projected.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms the baseline with the account team before planning from it. A disputed baseline invalidates every milestone built on top of it, and the dispute always surfaces later than it should.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its consumption commitment; access to current consumption data; the commitment term and how much of it remains.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account with a consumption commitment.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate measured consumption from projected consumption everywhere it appears.
5. Calculate the gap honestly, including the time remaining to close it.
6. Do not build the plan yet. Get agreement on the baseline first, because a plan built on a disputed number will be relitigated.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most consumption plans fail because they were built on an optimistic starting number nobody agreed to. The argument you avoid now happens in a review instead.

activities.name: Sequence the milestones that close the consumption gap
activities.description: Break the gap between commitment and current usage into milestones with owners, dependencies and dates that hold.
activities.prompt: Using this consumption baseline for the account or account identifier, help me build the milestone sequence that closes the gap. For each milestone: the workload, what the customer must do and what Microsoft must do, the technical dependency most likely to block it, a realistic date given that dependency, and the evidence that would show it is genuinely progressing rather than merely scheduled. Sequence them so the dependencies resolve in order, and tell me which single milestone carries the most of the gap. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced milestone plan with paired owners, blocking dependencies, dependency-aware dates, progress evidence, and the milestone carrying most of the gap identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms each date with the person who owns the dependency. A plan full of dates nobody has agreed to is the most common form of consumption planning, and the least useful.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed consumption baseline; the technical dependencies you know about; the Microsoft and customer roles who could own each milestone.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the agreed baseline.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Test every date against the dependency named beneath it. A date without a resolved dependency is a wish.
5. Assign a named owner on both the Microsoft and customer side. A team is not an owner.
6. Record the milestones where the v-team will actually see them.
activities.whyThisMatters: A consumption plan without owned milestones is a forecast. The milestone is the unit of work someone can actually be held to.

activities.name: Find the milestone that is quietly slipping
activities.description: Check the consumption plan against what has actually happened, and surface the milestones that have stopped moving before they become a shortfall.
activities.prompt: Review this consumption plan against what has actually happened since it was built. Identify milestones with no evidence of progress, dates that have passed without being reset or explained, dependencies that were assumed resolved and are not, and any workload where the deployment has started but usage has not followed. For each, tell me what the evidence shows and what I would need to confirm before raising it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A slip analysis distinguishing late milestones from stalled ones, with unresolved dependencies and deployment-without-usage cases identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides whether a slip is technical, commercial or customer-driven before assigning it. Routing a customer-priority problem to a technical owner wastes a cycle and the deadline does not move.
activities.requiredContext: The current consumption plan with its milestones and dates; recent consumption and deployment data; what you know about customer-side changes.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the consumption plan and the current consumption data.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Separate a milestone that is late from one that has stopped. They need different interventions.
4. Check whether deployment without usage is a technical issue or an adoption one, because the owner differs.
5. Raise the largest slip with the account team before the next review, not in it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Consumption shortfalls are visible in the milestone plan months before they are visible in the number. By the time the number moves, the runway to fix it has gone.

activities.description: Look past deployment milestones to whether people are using what was deployed, since a deployed workload nobody uses will not renew.

Identify workloads where deployment completed but usage is flat or declining, where usage is concentrated in a small group rather than spreading, and where the pattern suggests the deployment technically succeeded but adoption did not follow. Tell me what the data supports and what would need investigating with the customer. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A deployment-versus-usage comparison identifying flat or concentrated usage and separating technical from organizational adoption gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms with the customer team before concluding adoption has failed. Low usage can reflect a deliberate phased rollout, and treating a plan as a failure damages credibility.
activities.requiredContext: An account with completed deployment milestones; usage data for those workloads; who owns adoption on the customer side.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account where deployment milestones have completed.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate technical adoption problems from organizational ones.
5. Identify who owns adoption on the customer side; it is rarely the person who owned deployment.
6. Raise flat usage as a finding, not as a criticism of the deployment.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deployment is the milestone Microsoft measures; usage is the one the customer renews on. They are not the same, and the gap between them is invisible unless you look.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A customer commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. Focus on the plan that converts one into the other, and about being honest where that plan has stopped being real.
keyTalkingPoints: The ATS owns the technical plan behind the consumption number. Milestones without a named owner and a dependency-aware date are forecasts, not plans. Deployment and usage are different measures, and only one of them renews.
discussionQuestions: Which of your accounts has committed spend that is not converting, and do you know technically why?
Which milestone dates in your current plan would you personally bet on?
Where has something been deployed that nobody is actually using?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Establish what the customer committed to and what they have actually deployed'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the baseline to the single milestone each ATS will resequence or re-own this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test whether deployment is actually turning into usage', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Consumption plans are credible when milestone dates rest on confirmed dependencies and accepted ownership. Proposed dates should change when evidence no longer supports them. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account with a consumption commitment, the current plan if one exists, and the most recent consumption data you can reach.
facilitatorQuestions: Is your baseline a number the account team would agree with?
Which milestone carries most of the gap, and who actually owns it?
Where has deployment completed without usage following?
How does another ATS tell deployment completion from consumption progress when resequencing milestones?
listenFor: Baselines nobody has agreed, dates set without checking the dependency beneath them, teams named as owners instead of people, and deployment milestones being treated as evidence of adoption.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one consumption milestone sequence: customer commitment, baseline or unknown, dependency, owner, deployment state and usage evidence needed. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which date in your plan turned out to rest on an unconfirmed dependency, and what did you do about it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, confirm a milestone dependency with its owner and ask the plan owner to validate or revise the proposed date; do not commit timing for someone else. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized dependency checked and whether owner confirmation changed sequence or timing; actual customer dates are unnecessary. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

ATS-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

activities.name: Find out which recorded sponsors are still actually engaged
activities.description: Check the senior relationships your account depends on against real engagement, and find the ones that have gone quiet without anyone noticing.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, focus only on the senior stakeholders recorded as sponsors, executive contacts or decision makers, not the full contact list. For each, show me when they were last genuinely engaged, whether that engagement was with me or with someone else at Microsoft, and whether it has become less frequent over time. Separately, identify any senior person now appearing regularly in meetings or correspondence who is not recorded as a sponsor at all. I am testing whether the sponsorship this account depends on still exists, not building a contact list. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each recorded sponsor covering last genuine engagement, who at Microsoft holds it, and whether it is declining, plus any unrecorded senior contact now engaging.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what absence means. A sponsor who has not been in a meeting may still be engaged through a colleague, and the seller judges that rather than the activity data.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the senior stakeholders currently recorded as sponsors or decision makers; the outcomes the account depends on them for.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account, ideally one you feel confident about.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Look first at recorded sponsors with no recent engagement. That is the dangerous category.
5. Note whether the engagement that does exist is yours or a colleague's, because a relationship held by someone else is not yours to rely on.
6. Look last at unrecorded senior contacts. You may be misreading who holds influence.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsorship decays quietly. The person your account depends on may have changed role or priority months ago, and the account plan will keep listing them as your sponsor until someone checks.

activities.name: Separate real sponsorship from polite interest
activities.description: Apply an honest test to each senior relationship, distinguishing executives who would act on your behalf from those who merely take the meeting.
activities.prompt: Here are the senior stakeholders on the account or account identifier and what I know about each: the supplied list with what each has actually done. Help me test each one honestly. For each, tell me what evidence exists that they would spend their own political capital for this, what evidence suggests they are merely being courteous, and what I would need to see to be confident either way. Be direct where the evidence is thin. Do not soften a weak relationship into a strong one. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: An honest assessment of each senior relationship separating evidenced sponsorship from courtesy, with the evidence gap named for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns the honesty of the input. An overstated relationship produces a confident assessment of something that does not exist, which is worse than no assessment.
activities.requiredContext: The senior stakeholders on the account; what each has actually done rather than said; the outcomes the account depends on them for.
activitySteps: 1. List each senior stakeholder and what they have actually done, not what they have said.
2. Paste that into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest in what you supply. This exercise is worthless if you overstate the relationship.
4. Identify the single relationship the account most depends on.
5. If no relationship passes the test, that is the finding, and it is worth knowing now.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most accounts believe they have executive sponsorship. Far fewer have someone who would spend their own credibility to unblock something. The difference only becomes visible under pressure.

activities.name: Design the investment that earns sponsorship
activities.description: Plan what you will give an executive relationship over the coming quarter, so sponsorship is earned before it is needed rather than requested when it is.
activities.prompt: I want to deepen the relationship with the executive name and role at the account or account identifier over the next quarter. Here is what I know about their priorities and here is what I am genuinely able to offer them, whether that is access, insight, introductions or influence: the supplied their priorities and your realistic offer list. Using only what I have supplied, help me sequence the investment across the quarter: what to lead with, what earns the right to the next conversation, and what would signal the relationship is strengthening. Do not suggest anything I have not told you I can actually provide, and do not give me generic executive engagement advice. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced quarter of relationship investment built only on what you can genuinely provide, with what to lead with, what earns the next conversation, and the signals that sponsorship is strengthening.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what can actually be offered and delivered. Sponsorship built on something you cannot provide costs more than the relationship you were trying to build.
activities.requiredContext: The executive and their role; what the record and your own knowledge show about their priorities; what you can genuinely offer, meaning access, insight, introductions or influence you actually control.
activitySteps: 1. Write down what this executive appears to care about, and separately what you can genuinely offer them.
2. Paste both into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Discard anything that would be true of any executive at any company. That is the test of whether it is useful.
4. Sequence it across the quarter rather than planning a single meeting; sponsorship is built over time.
5. Put a date on the first step. An intention to deepen a relationship is not a plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: Executive relationships deepen through usefulness delivered over time, not through contact frequency or a single well-prepared meeting. The investment has to start from what they need and what you can actually give.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate real sponsorship from polite interest

activities.name: Work out what happens when your sponsor leaves
activities.description: Establish how much of an account rests on one person, and what would survive if that person moved on.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, I want to understand my exposure if a key relationship ended. Here is who I rely on and what each of them does for us: the supplied senior relationships and what each one enables. For each person, tell me what would stop working if they left tomorrow, whether anyone else at the customer could carry that, and how much of our position depends on that single individual. Then tell me which relationship I should be building now as insurance. Be blunt about concentration. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: An exposure read per key relationship covering what would stop working, who could carry it, the degree of single-person dependency, and the relationship to build as insurance.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller judges how much concentration is tolerable. Some accounts genuinely run through one executive, and the decision is whether to accept that risk or invest in reducing it.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the senior people you rely on and what each one enables; who else at the customer operates at that level.
activitySteps: 1. List the senior people you rely on and what each one actually enables, from renewals to unblocking decisions.
2. Paste that into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much depends on one person. Most accounts depend on more than the seller admits.
4. Identify the second relationship you would need if the first one ended.
5. Start building that relationship now, while it is insurance rather than emergency.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsors leave, get promoted and change priorities, and the account discovers its dependency at the worst moment. The insurance relationship has to be built before it is needed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every account plan claims executive sponsorship. Far fewer accounts have someone senior who would actually spend their own credibility to unblock something. Focus on finding out which kind you have.
keyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps age quietly; the person you are counting on may have changed role or priority. Sponsorship is built over quarters and cannot be assembled in the week you need it. An executive relationship you only use when you need something is not sponsorship.
discussionQuestions: Who on your biggest account would take your call today, and when did you last test that?
Which senior relationship are you assuming is stronger than it is?
When did a sponsor last change without you noticing?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find out which recorded sponsors are still actually engaged'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the tested map to the one relationship each person will act on, and what they will offer. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Work out what happens when your sponsor leaves', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Executive relationships need engagement evidence, not contact lists or presumed sponsorship. A useful contribution tests the relationship without demanding endorsement. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account you feel confident about, and its current stakeholder map. Confidence is what makes this exercise useful.
facilitatorQuestions: Which recorded sponsor has not actually engaged recently?
Which relationship would hold under pressure, and what is your evidence?
What could you offer that this executive cannot easily get elsewhere?
What behavior would convince a peer that sponsorship is more than polite engagement?
listenFor: Sponsorship asserted without evidence, relationships described by meeting frequency rather than by what the person has done, engagement plans that would suit any executive at any company, and sellers softening a weak relationship rather than naming it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one sponsor evidence row: senior stakeholder role, observed action, unsupported sponsorship claim, offered value and next relationship test. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which relationship turned out to be thinner than you assumed, and what will you do about it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one assumed executive relationship by offering something useful and seeing what comes back. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized engagement lesson and whether it changed the plan; a single reply or silence does not prove sponsorship. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Work out whether your territory actually covers your number
activities.description: Do the arithmetic between what your territory can realistically produce and what you have been asked to deliver, and quantify the gap.
activities.prompt: Help me test whether my territory covers my number. Here is what I have: the supplied quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rate your team actually achieves at each stage. Using the conversion rates I supplied rather than any assumed benchmark, work out what the existing pipeline could realistically produce, and show the arithmetic so I can check it. Keep the renewal base separate from new business in your working rather than netting them together, because how renewals count toward quota depends on how my plan is structured. Then tell me how much new pipeline would be needed to close the remaining gap, and by when it would have to exist in order to close within the year. Derive a latest pipeline-creation date only from the sales-cycle durations or milestone timing I supply. If that timing basis is missing, show the required question instead of inventing a date. Do not double-count pipeline and renewal amounts that overlap. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A coverage calculation with the arithmetic shown, new business and renewal base kept separate, the remaining gap quantified, and the date by which new pipeline must exist.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns both the conversion rates and the treatment of renewals. Optimistic conversion produces a plan that looks covered and fails in the second half, and how renewals count toward attainment varies by plan rather than being a universal rule.
activities.requiredContext: Your quota for the year; current pipeline by stage with values; your renewal base; the conversion rates your team actually achieves at each stage; how renewals are treated in your own compensation plan. Include observed sales-cycle or confirmed milestone timing needed for a latest-start calculation, and any renewal/pipeline overlap.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rates your team actually achieves.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it. Without your own conversion rates it will have nothing to calculate from.
3. Check the arithmetic yourself. This is the number you will be held to.
4. Check how renewals count toward your own quota before treating the renewal base as coverage; that varies by plan and the calculation deliberately keeps them separate.
5. Note the date by which new pipeline must exist, not the date it must close.
activities.whyThisMatters: A territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. Most are never tested against arithmetic until a review tests them, which is the worst moment to find out.

activities.name: Find where the growth is most likely to come from
activities.description: Identify which accounts in your territory have the strongest evidence for growth, so coverage planning is based on signal rather than familiarity.
activities.prompt: Across my assigned accounts, help me find where new pipeline is most likely to come from. Consider consumption trending against commitment, workloads the customer owns but has not deployed, renewal timing, recent engagement levels, and any account where activity has increased without a corresponding opportunity. Rank by strength of evidence rather than account size, and tell me what the evidence actually is in each case. Flag accounts where I have no basis for a judgment either way. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Accounts ranked by evidenced growth potential with the evidence named, accounts lacking any basis flagged, and the top three matched to a specific play.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides which evidenced opportunity is realistic given their capacity. A ranked list that exceeds the hours in the year is not a plan, and the seller owns that trade-off.
activities.requiredContext: Your assigned account list; consumption and renewal data; your coverage gap from the previous practice.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your assigned accounts.
2. Compare the ranking against your own instinct, and take seriously anywhere they disagree.
3. Note the accounts flagged as having no basis for judgment. Those need research, not a forecast.
4. Pick the top three and name the specific play for each.
5. Check the total against the coverage gap you calculated. If it does not close, say so now.
activities.whyThisMatters: Territory planning defaults to the accounts you already know. The growth is often in the ones you have not looked at, and the evidence for that is usually already sitting in the data.

activities.name: Build the support ask you can defend
activities.description: Turn the coverage gap into a specific, evidenced request for the help you need, rather than a general statement that the number is hard.
activities.prompt: I have a coverage gap and I need to ask for support. Here is what I have: the supplied gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what support you have already tried to get and what came back, and the specific resource or investment you think you need. Using only what I have supplied, help me turn this into a request a manager could act on: state the ask precisely, tie it to the specific accounts and evidence, show what has already been attempted, and set out what changes if it is not provided. Flag any part of the ask my evidence does not support, and do not invent a consequence I have not described. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A support request naming the specific ask, the accounts and evidence behind it, what has already been attempted, and the consequence of not getting it, with unevidenced elements flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what consequence to state. Overstating what happens without support costs credibility in the next review, and the seller is the one who will be there for it.
activities.requiredContext: Your coverage gap; your ranked growth opportunities; what support you have already tried to secure and the response; the specific resource, specialist or investment you need.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what you have already tried, and the specific support you need.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Cut anything you cannot evidence. An unevidenced ask weakens the parts that are real.
4. Check the consequence it states is one you would defend in a review.
5. Take it to your territory review or your manager rather than waiting to be asked.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support goes to the people who ask for something specific and evidenced. A general statement that the territory is difficult competes with everyone else saying the same thing.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find where the growth is most likely to come from

activities.name: Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong
activities.description: Find the single assumption your territory plan most depends on, and work out what happens if it does not hold.
activities.prompt: Here is my territory plan and coverage calculation: the supplied plan. Identify the single assumption it most depends on, whether that is a renewal landing, one large opportunity closing, a conversion rate holding, or a consumption ramp continuing. Then tell me what happens to my coverage if that assumption fails, how early I would know, and what I could do now to reduce the dependency. Be direct about how concentrated the risk is. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: The plan's most load-bearing assumption named, the coverage impact if it fails, the earliest warning signal, and a contingency to reduce the dependency.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides how much concentration is acceptable. Some territories are genuinely dependent on one renewal, and the judgment is whether that is a risk to manage or a plan to change.
activities.requiredContext: Your territory plan and coverage calculation; the largest single opportunities and renewals within it; the conversion assumptions you used.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your plan and coverage calculation.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much rests on one deal or one renewal.
4. Work out the earliest signal that the assumption is failing, and schedule a check.
5. Decide now what the contingency is, while there is still time to build one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most territory plans fail on one assumption, not many. Knowing which one, and how early it would show, is the difference between adjusting in month three and explaining in month nine.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. This session tests that claim against arithmetic, while there is still time to do something about the answer.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current fiscal planning and territory-review requirements for your organization. Test the plan against governed quota, pipeline and renewal evidence, preserving dates and metric definitions. Separate actuals, forecasts and assumptions, and name the dependency or support request that changes the plan.
discussionQuestions: Do you know, arithmetically, whether your pipeline covers your number?
What single deal or renewal is your year most dependent on?
What support would actually change your position, and have you asked for it specifically?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out whether your territory actually covers your number'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coverage gap to the specific, evidenced support request each person will make. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Territory planning makes coverage arithmetic and assumptions inspectable. An evidenced support ask informs the manager; it does not authorize staffing or assign capacity. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring your governed quota, current pipeline by stage and renewal base with scope, source and as-of date. Distinguish actuals, forecasts and assumptions, and bring one dependency or support request that could change the plan.
facilitatorQuestions: What is your uncovered gap, and by when would new pipeline have to exist to close it?
Where is the growth evidence strongest, and does it match where you spend your time?
What is the one assumption your plan cannot survive without?
Which conversion or capacity assumption would a colleague challenge before accepting the coverage plan?
listenFor: Optimistic conversion rates used to make a plan look covered, growth ranked by familiarity rather than evidence, concentration risk nobody has named, and support asks phrased as a general complaint about difficulty.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one territory coverage calculation: supplied target/baseline, explicit conversion assumption, concentration/capacity risk and evidenced support question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the arithmetic tell you that your instinct had not, and what changes because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, check a material coverage assumption and take an evidenced support recommendation to the manager or territory review, respecting staffing and capacity authority. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized manual scenario and report the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized coverage assumption checked and whether it sharpened the ask or changed the plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Find the thing you have already built that others keep needing
activities.description: Identify which of your own recent work is being asked for repeatedly, and would save colleagues the most time if it were reusable.
activities.prompt: Look across my own mail, meetings and chats from the last quarter and help me find what I have built that others could reuse. Start by telling me which of those sources you can actually reach, and skip anything you cannot rather than guessing at it. Then look for material I have sent to more than one person, questions colleagues have asked me more than once, and work I appear to have rebuilt rather than reused. Rank by how often it comes up, and for each tell me what evidence suggests it is repeatedly needed rather than a one-off. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of your own work that appears repeatedly needed, with the evidence for each, the account-specific items filtered out, and a statement of which sources could not be reached.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what is genuinely transferable. Something that worked because of a specific relationship or a specific customer situation may not survive being generalized, and packaging it anyway wastes everyone's time.
activities.requiredContext: Microsoft 365 Copilot with access to your own mail, meetings and chats; the material you have produced in the last quarter.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt. It works on your own recent activity, so there is nothing to fill in.
2. Check what it says it could not reach. A source it cannot see is a blind spot in the ranking, not an empty one.
3. Look for the thing you have sent to several people, not the thing you are proudest of.
4. Discard anything so account-specific it would not transfer.
5. Pick the one that would save a colleague the most time, and check whether something similar already exists before you package yours.
activities.whyThisMatters: The best candidate for reuse is rarely the work you are proudest of. It is the thing you keep sending to people, which is exactly the thing you stop noticing.

activities.name: Strip out what makes it yours and unusable
activities.description: Remove the customer detail, assumed context and personal shorthand that would stop a colleague using your work or make it unsafe to share.
activities.prompt: Here is something I want to make reusable: the supplied material. Review it and tell me what would stop a colleague using it. Identify customer-identifying detail that must be removed, context I have assumed the reader already has, shorthand or internal references that would not be understood, and anything that was true only for my specific situation. Then tell me what is genuinely reusable underneath. Be direct if the answer is that very little of it transfers. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A list of what blocks reuse covering customer-identifying detail, assumed context, unexplained shorthand and situation-specific content, plus what genuinely transfers.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller is accountable for the customer-identifying detail. An automated pass will miss context that only the person who wrote it recognizes as identifying, and a leaked customer specific in a shared asset is a real incident.
activities.requiredContext: The material you want to make reusable; your team's rules on what may be shared internally; the customers referenced in it.
activitySteps: 1. Take the asset you selected.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Remove every piece of customer-identifying detail it finds, and check yourself as well.
4. Fill in the context you had assumed rather than deleting the part that needs it.
5. If very little transfers, accept that and pick something else. A thin asset costs the next person more than no asset.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most shared assets are unusable because they carry the author's context invisibly. The person who wrote it cannot see what is missing, because to them nothing is.
