activities.name: Write what the next person needs to trust it
activities.description: Add the purpose, prerequisites, limitations and ownership that let a colleague judge whether your asset fits their situation.
activities.prompt: Here is the sanitized asset: the supplied information. Draft the wrapper a colleague needs in order to trust and adapt it: what job it does, when it is the right choice and when it is not, what they need before starting, what to change for their own situation, what it will not do, and who to ask if it breaks. Work out from the asset itself whatever you genuinely can. Where you cannot tell, and particularly for the limitations and the situations where it breaks, ask me rather than guessing, up to five short questions, one at a time. Then write the final version, short enough that someone would actually read it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A short wrapper covering purpose, fit, prerequisites, what to adapt, honest limitations and a named owner, stored where colleagues would look.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what the asset cannot do. An honest limitation is what makes it trustworthy, and only the person who built it knows where it breaks.
activities.requiredContext: Your sanitized asset; the situations where it does and does not apply; where your team actually looks for shared material.
activitySteps: 1. Take your sanitized asset.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Answer its questions honestly. The limitations are the part it cannot read off the asset, and they are the part that matters.
4. Put your name on it as owner. An asset nobody owns is one nobody trusts.
5. Store it where a colleague would look, not where it is convenient for you to put it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Assets go unused because nobody can tell whether they fit. The wrapper is the whole difference between a file in a folder and something a colleague will actually pick up.

activities.name: Draft a reusable skill specification from a repeated prompt
activities.description: Decide whether a repeated prompt is safe to generalize, then specify the parameters, access limits, human checkpoint and tests a skill owner would need.
activities.prompt: Here is a prompt I run repeatedly: the supplied prompt and describe when you use it. Help me decide whether this should become a reusable skill rather than something I retype. Tell me what would need to be parameterized so it works for someone else's accounts, what context it silently assumes, what could go wrong if a colleague ran it without understanding it, and what the human checkpoint should be. Then draft the version that would work for the team rather than only for me. Return a draft specification, not an installed or validated skill. Include one representative approved test case, expected output and pass/fail criteria, plus the owner who would implement and execute it in a supported environment. A walkthrough is not an execution test. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A decision on safe generalization and a draft skill specification with parameters, access boundaries, failure modes, human checkpoint, representative test and implementation owner; no installed or tested skill is claimed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides whether the prompt is safe to generalize. A prompt that works because of what the author knows about their own accounts becomes dangerous when someone runs it without that knowledge.
activities.requiredContext: A prompt you run repeatedly; the situations you use it in; what data access it depends on; the colleague who would test it.
activitySteps: 1. Choose a repeated prompt and describe its actual workflow.
2. Run the specification prompt using permitted, sanitized context.
3. Verify account parameters, access assumptions, failure modes and the human checkpoint.
4. Walk through one representative test case and record gaps; do not claim a skill has run.
5. Name the implementation owner. Test an actual implementation with recorded results before approving wider publication.
activities.whyThisMatters: The prompt you have retyped four times is a skill waiting to be written. Most never get written because nobody notices they are repeating themselves.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Everyone in this room has rebuilt something a colleague had already solved, and everyone has had their own work rebuilt by someone else. Focus on breaking that cycle with one thing you have already made.

discussionQuestions: What have you sent to more than one colleague in the last month?
What have you rebuilt that you suspect someone else had already done?
What would you need to see before you trusted a colleague's asset enough to use it with a customer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find the thing you have already built that others keep needing'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the chosen asset to what each person must write down before anyone else could use it. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Turn a repeated prompt into a reusable skill', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Reusable work needs purpose, provenance, limits and permission to share. Findability helps peers learn, but publication is a separate human decision, not a huddle requirement. Treat the next use as a small test of better work; share the benefit or correction, not just the draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one thing you have built that worked, ideally something you have already shared with at least one person.
facilitatorQuestions: What in your asset only makes sense because of what you already know?
What would you have to tell someone before they could safely use it?
What does it genuinely not do?
What prerequisite did another person discover only after trying to reuse an apparently finished asset?
listenFor: Assets chosen because the author is proud of them rather than because they are repeatedly needed, customer detail nobody has noticed, limitations left unstated, and material about to be stored where only its author would look.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one reusable-prompt or asset card: purpose, required context, sanitized inputs, limitations, provenance, rights gap and reviewer. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep reuse/publication on hold until rights, sanitization and actual validation are reviewed; no repository access is required for the draft.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you have to explain about your own work that you had never noticed you were assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, review an existing reuse candidate for purpose, provenance, prerequisites and limits. Ask rights and publication owners whether sharing is permitted; keep it a private draft if approval is missing. Publication is not required before the next huddle. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized reuse lesson or permission gap and whether it clarified when the method is useful; do not bring or publish the asset itself. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Check whether committed milestones are actually progressing
activities.description: Test each committed milestone against evidence of real delivery progress, rather than against its status field.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, review the committed milestones I own. First tell me which sources you can actually reach for this account: milestone records, delivery activity, deployment or consumption data, and customer engagement. Then for each milestone, tell me what evidence exists that it is genuinely progressing, and separate milestones with real evidence from those where only the status field has been updated. Flag any milestone whose date has passed or is approaching with no supporting evidence. Where you cannot see a source, say so and treat that milestone as unknown rather than as stalled. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each committed milestone separating evidenced progress from status-only updates and from milestones the agent could not see, with unsupported approaching dates flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM verifies with the delivery team before treating a milestone as stalled, and treats anything the agent could not see as unknown rather than as bad news. Delivery work often runs ahead of what is recorded, and raising a false alarm costs credibility with the people you need.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the committed milestones you own; access to delivery and consumption activity for that account.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account with committed milestones you own.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Read what it says it could not reach first. Unknown and stalled are not the same thing, and acting on the difference is the whole point.
4. Separate genuine progress from a status field somebody updated.
5. Check the dates approaching in the next month first; those are still recoverable, then pick the milestone with the weakest evidence and find out what is actually happening.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone status is a claim, not evidence. The ones that fail were usually failing quietly for weeks while the status said otherwise.

activities.name: Diagnose why a milestone stopped and route it correctly
activities.description: Establish what is actually blocking a stalled milestone and get it to the person who can move it, rather than escalating in the wrong direction.
activities.prompt: A committed milestone has stalled. Here is what I know: the supplied milestone, its dates, what has and has not happened, and any blocker i am aware of. Help me work out what is most likely blocking it: a technical dependency, a customer-side resource or decision, a Microsoft delivery constraint, or a commercial issue. For each possibility, tell me what evidence would confirm or rule it out, and which role or function would own it at Microsoft and at the customer. Name the role rather than a person, since you cannot know either org chart; I will map the role to a name. Do not guess at a cause the evidence does not support. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked set of likely causes with the confirming evidence and the owning role at Microsoft and at the customer for each, the person you have mapped each role to, and the cause you have chosen to act on.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms the cause before routing. Every misrouted milestone costs a cycle, and the commitment date does not move to accommodate the mistake.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled milestone with its dates; what has and has not happened; any blocker you already know about; your Microsoft and customer contacts for that workload.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the milestone with the weakest evidence from the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Rule out causes before acting on one. Routing a customer-side problem to a technical owner loses a week.
4. Map each named role to an actual person yourself, and confirm the likely cause with someone closer to the work.
5. Hand it to that person with the evidence attached, not just the problem.
activities.whyThisMatters: Stalled milestones usually have one cause and three plausible explanations. Picking the wrong one costs a week you did not have.

activities.name: Test whether completed milestones produced real usage
activities.description: Check that milestones marked complete actually resulted in the customer using what was delivered.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, look at the milestones marked complete in the last two quarters and compare them against actual usage of what was delivered. Here is the intended rollout scope as far as I know it: the supplied intended scope, and say plainly where you do not know it. Tell me first which usage data you can actually reach. Then identify anything marked complete where usage is flat, where usage started and then declined, or where adoption sits with a much smaller group than was intended. Tell me what the data supports and what would need checking with the customer before I draw a conclusion. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A comparison of completed milestones against real usage, identifying flat, declining or narrowly concentrated adoption, with what needs customer confirmation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms the intended rollout before calling adoption a failure. A deliberately phased deployment looks identical to a failed one in the data.
activities.requiredContext: An account with recently completed milestones; usage data for the delivered workloads; the customer's intended rollout scope, or an honest statement of where you do not know it.
activitySteps: 1. Bring an account with milestones completed in the last two quarters.
2. Supply your account and intended rollout scope as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Distinguish a phased rollout from an adoption failure before reacting. If you did not know the intended scope, that is the first thing to go and find out.
4. Identify who owns adoption on the customer side; it is rarely whoever owned the deployment.
5. Raise flat usage as a finding to work on together, not as a criticism of the delivery.
activities.whyThisMatters: Completed delivery is not adoption; verified rollout scope and usage expose value gaps before they undermine renewal confidence.

activities.name: Prepare the conversation that unblocks a customer-side delay
activities.description: Plan how to raise a milestone stalled on the customer's side without turning it into a complaint about them.
activities.prompt: A committed milestone is stalled because of something on the customer's side. Here is the situation: the supplied milestone, the blocker, who at the customer is involved, what i am genuinely able to offer to help, and the customer outcome this milestone supports. Help me prepare the conversation: how to raise it as a shared problem rather than a failure on their part, how to use what I have told you I can offer to make it easier for them, what specifically I need from them, and what the consequence is for them, in their own terms, if it does not move. Do not invent resources, funding or commitments I have not told you I can make. Keep it customer-safe and avoid anything that sounds like chasing a Microsoft number. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A conversation plan framing the delay as a shared problem, with what you will offer, the specific ask, and the consequence expressed in the customer's terms.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides how hard to push. A milestone date that matters to Microsoft may not matter to the customer, and pressing on Microsoft's timeline damages the relationship the renewal depends on.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled milestone and its customer-side blocker; who at the customer is involved; what you are genuinely authorized to offer; the customer outcome the milestone supports.
activitySteps: 1. Take a milestone stalled on the customer side.
2. Decide what you can genuinely offer before you run anything. If you do not tell it, it will invent something you cannot deliver.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Check the consequence is stated in the customer's terms, not Microsoft's.
5. Have the conversation with the person who can actually move it, not the person you usually speak to.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most committed milestones stall on the customer side, and most of those conversations go badly because they sound like Microsoft chasing its own number.

preparationChecklist: Bring one account with committed milestones you own, their current dates, and whatever delivery or consumption data you can reach.
facilitatorQuestions: Which milestone has a status but no evidence behind it?
What is actually blocking the one that stopped, and who owns that?
Where has something completed without anyone using it?
How does a peer distinguish a genuine stalled milestone from a deliberately phased rollout?
listenFor: Status fields treated as evidence, causes guessed at rather than confirmed, milestones escalated to the wrong owner, and phased rollouts being mistaken for failed adoption.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one milestone diagnosis: status versus evidence, stalled dependency, phased-rollout alternative, accountable role and usage check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which milestone turned out to be stalled for a different reason than you assumed, and what did that change?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one committed milestone with no supporting evidence and find out what is actually happening with it. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized difference between assumed and confirmed blocker and whether it changed the owner conversation. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires
activities.description: Check each uncommitted milestone against the criteria a commitment is supposed to satisfy, and identify which criteria are not yet met.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, review the uncommitted milestones I own. A milestone should not be committed until there is a named sponsor who has agreed the outcome, an agreed value and date, confirmed feasibility, available customer and delivery resources, an available budget, and a chosen delivery model. Tell me first which sources you can actually reach. For the sponsor, outcome, value, date and budget, tell me which are evidenced in the record, which are asserted without evidence, and which are simply absent. For feasibility, resources and the delivery model, tell me only whether each is recorded as confirmed and by whom; do not assess the technical position yourself, because the Solution Engineer owns settling those and you do not have the technical context. Rank the milestones by how close they are to being genuinely committable, and do not treat a populated field as evidence on its own. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Each uncommitted milestone scored against the commitment criteria, with sponsor, value, date and budget separated into evidenced, asserted and absent, the technical criteria reported only as recorded or not and by whom, a readiness ranking, and the unreachable sources named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides what counts as evidence of sponsorship, and routes the technical criteria rather than judging them. A named contact in a field is not a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, and a feasibility box ticked by nobody in particular is not confirmed feasibility.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the uncommitted milestones you own; the sponsor, value, date and budget position on each as far as you know it.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account with uncommitted milestones you own.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Separate a populated field from an evidenced one. Most milestones fail on evidence, not on data entry.
4. Take the closest milestone to commitment, not the largest one.
5. Split the missing criteria into the ones you close and the ones your SE closes, and send the technical half to them today rather than carrying it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone gets committed once. Everything after that is measured against it, so the cost of committing an unready one lands months later on someone who did not make the call.

activities.name: Build the case the sponsor has to agree to
activities.description: Turn the milestone into the outcome, value and commitment a named sponsor would actually put their name to.
activities.prompt: I need a sponsor to commit to a milestone. Here is what I have: the supplied milestone, the outcome it is meant to produce, the sponsor and what i know about what they are measured on, and the value and date i am proposing. Help me build the case in the sponsor's terms rather than in ours: what outcome they are being asked to own, what they get, what they have to put in including budget and their own people, and what happens to their outcome if the date slips. Tell me which parts of this I have not actually given you, and ask me for them rather than filling them in yourself. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A sponsor-facing case stating the outcome they would own, what they receive, what they must contribute, and the consequence to their outcome if the date moves, with the gaps you still need to fill named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP judges whether this person can actually commit. Agreement from someone without budget or authority reads identically in the record and fails identically later.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and the outcome it produces; the named sponsor and what they are measured on; the value and date you intend to propose; what the customer would need to contribute.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the milestone you took forward in the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Answer whatever it asks for rather than letting it assume. What the sponsor is measured on is the part that decides this.
4. Check the ask is proportionate to what they get. A commitment that costs them more than it returns will be agreed and then quietly dropped.
5. Take it to the sponsor directly. A commitment relayed through someone else is not a commitment.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsorship is the criterion most often recorded and least often true. The test is not whether they are supportive; it is whether they would defend the date to their own leadership.

activities.name: Pressure-test the value and the date before you commit to them
activities.description: Challenge the value and date on a milestone against the evidence behind them, before they become a commitment you are measured on.
activities.prompt: Here is the value and date I am about to commit to on a milestone: the supplied milestone, the value, the date, and how i arrived at each. Challenge both from the commercial side. For the value, tell me what it assumes about scope, adoption and timing, and which of those assumptions I have evidence for. For the date, work only on what the customer and I control: budget cycle, approval and procurement timing, the customer's own decision cadence, and any contractual or fiscal date it depends on. Do not construct the technical delivery sequence behind the date; the Solution Engineer owns that and you do not have the technical context for it. Then tell me what the value and date would look like if the least-evidenced assumption turned out to be wrong. Do not propose a different number; show me what mine depends on. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: The commercial assumptions the value and date rest on, which are evidenced and which are not, the approval, budget and customer-timing dependencies on the date, and what both would become if the weakest assumption failed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP owns the number and knows to get the delivery sequence from the SE rather than from a model. The decision to commit a value and a date in front of a customer and a forecast is not one to take on a commercial read alone.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone with its proposed value and date; how you arrived at each; the scope and adoption assumptions behind the value; the budget, approval and customer decision timing the date depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value and date you intend to commit to, and how you arrived at each.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Look for the assumption carrying the most of the number. There is usually one.
4. Get the technical side of the date from your SE rather than from the model. A commercial date that ignores the delivery sequence is half a commitment.
5. Record what the commitment depends on alongside it, so the reason is still there when someone asks in a quarter.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recording the evidenced commercial and technical assumptions lets the account team challenge the estimate before it becomes a commitment.

activities.name: Find the uncommitted milestones that are never going to commit
activities.description: Identify uncommitted milestones that have stopped moving and should be closed or reset rather than carried.
activities.prompt: For the account or account identifier, look at my uncommitted milestones and find the ones that are not progressing: dates that have been moved more than once without the underlying position changing, and milestones with no logged activity against them since they were created. For each of those, also tell me who is recorded as the sponsor and when that contact record was last updated, so I can check myself whether they are still in the role. Do not tell me whether anyone has left; you only know what someone typed into the record. For each milestone, tell me what the record shows and what it does not, and whether the honest action is to reset it with a new basis or close it. Do not recommend closing anything on absence of data alone; say what you would need to see. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: The uncommitted milestones with repeated date moves or no logged activity, the recorded sponsor and how stale that record is, what the record does and does not show, and a reset-or-close recommendation with the evidence still needed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides what to close. Closing a milestone removes it from the picture everyone else is working from, and a quiet customer is not the same as a dead opportunity.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; your uncommitted milestones with their date history; the recorded sponsor on each; what you know yourself about recent customer engagement.
activitySteps: 1. Use the same account and its uncommitted milestones.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Check the recorded sponsors yourself. A stale contact record looks identical to a current one, and the agent cannot tell them apart.
4. Check each candidate before acting. A milestone can be quiet because the customer is quiet, not because it is dead.
5. Reset the ones with a real basis and a stale date, close the ones without, and say why in the record. A closed milestone with a reason is reusable evidence; one without is just a gap.
activities.whyThisMatters: Uncommitted milestones that nobody will close make the consumption picture look healthier than it is, and the sponsor who left is usually discovered by the person who inherits the milestone rather than the one who carried it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A milestone commitment gives others a date and outcome to plan against. Focus on checking the evidence before committing, and making unresolved dependencies explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: A milestone is ready to commit when there is a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, an agreed value and date, confirmed feasibility, available customer and delivery resources, an available budget and a chosen delivery model. A populated field is not evidence. Once the milestone is committed it transfers to customer success to be driven to completion, so what you commit becomes someone else's number to defend.
discussionQuestions: Which of your uncommitted milestones would you personally defend the date on?
When a milestone gets committed early, what usually forces it?
Which committed milestone in your patch was committed before it was ready, and what did that cost?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the readiness read to the single milestone each person will either take to a sponsor or deliberately hold. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find the uncommitted milestones that are never going to commit', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Uncommitted milestones advance only when customer and technical evidence support the criteria. Holding is valid; AI cannot create sponsorship, budget or commitment. Make that evidence check part of recurring work; share a safe example of what changed so peers can adapt the habit.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account with uncommitted milestones you own, and for one of them the sponsor, the value, the date and how you arrived at each.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commitment criteria are populated on your milestone but not actually evidenced?
Would your sponsor defend this date to their own leadership?
Which single assumption is carrying most of your value?

activities.name: Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed
activities.description: Establish which parts of the technical path behind a milestone are proven and which are still assumptions carrying the date.
activities.prompt: Here is a milestone we are considering committing to: the supplied milestone, the workload, the target architecture or approach, and what has been proven so far. Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed. For each assumption, tell me what would prove or disprove it, roughly how hard that is to establish, and what breaks if it turns out to be false. Then tell me which single assumption carries the most of the date. Do not treat something we have done at another customer as confirmed here; say what would make it transferable. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A split of the technical basis into confirmed and assumed, what would settle each assumption and at what effort, what breaks if it fails, and the assumption carrying most of the date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides what counts as proven in this environment. A pattern that worked elsewhere is a hypothesis here, and the difference is invisible in the record once the milestone is committed.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and its workload; the target architecture or approach; what has already been proven and where; the customer's environment constraints as far as you know them.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one uncommitted milestone with a technical dependency you are not certain about.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Check that it has not quietly promoted a pattern from another customer into a confirmed fact here.
4. Take the assumption carrying the most of the date and work out what would settle it.
5. Say plainly which assumptions remain open. That sentence is what protects the date.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical commitments fail on the assumption nobody wrote down. Naming them before the commitment is the only point at which naming them is cheap.

activities.name: Name the dependencies and resources the date actually needs
activities.description: Work out what the customer and Microsoft must each provide for the milestone to land, and where those are not yet secured.
activities.prompt: For this milestone: the supplied milestone, the technical approach, and the open assumptions from the previous practice. Work out what the date actually depends on. Separate what the customer must provide, including people, environment access, data and decisions, from what Microsoft or a partner must provide, and from what depends on the chosen delivery model. For each, tell me whether it is secured, requested or not yet raised as far as I have told you, and flag anything you cannot tell from what I have given you rather than assuming it is in place. Then tell me which dependency, if it is not secured this month, makes the date unachievable. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: The dependencies split into customer, Microsoft or partner, and delivery model, each marked secured, requested or not yet raised, with the dependency that decides the date identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE confirms what the customer has actually agreed to provide rather than what was discussed. Assumed customer resource is the most common reason a technically sound milestone misses its date.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and its technical approach; the open assumptions; what the customer has agreed to provide; the intended delivery model; which partner or Microsoft resources are involved.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the assumptions you produced in the previous practice.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Check the customer-side list honestly. It is the half that is usually assumed and rarely secured.
4. Identify the dependency that decides the date and who owns it on the customer side.
5. Raise the unsecured ones now, while the milestone is still uncommitted and the date can still move.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone date depends on secured customer resources, environment access and delivery ownership as well as technical feasibility.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed

activities.name: Turn the proof result into a commit or hold recommendation
activities.description: Convert what a proof of concept or pilot actually showed into a clear recommendation on whether the milestone can be committed.
activities.prompt: Here is what our proof of concept or pilot actually produced: the supplied what was tested, what the results showed, what was not tested, and any conditions that differed from production. Turn this into a recommendation on whether the milestone can be committed. Tell me what the result genuinely supports, what it does not support because it was not tested, and what would behave differently at production scale or under production conditions. Then give me the recommendation, either commit, commit with a named condition, or hold, with the reason in one sentence I could say out loud to the account team. Do not extrapolate beyond what was tested. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: What the proof result supports and what it does not, what would differ at production scale, and a commit, commit-with-condition or hold recommendation with a one-sentence reason.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns the recommendation. A proof result is routinely reported as broader than it was, and the person who ran it is the only one who can say where the boundary is.
activities.requiredContext: The proof of concept or pilot scope and results; what was explicitly not tested; how the test conditions differed from production; the milestone the result is meant to support.
activitySteps: 1. Bring a proof of concept or pilot result behind an uncommitted milestone.
2. Paste what was tested and what was not into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Pay attention to what it says was not tested. That is the part the account team will hear as proven.
4. Take a position. Commit, commit with a stated condition, or hold.
5. Give the account team the one-sentence reason as well as the recommendation, so it survives being repeated.
activities.whyThisMatters: A narrow proof supports only the conditions tested; recording its limits protects the milestone from overbroad retelling.

activities.name: Work the date backwards from the technical path
activities.description: Build the sequence of technical work a milestone date implies and find where it has no room to absorb a delay.
activities.prompt: Here is a milestone date being proposed and the technical work behind it: the supplied date, the work that has to happen, and the dependencies from the previous practice. Work backwards from the date. Lay out what has to happen in what order, what can run in parallel and what genuinely cannot, and where a delay in one step consumes the whole margin. Tell me which step has the least certainty and the most consequence. Do not invent how long anything takes; where you need a duration, ask me for it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A backwards-planned sequence from the proposed date showing order, genuine parallelism, where the margin is consumed, and the step with the least certainty and most consequence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE supplies the durations and owns the sequence. The model can structure the dependencies but has no basis for estimating how long work takes in this customer's environment.
activities.requiredContext: The proposed milestone date; the technical work required; the dependencies and who owns each; your own estimate of how long each step takes.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the proposed date and the dependency list from the previous practice.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Supply the durations yourself when it asks. It has no basis for guessing them and a guessed sequence is worse than none.
4. Find the step with the least certainty and the most consequence.
5. Take the sequence to whoever proposed the date, before it is committed rather than after it is missed.
activities.whyThisMatters: A date is usually set from when it is needed rather than from when the work can be done. Laying the sequence out is how that gets discussed while it can still change.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You are usually the person in the room who knows whether the date is achievable. Focus on the window where saying so still changes the outcome rather than explaining the miss.
keyTalkingPoints: Feasibility, resources and the delivery model are part of what makes a milestone committable, and they are the part most often assumed. A pattern that worked at another customer is a hypothesis here, not a proven fact. A proof of concept proves what it tested and nothing else, and it gets retold as broader than it was.
discussionQuestions: Which milestone in your patch has a date nobody has worked backwards from?
What is the last thing you assumed the customer would provide and they did not?
Where has a pilot result been repeated back to you as more than it actually showed?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the confirmed-versus-assumed split to the one dependency each person will secure or escalate before the date is committed. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Work the date backwards from the technical path', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical milestone dates distinguish confirmed proof from assumptions about dependencies and capacity. Honest open conditions are more useful than unsupported dates. activities.name: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year
activities.description: Separate the deals that can still be fully executed and processed before the period ends from the ones that are already next year's.
activities.prompt: For my patch, or a named account or TPID, list the opportunities with a close date in the current fiscal period. For each, tell me what the record shows about its approval state, what is still outstanding, whether it has been signed, and whether anything indicates it will arrive for processing after a cutoff explicitly confirmed in the guidance I supply. Tell me first which of these you can actually see. Do not tell me whether it will book, because the rule that decides that is set by my own segment's bookings policy and you do not have it. Tell me what still has to happen for each deal to be capable of booking in the period. If no cutoff or bookings rule is supplied, mark the timing question unknown and route it to Deal Desk/operations; do not invent a guaranteed processing date. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Each in-period opportunity with its approval state, what is still outstanding, its signature position, any indication it will miss the processing cutoff, and what still has to happen for it to be capable of booking.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the bookings rule locally and decides what is genuinely closeable. An approval state in the record is a snapshot, and only the person in the deal knows whether the customer will actually sign in time or is simply being polite about the date.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; the opportunities you expect to close in the period; their current approval state; what each is waiting on; your Deal Desk or operations contact for the bookings rule that applies to your segment.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your own patch or one account, and the deals you believe are landing this period.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Confirm the bookings rule that applies to your own segment with Deal Desk or operations rather than assuming it. What has to be true for a deal to book in a period, and by when, is set locally.
4. Separate deals waiting on Microsoft approvals from deals waiting on the customer. Confirm who can act on each and check verified processing runway rather than only the signature date.
5. Decide which deals you are deliberately leaving in the new year, and say so out loud rather than carrying them as hope.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every year some deals get forced into June that were always going to close in July, and are discounted for the privilege. The deals worth pushing are the ones that only need a signature, not the ones that still need a decision.

activities.name: Find the renewals whose expiration timing will cost you the booking
activities.description: Identify renewals whose expiration date sits at the period boundary, where how they are handled decides whether they land in this year or the next.
activities.prompt: For my patch, or a named account or TPID, list the renewals with expiration dates at or near the end of the current fiscal period. For each, tell me the actual expiration date, whether it has been committed as on-time, what is still outstanding to complete it, and what the record shows about customer engagement on it. Flag any renewal where the expiration falls on the final day of the period, so I can confirm any booking/billing-calendar difference with the authoritative operations owner. Tell me what you cannot see rather than assuming it is fine. State a calendar rule only where the current guidance I supply confirms it. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewals at the period boundary with their actual expiration dates, commitment status, outstanding work and customer engagement, with last-day expirations flagged for deliberate handling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the processing runway with the person who owns it. Renewal processing has a real lead time and the deadline that matters is when the work has to arrive, not when the agreement expires.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; renewals with expiration dates near the period end; their commitment status; your renewals or operations contact.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your patch or one account with renewals near the period boundary.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Flag last-day expirations for an operations check; do not assume a different treatment without current authoritative guidance.
4. Confirm the processing runway with your renewals or operations contact rather than assuming it.
5. Commit the ones that are genuinely on-time and stop describing the others as on-time.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal at the period boundary is the easiest booking to lose and the hardest to explain, because nothing about it looked at risk until it was.

activities.name: Prioritize record corrections against verified fiscal deadlines
activities.description: Find apparent record discrepancies and distinguish corrections with a confirmed fiscal deadline from year-round hygiene or timing that still needs verification.
activities.prompt: For [patch / account / TPID], inspect the authorized records and agreement evidence available or supplied for apparent discrepancies in agreement, licensing, enrollment, amounts, forecast dates and commitments. State what the record shows, what the authoritative evidence shows and what remains uncertain. Using current correction-window guidance I supply, separate items with a confirmed fiscal-close deadline, year-round hygiene and items whose deadline is unverified. Cite the rule behind a deadline; do not assume a field becomes uneditable at year end. Identify which owner must verify or correct each item. Do not change any record. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidence-backed correction list with confirmed fiscal deadlines, year-round hygiene and unverified timing separated; each discrepancy has an accountable verification/correction owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller verifies the correct position against the agreement before changing anything. A confidently inferred correction is still a guess, and a wrong correction made in the last week of the year is materially harder to undo than a wrong original.
activities.requiredContext: Authorized account/patch and identifiers; authoritative agreement/licensing evidence; current correction-window guidance if available; operations or Deal Desk contacts. Missing guidance leaves the deadline unverified.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one authorized account/patch and the executed agreement or other authoritative evidence.
2. Confirm current correction-window guidance with operations or Deal Desk.
3. Run the prompt and verify each apparent discrepancy and deadline.
4. Prioritize confirmed deadline-sensitive items by consequence and remaining runway; leave unverified deadlines as questions.
5. The authorized owner approves and makes exact corrections through the usual process, or routes them to the team that can act.
activities.whyThisMatters: Verified correction windows let the seller prioritize material discrepancies without treating an assumed fiscal cutoff as policy.

activities.name: Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented
activities.description: Sort your year-end pressure into work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar and work that belongs on the customer's own timeline.
activities.prompt: Here is everything I am treating as urgent because of year end: the supplied list, and for each say what i believe the deadline is and where that deadline comes from. Sort it into two groups. The first is work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar, meaning it must happen before the period closes because a system, an approval chain or a booking rule requires it. The second is work I am pulling forward into this month even though the real driver is the customer's own decision, contract or delivery timeline. For anything in the second group, tell me what it would cost to force it early. Where I have not said where a deadline comes from, ask me rather than assuming there is one. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Your year-end work sorted into genuinely fiscal-dated and customer-dated, the cost of forcing each item that is being pulled forward, and an owner and date for the items that are genuinely fixed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to force. Some work is worth pulling forward even at a cost, and that is a judgment about the customer relationship and the number, not one a model can make.
activities.requiredContext: Your own list of what you are treating as year-end urgent; where you believe each deadline comes from; the customer decision or contract timing behind each item.
activitySteps: 1. Write down everything you are treating as urgent because of year end, and where you think each deadline comes from.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about the ones where the only deadline is that it is June.
4. For anything you are pulling forward, decide whether the cost of forcing it is worth it. Often it is; the point is to decide rather than to drift.
5. Take the genuinely fiscal-dated items and make sure each one has an owner and a date that is earlier than the cutoff.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of what feels like a June deadline is a deal on its own clock being pulled forward. Doing that deliberately is fine. Doing it because the month feels urgent is how good deals get discounted and customers get pushed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Year end generates a lot of urgency and only some of it is real. This session separates the part that is genuinely fixed by the calendar from the part that only feels that way, and acts on the first while there is still room.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current local systems-close calendar and authoritative booking, billing and approval guidance; historical dates do not establish current deadlines. Work backward from the applicable cutoff and allow the confirmed processing runway. Verify period-end renewal handling with the responsible owner. Check any ECIF or milestone calendar for its region and motion rather than treating it as a worldwide rule.
discussionQuestions: Which of the things you are rushing right now would still be urgent if it were March?
What did you find out too late at the last year end?
Which deal did you pull forward last year, and what did it cost to do it?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use the chosen result to identify one evidenced close-period action or deliberate carry-forward decision; do not require both a full deal review and record repair live. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Fiscal close depends on verified cutoffs, customer reality and authorized record ownership. Calendar pressure cannot justify forced period timing or unsupported commitments. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring your own patch or one account, the deals and renewals you expect to land in this period, and a written list of everything you are currently treating as year-end urgent.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your in-period deals is waiting on Microsoft, and which is waiting on the customer?
What could you correct today that stops being correctable after close?
Which of your urgent items has a deadline you could actually point to?
How does a peer distinguish a real processing deadline from urgency inferred only from the fiscal calendar?
listenFor: Signature dates being treated as booking dates with no processing runway, renewals at the period boundary assumed to be fine, corrections being deferred to the week when every queue is longest, and deadlines whose only source is that it is June.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one fiscal-close workback: processing deadline requiring current confirmation, customer/Microsoft dependency, correctable record and carry-forward rationale. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your year-end deadlines turned out to have no source other than the month it is?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, verify the applicable close cutoff and inspect a record or timing assumption at risk. Make an authorized correction or route it, and have the accountable person review any proposed customer timing message. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized manual scenario and report the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized cutoff or timing assumption checked and whether it prevented a rushed correction or unsupported year-end commitment. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

ALL-CLOSE.keyTakeaway: A close is complete when each material record is evidence-backed, owned, and dispositioned.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on producing a forecast the PSS can defend without treating partner stage as verified customer progress.
keyTalkingPoints: Limited to pinned/associated partner opportunities in PSS scope; the partner retains its forecast and opportunity decisions.
Current execution: Use Partner Center/Partner Timeline for partner-reported stage and MSX for Microsoft opportunity/forecast.
Fallback: Use a dated reconciliation table based on partner confirmation and MSX when cross-system reporting is unavailable.
System of record: MSX is the Microsoft forecast record; Partner Center is the partner-side co-sell source.
Optional AI boundary: AI may compare supplied records but must not infer customer stage, modify records, or collapse source differences.
discussionQuestions: Where do partner and Microsoft stage/date views disagree?
What is customer-confirmed versus partner-reported?
What correction belongs in each system?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test whether partner stages are evidenced'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect one decision-changing evidence gap in the selected artifact, then compare a peer's approach and name the accountable next action. Drafts do not prove acceptance, approval or a completed system update. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Correct the Microsoft forecast narrative', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pipeline inspection reconciles contradictions and customer evidence before forecast changes. Partner stage is not verified Microsoft forecast state. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one partner-associated opportunity, dated partner stage/forecast evidence, the corresponding MSX record and unresolved differences. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.
facilitatorQuestions: What evidence supports the partner's stage and next customer action? Which stalled dependency has an accountable owner? How does a colleague reconcile the partner view with the Microsoft forecast without silently overwriting either?
listenFor: Work starting without the stated trigger, partner involvement treated as universal, an unaccepted owner presented as coverage, AI output presented as system evidence, or Partner Solution Sales absorbing a decision outside this role boundary.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one partner/Microsoft pipeline reconciliation: supplied stage evidence, conflict, stalled dependency, owner and forecast question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which contradiction changed your forecast interpretation, and what remains unconfirmed?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, check a material pinned-partner contradiction or stall and ask the authorized record or forecast owner to validate correction or risk note. Use Microsoft 365 Copilot only for permitted drafting or analysis; otherwise review manually. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. If inputs are unavailable, use a sanitized example and name the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized contradiction clarified and whether it improved forecast confidence or follow-through. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on agreeing a joint plan the partner can execute and Microsoft can support.
keyTalkingPoints: Use only for selected partners/opportunities aligned to the solution area; do not impose one joint plan on every partner.
Current execution: Use MSX partner-associated pipeline, Partner Center/Partner Timeline, current partner-performance sources, and authoritative program guidance.

System of record: MSX for Microsoft opportunity/forecast; Partner Center for partner-side co-sell; route-specific system for approved programs.
Optional AI boundary: Know Your Partner may assemble permitted partner context where accessible. ECIF/program tools remain route- and access-specific.
discussionQuestions: Which joint-plan outcome can the partner execute?
What capacity or program dependency is unconfirmed?
Which party must accept each proposed commitment?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prioritize by demonstrated movement and solution fit'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect one decision-changing evidence gap in the selected artifact, then compare a peer's approach and name the accountable next action. Drafts do not prove acceptance, approval or a completed system update. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Attach the scalable program or investment route', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Partner plans are executable when selected plays match evidence, accepted ownership and a viable route. Plans cannot commit either party capacity. Agree where this fits in recurring work and how a small, safe signal will help the team learn together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one selected partner, approved joint-plan priorities, dated pipeline/capacity evidence and applicable current program guidance. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.
facilitatorQuestions: Which partner and deal demonstrate solution fit and movement worth PSS attention? What reciprocal action and route dependency remain unaccepted? How does a peer turn a joint plan into execution without taking over partner economics?
listenFor: Work starting without the stated trigger, partner involvement treated as universal, an unaccepted owner presented as coverage, AI output presented as system evidence, or Partner Solution Sales absorbing a decision outside this role boundary.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which play changed after checking partner acceptance and actual outcome?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, validate a selected play, route or ownership assumption and agree your own action with its partner or Microsoft owner. Use Microsoft 365 Copilot only for permitted drafting or analysis; otherwise review manually. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. If inputs are unavailable, use a sanitized example and name the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized assumption checked and whether it focused execution or exposed an unaccepted obligation. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

DSE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Explore how peer-led huddles connect business outcomes, recurring workflows, and responsible AI experimentation, including what to try and share between sessions.
DSE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.
DSE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Participate confidently in the motion, starting with a meaningful workflow and testing improvements in real work while retaining human judgment and learning from evidence.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Home
primaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
primaryAgents.whatItIs: SME&C Seller surface within Sales Agent
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

DCSA-ORIENT.todayObjective: Explore how peer-led huddles connect business outcomes, recurring workflows, and responsible AI experimentation, including what to try and share between sessions.
DCSA-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.
DCSA-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Participate confidently in the motion, starting with a meaningful workflow and testing improvements in real work while retaining human judgment and learning from evidence.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

activities.name: Record acceptance and monitoring signal
activities.description: Compare supplied handoff and milestone evidence to separate actual acceptance, started work, changed risks and missing result evidence.
activities.prompt: Produce an unactivated, read-only proposal, not a running monitor. Use authorized dated snapshots, a user-maintained baseline and previous report supplied for this review; do not retrieve unsupplied records, create automation, retain agent memory or notify anyone. Missing history is baseline-only or comparison unavailable, not no change. Record proposed scope, source permission, owner, cadence, recipients, review/expiry and approved change criteria without inventing values. Future monitoring requires separate explicit approval and verified access/state capabilities. If one essential detail is missing, ask one concise question. Compare the supplied handoff response, accepted owner, committed start date, milestone evidence, intended result, and escalation route. If two comparable dated snapshots are supplied, return only newly started or still-not-started work, changed ownership, new or resolved risk, changed result evidence, and overdue escalation. Do not assign ownership, judge implementation quality, or update a system.
