Keep it to one gap. Use only supplied material or reachable sources I am authorized to access and share through this tool; name access gaps rather than inventing evidence. Draft or analyze only: do not send, publish, change records, submit requests or make commitments. Treat any owner, date or approval not established by the sources as unconfirmed; do not convert a proposal or discussion into an agreed commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A one-gap credibility plan with a first step and a date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA keeps this to one gap. A plan covering every gap is a plan that closes none of them before the customer needs the answer.
activities.requiredContext: Gap map, customer timeline, available time; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.

3. Name the smallest first step.

activities.whyThisMatters: One closed gap before the customer needs it beats a broad plan that arrives after they asked.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You get called in when you are the person who can answer the question. Focus on deciding which questions those will be.
keyTalkingPoints: Technical credibility is set by the customer's roadmap, not by our product releases.
The gap worth closing is the one the customer hits next, not the most interesting one.
Being able to say what you do not know is part of being trusted, not the opposite of it.
discussionQuestions: What will this customer be building in six months that you could not advise on today?
Where have you been the bottleneck because the answer had to come from someone else?
Which technical topic do you avoid, and what does avoiding it cost?

Move from general capability to one customer, one upcoming technical decision, and one gap. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find where you were the bottleneck', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical advisor credibility grows by closing a customer-relevant gap and knowing when a specialist should lead. Learning is not certification or proven expertise. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one customer, what you know of their technical direction, and one question you were recently unable to answer.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next technical decision this customer faces, and could you hold that conversation today?
Which gap is real and which is imagined?
What is the smallest step that would make you credible on it?
How did a colleague decide between closing a technical gap personally and bringing in a specialist?
listenFor: Gaps chosen by personal interest rather than by customer need; plans to learn everything rather than one thing; and cases where the honest answer is to bring in a specialist rather than close the gap personally.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which customer-relevant knowledge gap should you close, and where is specialist advice the more credible step?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, choose a technical topic relevant to an upcoming customer decision and take a bounded learning or specialist-review step; advise only on what you can substantiate. If evidence is unavailable, use a sanitized manual scenario and report the gap.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized learning gap addressed and whether it improved advice or clarified the need for a specialist. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

PLC-ENT-AE-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on evidence from the guided Role Path and choose the team's next workflow priorities, using relevant existing topics or a custom huddle.
PLC-ENT-AE-W09.whyItMatters: Teams sustain change when they use evidence from practice to set their next learning priorities rather than continuing a fixed path by default.
PLC-ENT-AE-W09.desiredOutcome: Sustain a team-owned cycle of workflow improvement, using shared experience to choose relevant huddles, test changes in real work, and revisit priorities as evidence develops.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about three minutes reconnecting to why the Huddle Motion matters to the work.
2. Recognize the shift from guided Weeks 1-8 to team-owned learning, not the end of the motion.

3. Preview the shared transition: reflect on experience, choose the next focus, and close with participant feedback. These are coordinated session components, not four alternative practices to complete.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about ten minutes comparing experiences using examples the group may discuss.
2. Explain what changed in the workflow or why a practice did not help yet; no success story is required.
3. Identify a habit worth repeating and a friction point or support need.
4. Use these observations to inform the next-focus discussion, without ranking participants.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: AI in Action: choose the next team focus
activities.description: Choose a next work priority and an existing or custom huddle starting point, using tools and content permitted for the team.
activities.expectedOutput: An agreed next priority, a suitable huddle or draft starting point, and an owner; optional backlog ideas remain separate.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the ten-minute AI-in-Action segment to connect the reflection to work where a change would be useful.
2. Choose the priority to try first; keep up to two other ideas as an optional backlog rather than simultaneous commitments.

3. In All Topics, compare relevant outcomes and activities, filtering by Segment, Role, Focus Area, and tools permitted for the team and project. Select one Featured practice for the next ordinary huddle; Extended practices remain optional.
4. If no topic fits, use Huddle in a Box to outline a draft for later review, not to create or publish a finished huddle in this session.
5. Confirm an owner and a practical next step. Without app access, record the priority and locate the content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear next-focus commitment and a participant-owned feedback opportunity, with any unfinished survey completed after the huddle.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Use the final five minutes to restate the useful habit, friction point, and chosen next focus.
2. Confirm who will take the next step and when the team will revisit what it learned.
3. Open the Team Member Impact Survey and let participants complete their own responses. If time or access is insufficient, finish after the huddle rather than extending the live session.
4. Continue the team-owned motion; this transition is not a final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided activation to team-owned practice. The team has completed the eight-week activation journey. Use this huddle to recognize what changed, address friction, and choose what to focus on next.
keyTalkingPoints: This is the same participant experience for every role. Overview: 3 minutes - reconnect to the motion and the transition to team ownership. Share Your Experience: 10 minutes - reflect on useful changes, friction, and support needs. AI-in-Action: 10 minutes - choose the next team priority and a relevant existing or custom huddle starting point. Closing & Next Steps: 5 minutes - confirm the owner and next action, then allow participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey.
discussionQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent?
Which two or three team priorities would be most useful next?
suggestedTransitions: Use the coordinated Transition agenda: Overview, Share Your Experience, AI-in-Action, and Closing & Next Steps. Reflect on real work, agree the next focus and owner, and use the final five minutes for participant-owned survey completion. Review All Topics or a custom-huddle idea only if time and access permit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close the guided path by naming one useful habit, one unresolved friction point, and two or three priorities for team-owned huddles. Assign a follow-up owner for each priority. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately; if access is blocked, record the blocker for follow-up.
preparationChecklist: Before joining, bring one concrete example where AI changed your work, one friction point or challenge, and one idea for what comes next. Keep examples appropriate to share. No separate role-specific Week 9 preparation is needed.
facilitatorQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent, and what support or practice would help?
Which two or three priorities are most useful now?
Which All Topics huddle or custom huddle could help with each priority?
listenFor: Concrete examples of work changed, one useful habit to keep, and a specific friction point. Keep reflection conversational, not a scorecard. priorities grounded in team work and an owner or next step. Remind the group to share only information it is authorized to discuss.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If examples are vague, compare one task before and after and keep tool discussion anchored to the work. If the app, search, download or survey is inaccessible, capture the useful habit, friction point, next priority and follow-up owner manually; do not require Create your own huddle or Huddle in a Box to complete the conversation. A sanitized or clearly labeled synthetic task can demonstrate the reflection method, but is not personal impact evidence or a substitute survey response. Record the access gap and use the approved link/process later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which habit should the team keep, what evidence supports it, and what friction remains? Which two or three priorities should shape the next huddles?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next team-owned huddle, test one chosen habit on real work and decide what to keep, revise or stop. Agree the next topic and owner. Use the Frontier Accelerator topic library or Huddle in a Box if useful; otherwise plan manually. Use approved tools and permitted inputs only. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately, or record an access blocker.
bringBackEvidence: At the next huddle, share one brief, anonymized observation: what changed, what remains uncertain, and what to adjust next. Keep restricted details in approved systems. If untested, share the blocker and next check. Survey completion is not evidence of workflow benefit.

topicResources.description: Open Run a Huddle, choose the relevant view, then switch from Role Path to All Topics. Search and filter by Segment, Role, Focus Area, and AI Tool. For an uncovered team need, select Create your own huddle and download Huddle in a Box.

topicResources.description: Participant survey to complete at the close of the Week 9 transition huddle; allow about five minutes.

PLC-ENT-ATS-W09.roleTopicDescription: Reflect on the first eight weeks, name a useful habit to keep and a friction point to address, then agree on two or three team priorities and connect them to the next topic or a custom huddle. This transition is shared across all roles.
PLC-ENT-ATS-W09.wiifm: Team-owned priorities keep huddles useful as work changes, helping you retain valuable habits and address friction instead of continuing a fixed learning path by default.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion

activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.

activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about three minutes reconnecting to why the Huddle Motion matters to the work.

activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about ten minutes comparing experiences using examples the group may discuss.

3. Identify a habit worth repeating and a friction point or support need.

activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: AI in Action: choose the next team focus
activities.description: Choose a next work priority and an existing or custom huddle starting point, using tools and content permitted for the team.
activities.expectedOutput: An agreed next priority, a suitable huddle or draft starting point, and an owner; optional backlog ideas remain separate.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the ten-minute AI-in-Action segment to connect the reflection to work where a change would be useful.

activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear next-focus commitment and a participant-owned feedback opportunity, with any unfinished survey completed after the huddle.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Use the final five minutes to restate the useful habit, friction point, and chosen next focus.

activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.

activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activitySteps: 1. Spend about ten minutes comparing experiences using examples the group may discuss.

activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Account planning fails when it becomes an inventory. Focus on a short operating plan that helps you decide where attention goes this week.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritization requires saying no. AI can assemble customer, pipeline, renewal, whitespace, partner, and investment signals. You decide which account deserves action and why.
discussionQuestions: Which accounts get your attention by habit rather than evidence? Where is the account plan missing a decision? What signal would change your priority list?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prioritize account action for this week'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from account list discussion to one AE selecting a top account and naming the next action. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the account priority list', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Prioritization improves when account signals change where you spend attention, not when the list grows. Separate supported priorities from assumptions before choosing the next account action. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one territory or account list and one account where the next action is unclear. For the account-plan practice, bring its TPID, current account plan, and approved supporting evidence as user-provided inputs, with source, scope, and as-of date. A human verifies the records and decides.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account deserves attention that it is not getting? Which account gets attention mostly by habit? What evidence would change your top three?
How does another AE distinguish evidence-led priority from an account that gets attention by habit?
listenFor: Planning as annual documentation, prioritization by revenue alone, unclear next actions, missing role coverage, and customer priorities not connected to pipeline.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-account priority table: dated signal, customer priority, role gap, next action and AE judgment. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, use AI to build or refine one account priority view, then choose one next action you will actually take. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share one priority you checked and whether it clarified the next action. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on restoring trust in the pipeline signal before it becomes a forecast argument.
keyTalkingPoints: Bad data creates bad inspection. Stage, close date, next step, customer engagement, and partner attach should reflect reality. AI can flag issues; you verify and decide the correction.
discussionQuestions: Where does your pipeline data most often mislead you? Which field do you trust least? Which opportunity would you hesitate to defend in a review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Ask what the certified business data says'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the individual records the check surfaced to the aggregate gap they add up to, then decide which correction would change the forecast conversation. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Tell the applied fixes apart from the ones waiting on you', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Pipeline trust comes from checking material signals and routing corrections to the record owner. An AI explanation is a hypothesis, not a verified stage or forecast change. Treat the next use as a small test of better work; share the benefit or correction, not just the draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring the scope you normally inspect for pipeline reviews and one opportunity you suspect may be stale or misrepresented.
facilitatorQuestions: Which opportunity would you not want inspected right now? What field, date, or next step might be telling the wrong story? What correction would change the forecast conversation?
What recurring inspection check has a peer used to catch a misleading date or next step before the review?
listenFor: Manual reconciliation, stale dates, close-date optimism, missing customer engagement, and records corrected only right before reviews.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or approved context is unavailable, use a sanitized supplied example or a clearly labeled synthetic case. On paper, complete one pipeline record check: field/date, definition, supporting evidence, discrepancy, correction owner and verification gap. Mark evidence, assumptions and unknowns; the exercise does not establish live pipeline status or authorize a correction. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient. Any later AI run must use project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot and approved supplied inputs.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did inspection reveal about the pipeline or forecast story, and which correction or caveat changes the decision?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, run one pipeline signal-quality check and correct or flag one material issue. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share the type of issue verified, corrected or routed and whether it reduced a misleading pipeline signal. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Create the forecast follow-through plan
activities.description: Turn the forecast inspection into the specific actions and dates that change the position before the next review.
activities.prompt:
Turn the forecast narrative into a follow-through plan. For each at-risk commit and gap driver, define the action that would change it, the owner, the date it must move by, and the evidence you will check. Set the rhythm you will use to inspect it before the next forecast call. Work from the material I have supplied rather than looking it up, and where a piece of it is missing, name the gap instead of filling it.

USPSI project practice: Use only minimum necessary supplied inputs approved for this Copilot use, account scope and audience; sanitize sensitive internal, customer, commercial or personal content before entry and withhold classified or restricted material unless explicitly permitted. Include source and as-of date. No CRM/MSX, mailbox, meeting or live-system connector access, scheduled checks, persistent memory or writes are assumed. Return draft text/tables; native artifacts are not assumed. Cite evidence; mark stale, missing or conflicting facts unknown. Label unconfirmed owners, dates, eligibility and conclusions as proposals or questions. Authorized humans retain procurement/policy judgments, commercial/investment approvals, commitments, implementation and publication. If Copilot or sharing is not permitted, use approved evidence manually or a fictional example; do not bypass restrictions.
activities.expectedOutput: A forecast follow-through plan with actions, owners, dates, evidence checks, and an inspection rhythm.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE owns the dates in this plan and confirms them with the people named before it is shared. A follow-through plan built on dates nobody has agreed to reads as commitment and behaves as fiction.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. The reviewed forecast narrative; the at-risk commits and their owners; the date of your next inspection.
activities.whyThisMatters: Confirmed actions and evidence checks make the next forecast inspection useful.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A forecast narrative explains what changed, what is at risk, and what decision is needed. Focus on building that story from evidence.
keyTalkingPoints: The number alone does not create confidence. Movement, risk, timing, and inspection questions need to be visible. AI can draft the story, but you own the commitment and caveats.
discussionQuestions: What changed since the last review? Which commit has the weakest evidence? What question from your manager would be hardest to answer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Analyze certified forecast movement'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from report output to the narrative the AE would actually use in a forecast review. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the forecast narrative', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: A useful forecast narrative exposes the evidence, uncertainty and decision behind the number. Carry unresolved risks into inspection rather than smoothing them out. Agree where this fits in recurring work and how a small, safe signal will help the team learn together.
preparationChecklist: Bring the current forecast scope and the report or meeting notes you use for weekly inspection.
facilitatorQuestions: What changed since last week? Which commit carries the most risk? What would your manager ask that the current narrative cannot answer?
How would another AE challenge your highest-risk commit using dated evidence rather than confidence?
listenFor: Forecast narrative built from memory, risk without evidence, unclear inspection questions, and confusion between confidence and wishful thinking.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one forecast movement brief: prior/current period, changed fact, risk, assumption, evidence needed and inspection question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did inspection reveal about the pipeline or forecast story, and which correction or caveat changes the decision?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, draft one forecast narrative for your scope and use it in your next inspection or manager discussion. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share one forecast caveat changed by human review and whether it improved the discussion; omit customer metrics and the full forecast. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Decide whether the satisfaction signal changes your ask
activities.description: Test the ask you were planning to make against the customer's current satisfaction and support experience, and change it if the evidence says you should.
activities.prompt:
Compare my intended customer ask with the satisfaction/support evidence I supply. Identify supported changes and gaps; do not infer health from missing data or guess metric meanings. Distinguish unresolved issues from those already resolved. Recommend proceeding, acknowledging an issue first or delaying the ask, with supporting evidence and one question to settle the main uncertainty. Do not quote internal metrics or identifiable verbatims in customer-facing wording. The AE decides timing and disclosure.

USPSI project practice: Use only minimum necessary supplied inputs approved for this Copilot use, account scope and audience; sanitize sensitive internal, customer, commercial or personal content before entry and withhold classified or restricted material unless explicitly permitted. Include source and as-of date. No CRM/MSX, mailbox, meeting or live-system connector access, scheduled checks, persistent memory or writes are assumed. Return draft text/tables; native artifacts are not assumed. Cite evidence; mark stale, missing or conflicting facts unknown. Label unconfirmed owners, dates, eligibility and conclusions as proposals or questions. Authorized humans retain procurement/policy judgments, commercial/investment approvals, commitments, implementation and publication. If Copilot or sharing is not permitted, use approved evidence manually or a fictional example; do not bypass restrictions.
activities.expectedOutput: A judgment on whether the intended ask is well timed, the issues a customer could raise that you are not ready for, and what to resolve or acknowledge before making the ask.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether to proceed with the ask. A written review may highlight a poorly timed ask, but only the AE knows what the relationship can carry and what has already been discussed offline.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Supplied sanitized satisfaction/support excerpts with metric definitions, source dates and account scope; intended ask, meeting date and known resolved issues.
activitySteps: 1. Write down the ask you intend to make before you run anything. The point is to test it, not to discover it.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt with that ask included.
4. Decide whether to proceed with the ask, soften it, or resolve something first.
5. Prepare an answer for anything the customer could reasonably raise.
6. Never quote the internal satisfaction data in the meeting. It shapes your preparation and stays out of the room.

If Copilot is unavailable or not permitted, complete the same bounded review manually from approved sanitized evidence or a fictional example; never bypass restrictions. Sending, publication, implementation or record updates are separate authorized human actions.
activities.whyThisMatters: Preparation usually fails at the ask, not the agenda. Walking a growth ask into a customer whose support experience is deteriorating is how a relationship gets set back a quarter.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer conversations are where decisions move. Focus on preparing the position, evidence, objections, and ask before the meeting starts.
keyTalkingPoints: A brief is not a recap. It should state the intended outcome, customer context, evidence, open questions, likely objections, and the ask. You validate tone and relationship nuance.
discussionQuestions: What do you often walk into a meeting still not knowing? What would change if the ask were explicit before the meeting? Which claim would need validation before customer use?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the account and conversation brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from preparation concept to one live meeting brief and the ask the AE will use. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the executive conversation plan', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Customer preparation is useful when grounded claims and a primary or fallback ask help the customer decide. Rehearsal does not replace judgment about what to say or promise. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming customer meeting, the desired decision, and any approved source materials you want to use.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the meeting move? What claim must be validated? What objection is likely but uncomfortable to prepare for?
What did a peer change after the executive questioned the value claim or meeting ask?
listenFor: Recaps instead of positions, meetings with no intended outcome, generic value language, unsupported claims, and missing fallback asks.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one executive meeting brief: intended decision, supported value claim, caveat, likely objection, primary ask and fallback. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence would make this customer conversation credible, and what decision or question still belongs to a person?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, prepare one customer conversation brief and validate the claims before use. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized claim validated or removed, or an ask sharpened, and whether preparation made the conversation more useful; a meeting result is optional. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Strategic deals stall when the next decision, blocker, or owner is unnamed. Focus on making the deal inspectable.
keyTalkingPoints: A close date is not a plan. Exit criteria, approvals, commercial dependencies, stakeholder coverage, and customer actions determine whether the deal can move. AI can organize the deal picture; you route decisions to the right owners.
discussionQuestions: What is your deal really waiting on? Which approval, customer action, or role gap is not yet explicit? What should not be decided by AI?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect deal context before customer action'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from deal summary to the next decision and owner map. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the deal inspection', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Deal inspection should expose the next decision and its accountable owner, not merely produce a blocker list. A routed ask is not accepted or approved work. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one live opportunity, current stage, and a seller-validated inspection naming the next customer decision, exit criteria, blockers, known owners and agreed or unconfirmed dates. If relevant and policy permits, bring approved agreement or enrollment details as a sanitized excerpt with its source and as-of date. Treat this as context only; it supplements the seller-validated inspection and does not establish the customer decision path or team ownership.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next decision, not the next task? Which blocker has no owner? Which commercial, technical, or partner decision needs another role?
How does another AE secure a decision owner without taking over CE, technical or partner authority?
listenFor: Close date as proxy for plan, approval paths discovered late, role gaps, unsupported deal assumptions, and AI outputs that overstep CE or SME authority.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one deal decision map: next customer decision, commercial/technical/partner blocker, evidence gap, accountable role and checkpoint. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal assumption changed when you inspected the evidence, and who owns the next decision or approval?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, inspect one strategic deal and route at least one blocker or decision to the right owner. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized decision routed to its owner and whether it clarified the next step; pending acceptance is valid. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Test renewal risk against how the customer actually feels
activities.description: Put the customer's satisfaction signal next to your own renewal risk read, and investigate every account where the two disagree.
activities.prompt:
Compare the supplied renewal risk ratings with sanitized satisfaction/support evidence. Use named metrics only with supplied definitions, scales, periods and source dates; prefer aggregate themes over identifiable verbatims. Missing data is unknown, not healthy. Identify disagreements, alternative commercial explanations and evidence needed to resolve them. Satisfaction alone does not establish renewal intent.

USPSI project practice: Use only minimum necessary supplied inputs approved for this Copilot use, account scope and audience; sanitize sensitive internal, customer, commercial or personal content before entry and withhold classified or restricted material unless explicitly permitted. Label unconfirmed owners, dates, eligibility and conclusions as proposals or questions. Authorized humans retain procurement/policy judgments, commercial/investment approvals, commitments, implementation and publication. If Copilot or sharing is not permitted, use approved evidence manually or a fictional example; do not bypass restrictions.
activities.expectedOutput: A satisfaction picture per renewing account ordered by deterioration, set against your own risk ratings, and the shortlist where the two disagree.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE owns the renewal risk call. Satisfaction is one input, not a verdict, and a satisfied customer can still leave for commercial reasons no CX metric will show.

Supplied renewal portfolio/risk ratings, sanitized satisfaction/support excerpts, metric definitions and periods, known commercial drivers and resolved issues; only necessary identifiers.

2. Compare the supplied approved evidence with your current human-assessed risk ratings; identify satisfaction-record gaps rather than assuming access.
3. Put any evidence-based ordering next to your own ratings and focus on disagreements.
4. For each disagreement, decide which evidence is reliable and what additional source would settle it.
5. Raise any renewal you downgrade with the account team before it appears in a review.
6. Bring the accounts where evidence and your judgment disagree to the huddle. Those are the ones worth the room's time.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Renewal risk is usually visible before the renewal conversation. Focus on finding it while there is still time to act.
keyTalkingPoints: Renewal health depends on value evidence, usage or consumption signals, relationship recency, commercial readiness, and expansion logic. AI can surface patterns; you validate intent and next action.
discussionQuestions: Which upcoming renewal has the weakest value evidence? What expansion hypothesis is already visible? Where do you need CSAM, CSA, CE, or SSP input?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Assess renewal risk and expansion readiness'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from renewal principles to one account and the action that changes risk this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the renewal assessment', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Renewal and expansion choices depend on evidenced value, risk and customer readiness. Available headroom is a hypothesis, not a customer commitment. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account renewing in the next planning window and the evidence you currently use to judge risk.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the largest renewal risk? What value evidence would the customer recognize? Which expansion signal is supported by usage, consumption, or customer priority?
What early evidence has a peer used to separate renewal risk from a supported expansion signal?
listenFor: Renewals treated as admin, value evidence built too late, expansion detached from customer outcomes, and unclear CSAM/CSA/CE ownership.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one renewal-risk card: agreement event, customer value evidence, risk, supported expansion hypothesis, role owner and next check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence changes the renewal or expansion approach, and which customer or owner decision must follow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, assess one upcoming renewal and take one action that reduces risk or strengthens value evidence. Verify evidence; commercial terms, forecast commitment and approval stay with accountable owners. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized renewal assumption checked and whether it changed the next customer or owner action. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

PLC-USPSI-AE-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on evidence from the guided Role Path and choose the team's next workflow priorities, using relevant existing topics or a custom huddle.
PLC-USPSI-AE-W09.whyItMatters: Teams sustain change when they use evidence from practice to set their next learning priorities rather than continuing a fixed path by default.
PLC-USPSI-AE-W09.desiredOutcome: Sustain a team-owned cycle of workflow improvement, using shared experience to choose relevant huddles, test changes in real work, and revisit priorities as evidence develops.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about three minutes reconnecting to why the Huddle Motion matters to the work.
2. Recognize the shift from guided Weeks 1-8 to team-owned learning, not the end of the motion.

3. Preview the shared transition: reflect on experience, choose the next focus, and close with participant feedback. These are coordinated session components, not four alternative practices to complete.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about ten minutes comparing experiences using examples the group may discuss.
2. Explain what changed in the workflow or why a practice did not help yet; no success story is required.
3. Identify a habit worth repeating and a friction point or support need.
4. Use these observations to inform the next-focus discussion, without ranking participants.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: AI in Action: choose the next team focus
activities.description: Choose a next work priority and an existing or custom huddle starting point, using tools and content permitted for the team.
activities.expectedOutput: An agreed next priority, a suitable huddle or draft starting point, and an owner; optional backlog ideas remain separate.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the ten-minute AI-in-Action segment to connect the reflection to work where a change would be useful.
2. Choose the priority to try first; keep up to two other ideas as an optional backlog rather than simultaneous commitments.

3. In All Topics, compare relevant outcomes and activities, filtering by Segment, Role, Focus Area, and tools permitted for the team and project. Select one Featured practice for the next ordinary huddle; Extended practices remain optional.
4. If no topic fits, use Huddle in a Box to outline a draft for later review, not to create or publish a finished huddle in this session.
5. Confirm an owner and a practical next step. Without app access, record the priority and locate the content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear next-focus commitment and a participant-owned feedback opportunity, with any unfinished survey completed after the huddle.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Use the final five minutes to restate the useful habit, friction point, and chosen next focus.
2. Confirm who will take the next step and when the team will revisit what it learned.
3. Open the Team Member Impact Survey and let participants complete their own responses. If time or access is insufficient, finish after the huddle rather than extending the live session.
4. Continue the team-owned motion; this transition is not a final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided activation to team-owned practice. The team has completed the eight-week activation journey. Use this huddle to recognize what changed, address friction, and choose what to focus on next.
keyTalkingPoints: This is the same participant experience for every role. Overview: 3 minutes - reconnect to the motion and the transition to team ownership. Share Your Experience: 10 minutes - reflect on useful changes, friction, and support needs. AI-in-Action: 10 minutes - choose the next team priority and a relevant existing or custom huddle starting point. Closing & Next Steps: 5 minutes - confirm the owner and next action, then allow participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey.
discussionQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent?
Which two or three team priorities would be most useful next?
suggestedTransitions: Use the coordinated Transition agenda: Overview, Share Your Experience, AI-in-Action, and Closing & Next Steps. Reflect on real work, agree the next focus and owner, and use the final five minutes for participant-owned survey completion. Review All Topics or a custom-huddle idea only if time and access permit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close the guided path by naming one useful habit, one unresolved friction point, and two or three priorities for team-owned huddles. Assign a follow-up owner for each priority. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately; if access is blocked, record the blocker for follow-up.
preparationChecklist: Before joining, bring one concrete example where AI changed your work, one friction point or challenge, and one idea for what comes next. Keep examples appropriate to share. No separate role-specific Week 9 preparation is needed.
facilitatorQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent, and what support or practice would help?
Which two or three priorities are most useful now?
Which All Topics huddle or custom huddle could help with each priority?
listenFor: Concrete examples of work changed, one useful habit to keep, and a specific friction point. Keep reflection conversational, not a scorecard. priorities grounded in team work and an owner or next step. Remind the group to share only information it is authorized to discuss.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If examples are vague, compare one task before and after and keep tool discussion anchored to the work. If the app, search, download or survey is inaccessible, capture the useful habit, friction point, next priority and follow-up owner manually; do not require Create your own huddle or Huddle in a Box to complete the conversation. A sanitized or clearly labeled synthetic task can demonstrate the reflection method, but is not personal impact evidence or a substitute survey response. Record the access gap and use the approved link/process later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which habit should the team keep, what evidence supports it, and what friction remains? Which two or three priorities should shape the next huddles?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next team-owned huddle, test one chosen habit on real work and decide what to keep, revise or stop. Agree the next topic and owner. Use the Frontier Accelerator topic library or Huddle in a Box if useful; otherwise plan manually. Use approved tools and permitted inputs only. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately, or record an access blocker.
bringBackEvidence: At the next huddle, share one brief, anonymized observation: what changed, what remains uncertain, and what to adjust next. Keep restricted details in approved systems. If untested, share the blocker and next check. Survey completion is not evidence of workflow benefit.

PLC-USPSI-ATS-W01.todayObjective: Explore how peer-led huddles connect business outcomes, recurring workflows, and responsible AI experimentation, including what to try and share between sessions.
PLC-USPSI-ATS-W01.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.
PLC-USPSI-ATS-W01.desiredOutcome: Participate confidently in the motion, starting with a meaningful workflow and testing improvements in real work while retaining human judgment and learning from evidence.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

activities.name: Build the account intelligence brief
activities.description: Combine work and public context into a meeting-prep brief. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt:
Act as my account intelligence analyst for the account. Build a meeting prep brief that summarizes business priorities, current technical strategy, stakeholder context, relevant KPIs, AI and cloud workload signals, open risks, recent customer commitments, and the top actions I should consider. Work only from approved records and excerpts I provide, with source, scope, and as-of date; identify missing records and leave those points open rather than inferring. Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and flag missing context. Mark every section that rests only on my own view of the account, and list the specific questions my v-team counterparts would need to answer to close those gaps.

USPSI project practice: Use only minimum necessary supplied inputs approved for this Copilot use, account scope and audience; sanitize sensitive internal, customer, commercial or personal content before entry and withhold classified or restricted material unless explicitly permitted. Include source and as-of date. No CRM/MSX, mailbox, meeting or live-system connector access, scheduled checks, persistent memory or writes are assumed. Return draft text/tables; native artifacts are not assumed. Cite evidence; mark stale, missing or conflicting facts unknown. Label unconfirmed owners, dates, eligibility and conclusions as proposals or questions. Authorized humans retain procurement/policy judgments, commercial/investment approvals, commitments, implementation and publication. If Copilot or sharing is not permitted, use approved evidence manually or a fictional example; do not bypass restrictions.
activities.expectedOutput: Account intelligence and meeting-prep brief with risks, priorities, and actions, plus a short list of questions to put to the v-team where the brief rests on one person's view.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which context is current enough to rely on. A brief assembled from work and public sources mixes material of different ages, and the stakeholder position that changed most recently is the one that matters most. The ATS also decides where one perspective is not enough, because a brief built from one person's sources can read as complete while missing what a teammate already knows.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. User-provided approved account records and excerpts, with source, scope, and as-of date; the minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or excerpts you want reflected; and relevant information already shared by v-team counterparts. Do not include restricted customer or personal data unless policy permits. A human verifies every source record and claim, makes all decisions, and performs any authorized updates; Microsoft 365 Copilot does not make record changes.
activities.whyThisMatters: Account intelligence is useful when it changes the next technical decision, not when it creates a longer dossier.

activities.name: Draft an intelligence-hub structure for human-maintained contributions
activities.description: Turn account intelligence into something the whole v-team feeds, so the picture reflects what each member can see rather than what one person could reach.
activities.prompt:
Using only the approved account excerpts and contributor roles I supply, draft a text-only intelligence-hub structure: priorities, opportunity context, stakeholders, estate, interactions and risks. Leave unsupplied contributor sections visibly empty. For supplied contributions record role, source, account scope and date. Keep conflicts separate with a resolution question. Draft contribution requests and a refresh checklist. Do not obtain contributions, retain memory, create a shared hub or publish. The ATS separately reviews contributions and maintains an authorized hub.

USPSI project practice: Use only minimum necessary supplied inputs approved for this Copilot use, account scope and audience; sanitize sensitive internal, customer, commercial or personal content before entry and withhold classified or restricted material unless explicitly permitted. Include source and as-of date. No CRM/MSX, mailbox, meeting or live-system connector access, scheduled checks, persistent memory or writes are assumed. Return draft text/tables; native artifacts are not assumed. Cite evidence; mark stale, missing or conflicting facts unknown. Label unconfirmed owners, dates, eligibility and conclusions as proposals or questions. Authorized humans retain procurement/policy judgments, commercial/investment approvals, commitments, implementation and publication. If Copilot or sharing is not permitted, use approved evidence manually or a fictional example; do not bypass restrictions.
activities.expectedOutput: Text-only structure with supplied sourced contributions, empty sections, conflicts, draft requests and human refresh checklist; no shared hub created.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS reviews the hub for accuracy before sharing with the v-team, and reviews each contribution before it reaches the shared hub rather than only at first build, confirming that no customer-confidential material sits where it should not. Where two contributors describe the same stakeholder or risk differently, the hub keeps both accounts with their sources and dates, and the ATS records which one the account plan proceeds on and why, or marks it unresolved. A difference between two contributors can be two accurate observations from different vantage points, and collapsing it early loses the signal.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Supplied sanitized account excerpts, contributor roles, intended audience and permitted contributions already received with sources/dates; human-maintained location.
activitySteps: 1. List the approved account-planning records available to provide, and identify missing records. For CRM/MSX-derived information, provide only the minimum necessary approved fields or excerpts, with source, scope, and as-of/freshness date.
2. List the v-team members who can see what you cannot, and what each of them holds.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Review the first hub build against what you already know about the account.
5. Check that nothing customer-confidential sits where the wider v-team should not see it, then send the contribution requests and give people a deadline they can meet.
6. As contributions come back, review each one before it reaches the shared hub and hold anything that should not sit there.
7. Add the approved contributions with their contributor, source and date, and chase the sections still empty.
8. Set the refresh cadence and agree with the v-team who reads the change summary.

If Copilot is unavailable or not permitted, complete the same bounded review manually from approved sanitized evidence or a fictional example; never bypass restrictions. Sending, publication, implementation or record updates are separate authorized human actions.
activities.whyThisMatters: An account picture assembled by one person is bounded by the records and context that person can provide. The hub's value is that the gaps stay visible until somebody who can see them fills them in.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on building an account intelligence and meeting-preparation brief.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is an account intelligence brief with technical risks, workload signals, stakeholder context, and next actions. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Which account are you least confident you could brief someone on right now?
Where does your current account picture come from, and how old is it?
Which part of your account picture exists only in a teammate's head?
What technical signal would change your priorities this week if you knew it today?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the account intelligence brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the assembled account picture to the single signal that should change this week's priorities. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Build a standing account intelligence hub the v-team contributes to', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Account intelligence improves technical priorities when missing context is reconciled with the v-team. The useful change is a decision informed by their answer, not a longer brief. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one account, its approved current plan or context, dated technical signals and the unresolved account question. Use approved user-supplied inputs with source, scope and date; review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: What is in your account brief that you could not source if challenged?
Which signal in the brief actually changes what you do next week?
What is missing that you only notice once it is written down?
What source-checking habit has a peer used when a polished brief hid stale stakeholder context?
listenFor: Briefs assembled from memory rather than systems, KPI figures quoted without their definition or date, technical risks with no named owner, and stakeholder context that is a year old. Also note the brief becoming an end in itself rather than driving a decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one account-intelligence brief: source/date, customer priority, stakeholder position, KPI definition, technical risk and v-team validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What intelligence gap changed the technical priority after v-team review, and which assumption remains unsupported?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, build an account intelligence brief for one account, ask one v-team counterpart the question your own sources could not answer, and put what they send back into the brief. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a safe description of the intelligence gap, what the counterpart could confirm, and whether it changed the technical priority. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

Prepare a CxO technical briefing for the account on the topic. Include customer outcomes, architecture direction, risks, proof points, executive talking points, likely questions, and the technical ask. State what this executive is personally backing if they say yes, and what it costs them if it goes wrong; where you have no source for that, say so and name who could tell me rather than inferring it. Present the realistic options side by side with their tradeoffs rather than one recommended path, and name the decision they are being asked to make.
