facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Bring one project whose direction is clear enough to discuss with PSA. The PTS task is not to solve the architecture in the huddle; it is to define why the work exists, what outcome and evidence are needed, where execution authority sits and when the scoped involvement ends. PSA must review feasibility and accept its own execution scope. The partner must confirm its delivery and post-activation responsibilities. AI can draft a scope contract or reveal an ownership gap, but it cannot allocate an architect, accept a handoff or approve release. Use the live practice to resolve one ambiguity.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Separate technical intent from implementation method. PTS supplies strategic outcomes and guardrails; PSA determines scoped CSA-specific architecture and execution.
2. Name deliverables, evidence gates, escalation triggers and exit criteria. A list of activities without an exit can turn scoped assistance into assumed ongoing operation.
3. Mark all proposed ownership and acceptance explicitly. Handoff readiness is a draft review judgment, not proof that PSA has capacity or the partner has accepted delivery obligations.
discussionQuestions: What must PSA understand about the technical intent without being told how to implement it?
Which decision must return to PTS because it changes scope or cross-solution direction?
What would show that the scoped work has ended and partner ownership is in place?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft a PTS-to-PSA scope contract'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use one minute to choose the handoff ambiguity, five minutes for one Featured scope, escalation or ownership practice, and two minutes to challenge the exit. Keep architecture design outside this segment. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Scope regional activation without rebuilding the global solution', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by reading the acceptance question and exit criterion aloud. Ensure everyone can distinguish PTS strategy ownership, PSA execution ownership and partner delivery/operation ownership. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one approved technical-plan decision, project brief, known constraints and any dated PSA intake or partner ownership notes. Include the intended deliverable and evidence gate if they exist. Supply approved extracts only; no assumed PMX connector, automated intake or task assignment. Decide whether the biggest gap is scope, escalation or ownership.
facilitatorQuestions: Is this a PTS guardrail or an architectural instruction PSA should own?
Can the exit criterion be checked from evidence rather than sentiment?
Which owner or acceptance is still proposed rather than confirmed?
listenFor: PSA being treated as indefinite delivery capacity, partner operations assigned to Microsoft, and acceptance inferred because a name appears in a draft. Ask participants to make the stop or escalation boundary as concrete as the deliverable.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Write one handoff row manually: technical intent, expected evidence, in/out scope, proposed owner, escalation trigger and exit. Leave acceptance unconfirmed. If strategic intent itself is unclear, return to the technical-plan decision rather than fabricate intake detail. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which phrase in the original handoff could have made scoped technical help look like an open-ended delivery commitment?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, review one handoff boundary with the relevant PSA or partner owner through the normal human process. Record the PTS-approved strategic guardrail, confirmed versus unconfirmed acceptance and any scope change required; do not send or assign automatically. If input or access is missing, use a permitted sanitized example or document the verification gap; do not infer approval, agreement or status.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized scope phrase or exit criterion clarified and whether it reduced ambiguity between PTS, PSA and partner ownership. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Audit milestone evidence without inventing a health score
activities.description: An evidence ledger exposes genuine progression without manufacturing precision or confusing activity with an achieved outcome.
activities.prompt: If one essential detail is missing, ask one concise question. Inspect at most three milestones for the partner project using only my approved plan row, original evidence gates and dated progress packet. First extract what each gate requires; then assess whether the supplied evidence supports, partially supports, contradicts or leaves it unknown. Keep activity completion separate from outcome proof and distinguish partner-provided evidence from Microsoft-side status. Return a progression ledger with source/date, evidence judgment, contradiction or gap, and the next human question. Do not invent traffic-light thresholds, completion percentages or missing results. I, the PTS, will validate the judgment and its roadmap implication. Stop before declaring a gate met if required evidence is absent or contradictory. No status writeback, alerts, task assignments or approvals.
activities.expectedOutput: Milestone progression ledger with supported/partial/contradicted/unknown judgments, source references and one prioritized review question.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates the evidence judgment and its strategic implication, not execution completion on behalf of PSA. Stop before declaring a gate met when required evidence is missing or contradictory.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/project; up to three milestones; original approved evidence gates; dated progress notes/exports; available partner evidence; previous decision record where available.
activitySteps: 1. Supply one project and no more than three milestones with original evidence gates.
2. Add approved dated progress evidence and label source origin.
3. Trace the most consequential judgment back to the gate and source.
4. Retain the PTS-reviewed ledger and one unresolved human evidence question.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: An evidence ledger exposes genuine progression without manufacturing precision or confusing activity with an achieved outcome.

activitySteps: 1. Select one blocked milestone and provide the approved evidence/constraint packet.
2. Ask Cowork to compare no more than three supported intervention responses.
3. Inspect decision rights and the assumption most likely to overturn the recommendation.
4. Record a PTS intervention or hold with a human validation owner and review trigger.

activities.description: A transparent rebaseline preserves learning and accountability while allowing the multi-horizon technical plan to respond to real evidence.
activities.prompt: If one essential detail is missing, ask one concise question. Compare the approved baseline and proposed revision for the partner project using only the dated change evidence and horizon definitions I supply. Produce a before-and-after plan row showing original outcome/gate, changed assumption, source of change, proposed horizon or scope, downstream dependency effects and decision still required. Separate a justified rebaseline from moving a date to conceal an unresolved blocker. Do not infer stakeholder acceptance, create dates or change the system of record. activitySteps: 1. Supply one baseline row, a proposed revision and dated change evidence.
2. Add existing horizon definitions and relevant downstream dependencies.
3. Review the before-and-after rationale for hidden blockers or invented acceptance.
4. Keep a PTS rebaseline decision draft that preserves the original row and remaining review requirements.

activities.description: A bounded snapshot variant detects regional divergence without assuming continuous access or turning strategic governance into automated operational monitoring.
activities.prompt: If one essential detail is missing, ask one concise question. Compare the two dated, user-supplied snapshots for the partner solution in the region against the approved global technical guardrails. activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates materiality against global intent. Stop when snapshots are not comparable or supporting evidence is absent; do not interpret missing rows as completed or cancelled work.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/solution and one region; two dated approved status exports; global technical guardrails; field-mapping notes if needed. User supplies all material; no live connector or scheduled monitor.
activitySteps: 1. Supply two comparable approved snapshots for one solution and one region.
2. Add the global guardrails and known field-name changes.
3. Inspect the drift log for false differences caused by missing rows or renamed fields.
4. Retain one PTS-validated exception or a no-material-change conclusion with evidence.

activities.name: Monitor one approved technical-plan dependency
activities.description: Watch an approved plan dependency on a human-approved cadence and report only evidence changes for PTS review.
activities.prompt: Produce an unactivated read-only proposal, not a running monitor. Use authorized dated snapshots, a user-maintained baseline and previous report supplied for this review; do not retrieve unsupplied records, create automation, retain agent memory or notify anyone. Missing history is baseline-only or comparison unavailable, not no change. Record scope, source permission, owner, cadence, recipients, review/expiry and supplied approved change criteria without inventing values. Future monitoring requires separate explicit approval and verified access/state capabilities. If one essential detail is missing, ask one concise question. Compare supplied snapshots for the technical plan dependency on the approved cadence using the approved evidence locations, the dated baseline, and the named review owner. For a baseline-only review, record the dated baseline and access state. For a comparison review, compare the supplied baseline and user-maintained previous report. Return change-only findings for new, changed, missing, or inaccessible evidence, with dates and possible plan impact. Do not infer completion, change the plan, send commitments, or assign work. the named review owner decides whether to intervene, rebaseline, or hold.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated baseline-only or change-only supplied-evidence review draft with source/history/access gaps and an unactivated proposal for the named reviewer; zero scheduled jobs or notifications.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The named owner reviews every report; PTS alone decides whether the technical plan changes.
activities.requiredContext: An approved dependency, human-approved cadence, approved evidence locations, dated baseline, and named review owner. Provide authorized dated snapshots and user-maintained baseline/prior report if available. Source permissions, scope, cadence, recipients, review/expiry and automation approval are explicit proposed fields; missing inputs remain gaps and no tool access/state retention is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm one bounded dependency/action and supply authorized dated snapshots; clearly labeled synthetic evidence is rehearsal-only.
2. Check the user-maintained baseline/prior report, comparable definitions and named reviewer; leave missing history, permission or criteria explicit.
3. Compare supplied evidence manually or with one already authorized tool; no schedule, live retrieval or persistent agent memory.
4. Produce a dated baseline-only/comparison draft and unactivated proposal with source, owner, cadence, recipients, expiry and approval fields.
5. Apply the unchanged HumanCheckpoint before interpretation/action; future automation, notifications and system changes require separate explicit authorization.

Fallback: Scout is optional and preview/prerelease. Compare supplied dated snapshots manually and retain the baseline/report yourself; no connector, persistent agent memory, scheduled job or notification permission is assumed.
activities.whyThisMatters: Persistent monitoring catches meaningful dependency movement without replacing the plan owner's judgment.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Select one project in the partner technical plan and compare its current evidence with the outcome and exit criteria already agreed. Do not ask AI to review everything or generate an overall partner health score. PTS governs cross-solution direction and the implications for the roadmap; PSA and project owners act on scoped execution issues, and the partner remains responsible for delivery and operation. Today's useful result may be confirmation that the milestone is supported, a targeted evidence request or a deliberate rebaseline. It is not a new promise about dates or resources.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Compare evidence against the original outcome gate, not the confidence of the latest status note. Keep source dates, contradictions and missing partner-side evidence visible.

2. Choose interventions by decision ownership. PTS changes direction or sequencing; PSA/project owners address execution within scope. Do not convert a governance review into automated task assignment.
3. Rebaseline only when a human decision changes the plan. Preserve the original assumption, the new evidence and the rationale so future reviews can see why the plan moved.
discussionQuestions: Which milestone appears complete because activity happened rather than because its evidence gate was met?
What is the smallest PTS intervention that could change the plan's trajectory?
When is a rebaseline honest governance, and when would it hide an unresolved dependency?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Audit milestone evidence without inventing a health score'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use one minute to select the milestone decision, five minutes for one Featured ledger, intervention or rebaseline practice, and two minutes to audit the critical evidence reference. Extended snapshot comparison is optional follow-on work. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Choose a strategic intervention rather than a task list', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Ask participants to state the evidence judgment, the PTS decision and who owns any subsequent execution action. Close with a specific review trigger instead of an open-ended request to monitor progress. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one project's approved plan row or scope contract, the previous review snapshot, current approved progress notes and the defined outcome/exit evidence. Include human-supplied PMX or other status exports only if approved and dated. Keep the review bounded to at most three milestones and one project.
facilitatorQuestions: What changed since the previous review, and which source proves it?
Is this an execution issue or a PTS direction/sequence decision?
What would you need before accepting the proposed revised milestone?
listenFor: Completed meetings or documents being used as proof of an outcome, missing evidence treated as failure, and revised dates accepted without human ownership. Coach participants to preserve uncertainty and identify the precise decision rather than announce a red status.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Manually compare one milestone's original evidence gate with the latest approved evidence. Mark supported, partial, contradicted or unknown and write one review question. If no prior snapshot exists, establish a dated baseline rather than fabricate a change history. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the evidence inspection change that a conventional status update would have missed?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, validate one progression judgment or proposed intervention with the relevant human owner. Record the PTS decision, the unchanged execution boundary and the evidence/date that will trigger reconsideration; make no automatic status updates or assignments. If input or access is missing, use a permitted sanitized example or document the verification gap; do not infer approval, agreement or status.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized progression claim checked and whether evidence changed intervention rather than just status. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Take one offering with useful technical learning, whether it succeeded fully, partially or exposed a limit. This week is not a graduation or a claim that the partner is ready to scale everywhere. It asks what can responsibly be reused, what evidence supports that reuse and what should change in the technical roadmap. PTS validates cross-solution learning and reuse direction. PSA contributes architecture and execution evidence. The partner leads delivery and post-activation operation. AI can assemble a package or compare lessons, but permission, accuracy, reuse decisions and any publication remain human responsibilities.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Separate reusable architecture decisions, bounded accelerators and context-specific implementation details. Keep rights, provenance, known limitations and support ownership attached to the artifact.
2. A successful activation or early win is not universal validation. Show the conditions under which it was observed and the evidence still missing for wider use.

3. Close the learning loop deliberately: retain, revise or retire one technical assumption and connect that judgment to the next roadmap review. Do not automatically publish proof points, update systems or transfer partner operation to Microsoft.
discussionQuestions: Which part of this offering would we reuse, and what context must travel with it?
What did the project teach us that should change a roadmap assumption?
Who owns delivery and operation after the scoped technical work ends?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Package one offering's reusable technical core'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Give one minute to choose the scale decision, five minutes for one Featured reuse, learning or ownership practice, and two minutes to check the evidence/permission boundary. The Extended variant is optional, not an additional live requirement. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test a reusable asset in one new context before scaling', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close with one reusable insight and its limit, one PTS roadmap implication and the human owner of the next validation. Do not frame the package as published, approved or operationally handed over. Treat the next use as a small test of better work; share the benefit or correction, not just the draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one offering's approved architecture/decision summary, validation or activation evidence, permission and asset-ownership notes, and one relevant technical-plan assumption. Include a human-supplied partner operating-owner statement where available. Remove customer identifiers and reuse-restricted content before the huddle. A partial outcome with clear limits is a valid case.
facilitatorQuestions: Which claimed reusable element has evidence and permission behind it?
What would fail if this artifact were applied in a different context?
Is the proposed next step PTS roadmap governance or partner delivery/operation?
listenFor: One early win being generalized to every partner context, reusable assets lacking rights or support owners, and an exit statement that assumes the partner has accepted operation. Encourage a bounded hold when the evidence or permission does not support scale.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Create a manual reuse card: artifact, original context, evidence, reusable boundary, known limit, rights/owner and next validation. If permission is absent, describe only the type of learning and hold the underlying material from reuse or publication. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What limitation would you now insist travels with an early win or reusable asset?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, validate one reuse boundary, roadmap-learning change or partner operating-owner gap with the appropriate human owner. Record the PTS retain/revise/hold decision and the permission/evidence needed before broader use. Do not publish or send the package automatically. If input or access is missing, use a permitted sanitized example or document the verification gap; do not infer approval, agreement or status.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized reuse limit or roadmap implication refined and whether it improved learning; publication or operational transfer is not required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Spend about ten minutes comparing experiences using examples the group may discuss.
2. Explain what changed in the workflow or why a practice did not help yet; no success story is required.
3. Identify a habit worth repeating and a friction point or support need.
4. Use these observations to inform the next-focus discussion, without ranking participants.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: AI in Action: choose the next team focus
activities.description: Choose a next work priority and an existing or custom huddle starting point, using tools and content permitted for the team.
activities.expectedOutput: An agreed next priority, a suitable huddle or draft starting point, and an owner; optional backlog ideas remain separate.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the ten-minute AI-in-Action segment to connect the reflection to work where a change would be useful.
2. Choose the priority to try first; keep up to two other ideas as an optional backlog rather than simultaneous commitments.

3. In All Topics, compare relevant outcomes and activities, filtering by Segment, Role, Focus Area, and tools permitted for the team and project. Select one Featured practice for the next ordinary huddle; Extended practices remain optional.
4. If no topic fits, use Huddle in a Box to outline a draft for later review, not to create or publish a finished huddle in this session.
5. Confirm an owner and a practical next step. Without app access, record the priority and locate the content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear next-focus commitment and a participant-owned feedback opportunity, with any unfinished survey completed after the huddle.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Use the final five minutes to restate the useful habit, friction point, and chosen next focus.
2. Confirm who will take the next step and when the team will revisit what it learned.
3. Open the Team Member Impact Survey and let participants complete their own responses. If time or access is insufficient, finish after the huddle rather than extending the live session.
4. Continue the team-owned motion; this transition is not a final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided activation to team-owned practice. The team has completed the eight-week activation journey. Use this huddle to recognize what changed, address friction, and choose what to focus on next.
keyTalkingPoints: This is the same participant experience for every role. Overview: 3 minutes - reconnect to the motion and the transition to team ownership. Share Your Experience: 10 minutes - reflect on useful changes, friction, and support needs. AI-in-Action: 10 minutes - choose the next team priority and a relevant existing or custom huddle starting point. Closing & Next Steps: 5 minutes - confirm the owner and next action, then allow participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey.
discussionQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent?
Which two or three team priorities would be most useful next?
suggestedTransitions: Use the coordinated Transition agenda: Overview, Share Your Experience, AI-in-Action, and Closing & Next Steps. Reflect on real work, agree the next focus and owner, and use the final five minutes for participant-owned survey completion. Review All Topics or a custom-huddle idea only if time and access permit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close the guided path by naming one useful habit, one unresolved friction point, and two or three priorities for team-owned huddles. Assign a follow-up owner for each priority. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately; if access is blocked, record the blocker for follow-up.
preparationChecklist: Before joining, bring one concrete example where AI changed your work, one friction point or challenge, and one idea for what comes next. Keep examples appropriate to share. No separate role-specific Week 9 preparation is needed.
facilitatorQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent, and what support or practice would help?
Which two or three priorities are most useful now?
Which All Topics huddle or custom huddle could help with each priority?
listenFor: Concrete examples of work changed, one useful habit to keep, and a specific friction point. Keep reflection conversational, not a scorecard. priorities grounded in team work and an owner or next step. Remind the group to share only information it is authorized to discuss.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If examples are vague, compare one task before and after and keep tool discussion anchored to the work. If the app, search, download or survey is inaccessible, capture the useful habit, friction point, next priority and follow-up owner manually; do not require Create your own huddle or Huddle in a Box to complete the conversation. A sanitized or clearly labeled synthetic task can demonstrate the reflection method, but is not personal impact evidence or a substitute survey response. Record the access gap and use the approved link/process later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which habit should the team keep, what evidence supports it, and what friction remains? Which two or three priorities should shape the next huddles?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next team-owned huddle, test one chosen habit on real work and decide what to keep, revise or stop. Agree the next topic and owner. Use the Frontier Accelerator topic library or Huddle in a Box if useful; otherwise plan manually. Use approved tools and permitted inputs only. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately, or record an access blocker.
bringBackEvidence: At the next huddle, share one brief, anonymized observation: what changed, what remains uncertain, and what to adjust next. Keep restricted details in approved systems. If untested, share the blocker and next check. Survey completion is not evidence of workflow benefit.

PLC-USPSI-SE-W01.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

activities.name: Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief
activities.description: Synthesize approved customer and technical context into a brief that names the customer decision, constraints, evidence gaps, and criteria. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt:
Using the selected approved customer and technical sources I am attaching, together with the confirmed attendee list I supply, prepare for the meeting. Summarize known outcomes, decisions, constraints, architecture context, open technical questions and missing evidence. Name the business outcome this work has to produce and who owns it. List who has to say yes for this to get funded and staffed, mark which of them is confirmed in the room, and state what each one is measured on where you have a source for it, marking the rest unknown alongside the person who could confirm it. Propose five discovery questions that advance the technical decision, including the questions that establish authority where it is unclear. Separate sourced facts from hypotheses. Include the decision criteria: distinguish criteria explicitly agreed by the customer, citing the supplied source, from proposed criteria that are still hypotheses. For each criterion name who must confirm it, or mark the owner unknown and ask who can confirm ownership. Do not present proposed criteria as customer agreement.

USPSI project practice: Use only minimum necessary supplied inputs approved for this Copilot use, account scope and audience; sanitize sensitive internal, customer, commercial or personal content before entry and withhold classified or restricted material unless explicitly permitted. Include source and as-of date. No CRM/MSX, mailbox, meeting or live-system connector access, scheduled checks, persistent memory or writes are assumed. Return draft text/tables; native artifacts are not assumed. Cite evidence; mark stale, missing or conflicting facts unknown. Label unconfirmed owners, dates, eligibility and conclusions as proposals or questions. Authorized humans retain procurement/policy judgments, commercial/investment approvals, commitments, implementation and publication. If Copilot or sharing is not permitted, use approved evidence manually or a fictional example; do not bypass restrictions.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical discovery brief with questions, evidence gaps, the business outcome and its owner, decision-maker coverage, and explicit decision criteria. Each criterion identifies customer-agreed versus proposed status, supporting source where available, and the person who must confirm it or an unresolved ownership gap.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides which questions are appropriate to ask this customer. A technically sound discovery question can be premature or presumptuous given where the relationship is, and discovery is where that costs most. The SE also decides how directly to ask who can approve, since the question is fair to ask and can still land badly depending on who is in the room.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Selected approved customer and technical sources; the confirmed attendee list for the meeting, and any sourced information you hold about how the decision-makers are measured. Include any recorded customer-agreed decision criteria and their source; otherwise identify criteria as hypotheses to confirm.
activities.whyThisMatters: Discovery becomes useful when it produces decision criteria the customer and team can inspect.

keyTalkingPoints: Start from the customer decision and work backward to criteria and evidence.
Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and open questions.
Capture what must be validated before architecture, demo, or PoC work begins.
discussionQuestions: Which decision is the customer actually trying to make?
Who has to say yes for this to happen, and were they in the room last time?
What evidence gap would make the next technical step unsafe?
What criteria need to be agreed rather than inferred?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief'. facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Technical discovery separates customer-agreed criteria from assumptions and identifies who can say yes. Write criteria before the conversation, then revise them as evidence changes. Keep the useful step in your normal rhythm and bring a permission-safe lesson back for the team to improve together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming or recent technical discovery conversation, approved context, known constraints, and any open technical questions.
facilitatorQuestions: Which discovery question would most change the technical decision?
What evidence is missing or only assumed?

listenFor: Vague decisions, inferred criteria, missing evidence, and questions that sound impressive but do not advance the decision.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A demo or workshop should advance a customer decision, not tour a product. Today narrows the experience to proof that matters.
keyTalkingPoints: Anchor the experience in the customer scenario and decision.
Prepare evidence, objections, roles, environment needs, and fallback plan.
Do not rely on demo energy to cover unclear criteria.
discussionQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop make easier?
Which scenario proves the most important customer concern?
Where could environment, permission, or data issues derail the experience?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the decision-centered demo or workshop plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from scenario selection to the demo or workshop plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate demo evidence and known limitations', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Demos and workshops should provide the smallest relevant proof for the customer decision. Cut feature tours that do not test the criterion and keep prerequisites, limits and fallback visible. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one demo, workshop, or technical customer session and the decision it needs to advance. Supply any available run logs or test results with their date and environment; if none are available, plan the verification and keep execution status unknown.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop advance?
Which scenario proves that decision?
What could fail because of data, tenant, permission, or environment constraints?
What fallback has a peer used when a demo environment failed without claiming the proof succeeded?
listenFor: Feature tours, unclear audience, unsupported claims, missing fallback plans, and proof not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or approved context is unavailable, use a sanitized supplied example or a clearly labeled synthetic case. On paper, create one demo or workshop storyboard: audience decision, proof scenario, environment prerequisite, known limitation and fallback explanation. Mark evidence, assumptions and unknowns. This is a storyboard, not an executed demo, successful test or permission to use an environment. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient. Any later AI run must use project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot and approved supplied inputs.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What decision does the scenario test, and what feature or unsupported claim did you cut because it did not help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, revise a demo or workshop scenario to test the customer criterion, checking prerequisites, limits and fallback. Building or running the whole session is not required. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized scenario retained or cut and whether review made the decision clearer; a customer session need not have occurred. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical responses move faster when supported answers, assumptions, confidence, exceptions, and required reviewers are visible.
keyTalkingPoints: Answer with sources and confidence, not just fluency.
Preserve unsupported areas instead of smoothing them over.
Use the response package to route review, not to bypass it.
discussionQuestions: Which technical answer needs evidence before it can be used?
Where do we usually hide uncertainty?
Who must review the response before it goes to the customer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft the sourced technical answer matrix'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from answer drafting to response governance and exception routing. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Route unsupported technical answers for review', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Grounded technical responses distinguish sourced answers, uncertainty and claims needing specialist or formal review. A defensible answer matters more than filling every box. Agree where this fits in recurring work and how a small, safe signal will help the team learn together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one technical ask, security or architecture question, or objection that requires a governed response. If a formal RFP or questionnaire is in play, bring the technical question inside it rather than the document; the formal response goes through the proposal process.
facilitatorQuestions: Which answer is most consequential?
What source supports it?
Where should the response show confidence, caveat, exception, or SME-needed flag?
What review habit has a peer used to catch an answer that sounded certain but lacked support?
listenFor: Confident but unsourced answers, hidden uncertainty, overbroad commitments, and missing reviewers.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one answer-matrix row: technical question, supplied authoritative source or unavailable, bounded answer or hold, caveat and SME reviewer. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which answer is supported by its source, and which uncertainty belongs with a specialist or formal reviewer?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, review a technical response for an upcoming conversation: verify a consequential answer, flag source or uncertainty, and route unsupported claims to technical or formal proposal review. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized answer qualified or routed and whether it prevented an unsupported technical claim. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical risk should be named while it is still a decision, not after it becomes a customer escalation.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect exit criteria, blockers, proof gaps, objections, dependencies, and handoffs.
Every risk needs evidence, owner, mitigation, checkpoint, and next decision.
Use AI to surface signals, but use your judgment to prioritize them.
discussionQuestions: What technical risk is blocking progression right now?
Which proof gap is being treated as if it were already closed?
Who owns the next technical action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect technical deal health and proof gaps'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from risk naming to action plan and handoff. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the blocker evidence and mitigation path', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Early technical risk management turns evidence into a timely owner conversation, mitigation or accepted handoff. Inference is not a confirmed blocker or escalation rule. Treat the next use as a small test of better work; share the benefit or correction, not just the draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one opportunity or technical workstream with a blocker, proof gap, objection, or dependency.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical risk is blocking progression?
What evidence would clear or confirm it?
Who owns the mitigation and next checkpoint?
How does another SE keep an untested proof gap visible in the technical handoff?
listenFor: Risks without owners, proof gaps treated as closed, delivery handoffs without requirements, and blockers framed too broadly.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one technical risk row: blocker, available evidence, untested proof gap, proposed mitigation owner, handoff requirement and next check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, identify one technical risk early enough to be a conversation rather than an escalation. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized concern checked and whether acting early clarified mitigation or avoided a later surprise. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

Remove sensitive content before reuse.

discussionQuestions: What did you build recently that another SE will rebuild?
What context would make someone trust and adapt it?
What should not be reused without review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Package a reusable technical asset with context'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Technical reuse depends on provenance, permissions, prerequisites and validation limits. A workflow outline or written workflow outline is a draft, not an implemented or tested capability. Agree where this fits in recurring work and how a small, safe signal will help the team learn together.
preparationChecklist: Bring one demo, script, architecture, checklist, response, or pattern that could become reusable. Supply available validation results, date, and environment for asset packaging. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided activation to team-owned practice. The team has completed the eight-week activation journey. Use this huddle to recognize what changed, address friction, and choose what to focus on next.
keyTalkingPoints: This is the same participant experience for every role. Overview: 3 minutes - reconnect to the motion and the transition to team ownership. Share Your Experience: 10 minutes - reflect on useful changes, friction, and support needs. AI-in-Action: 10 minutes - choose the next team priority and a relevant existing or custom huddle starting point. Closing & Next Steps: 5 minutes - confirm the owner and next action, then allow participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey.
discussionQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?
What do you do now that you did not do eight weeks ago?
Which example shows an impact worth repeating?
Where are you stuck or inconsistent?
Which two or three team priorities would be most useful next?
suggestedTransitions: Use the coordinated Transition agenda: Overview, Share Your Experience, AI-in-Action, and Closing & Next Steps. Reflect on real work, agree the next focus and owner, and use the final five minutes for participant-owned survey completion. Review All Topics or a custom-huddle idea only if time and access permit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close the guided path by naming one useful habit, one unresolved friction point, and two or three priorities for team-owned huddles. Assign a follow-up owner for each priority. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately; if access is blocked, record the blocker for follow-up.
preparationChecklist: Before joining, bring one concrete example where AI changed your work, one friction point or challenge, and one idea for what comes next. Keep examples appropriate to share. No separate role-specific Week 9 preparation is needed.
facilitatorQuestions: Where has AI changed the way you work?

listenFor: Concrete examples of work changed, one useful habit to keep, and a specific friction point. Keep reflection conversational, not a scorecard. priorities grounded in team work and an owner or next step. Remind the group to share only information it is authorized to discuss.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If examples are vague, compare one task before and after and keep tool discussion anchored to the work. If the app, search, download or survey is inaccessible, capture the useful habit, friction point, next priority and follow-up owner manually; do not require Create your own huddle or Huddle in a Box to complete the conversation. A sanitized or clearly labeled synthetic task can demonstrate the reflection method, but is not personal impact evidence or a substitute survey response. Record the access gap and use the approved link/process later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which habit should the team keep, what evidence supports it, and what friction remains? Which two or three priorities should shape the next huddles?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next team-owned huddle, test one chosen habit on real work and decide what to keep, revise or stop. Agree the next topic and owner. Use the Frontier Accelerator topic library or Huddle in a Box if useful; otherwise plan manually. Use approved tools and permitted inputs only. Complete the Team Member Impact Survey separately, or record an access blocker.

PLC-USPSI-SSP-W01.todayObjective: Explore how peer-led huddles connect business outcomes, recurring workflows, and responsible AI experimentation, including what to try and share between sessions.
PLC-USPSI-SSP-W01.whyItMatters: Access and usage do not equal transformation. Teams build durable capability when managers connect outcomes to the work, peers experiment together, and evidence from practice improves the next cycle.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the Frontier Accelerator Huddle motion. This shared 30-minute Orientation starts a continuing peer-learning path: begin with recurring work, surface friction, and consider one useful next test. It is not a tool demo or performance assessment.
keyTalkingPoints: Start with the workflow and real friction, not a product. Compare approaches before choosing a tool; tools and AI are optional. Use only authorized, non-sensitive inputs and permitted tools. Treat outputs as drafts for human review; people retain authority over decisions and actions.
discussionQuestions: Where does a familiar workflow slow down? What makes that step difficult? What have peers found helpful? What would we need to understand before trying a small change?
suggestedTransitions: Move from a workflow example to peer comparison, then consider a bounded next test. Offer a permitted tool or AI only if useful; otherwise continue manually. Before moving on, distinguish observations, assumptions, and drafts needing human review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Return to the workflow and name what peer learning clarified. Invite an optional next test or question, with appropriate authorization and human review. This begins a continuing learning motion; no deliverable, performance proof, or reporting obligation is created.
preparationChecklist: No prework, tool access, or artifact is required. A familiar or synthetic example is helpful but optional. Use only supplied or otherwise authorized non-sensitive inputs; never share sensitive customer or employee information. Listening or a manual explanation is enough to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What happens at this step, handoff, or decision? Where is the friction? How does someone else approach it? What small change might help, and what human review would be needed before using it?
listenFor: Listen for specific friction, useful peer comparisons, and clearly labelled assumptions. Keep privacy, permission, and human authority visible. Tool use, speed, and polished outputs are not measures of participation; a useful question or clearer workflow understanding also matters.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or suitable inputs are unavailable, stop the tool attempt and use a synthetic, non-sensitive example, manual walkthrough, or peer discussion. Do not bypass permissions or use sensitive information. Clearly label anything not executed; discussion remains valid participation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did another perspective help you notice? Which assumption still needs checking? What would you like to understand better before changing this workflow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, choose a small next test or question within your authority. Tools and AI remain optional, and any output stays a draft until appropriate human review. You may also keep reflecting or defer; no deadline, artifact, or follow-up report is required.
bringBackEvidence: If you return to the conversation, optionally share an observation, question, or peer insight using authorized, non-sensitive information. No artifact, completed practice, performance result, or report is required. Never share sensitive customer or employee information.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Lead and account signals are noisy. Focus on turning them into a focused follow-up plan.
keyTalkingPoints: Qualification is evidence work. Solution relevance, owner, message, consent, and next action must be explicit.
discussionQuestions: Which lead or signal deserves attention first? What evidence makes it real? Who owns the next action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from noisy signals to one prioritized follow-up plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Lead prioritization matters when credible demand leads to appropriate, consent-aware follow-up. Activity or a high AI ranking alone does not establish customer intent. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one lead or account signal, dated qualification evidence and the proposed follow-up owner. Use approved user-supplied evidence with source and date; review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: Which lead has the strongest dated evidence of solution relevance, and what is only inferred? Who owns the first follow-up? How does a peer distinguish a buying signal from marketing activity before outreach?
listenFor: Undifferentiated lead lists, vague ownership, weak message fit, and missing consent/context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-lead ranking: dated solution signal, customer relevance, missing context/permission, follow-up owner and next question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which signal warrants a customer action rather than just a new record, and what evidence would disprove the opportunity?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, turn your top-priority lead into an actual first contact this week. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized lead signal and whether the reviewed follow-up clarified interest or avoided a poor contact; no sent message is required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

activities.name: Turn the conversation into decisions and commitments
activities.description: Convert meeting notes into what changed, what was agreed, and what the customer actually committed to.
activities.prompt:
Here are my notes from the customer conversation: the supplied notes or transcript summary. Produce three separate lists: what we learned that changes our understanding, what was explicitly agreed and by whom, and what remains open. Then draft a short follow-up note to the customer confirming only what was actually agreed. Do not record something as agreed if the notes only show it was discussed. Flag anything ambiguous rather than resolving it.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP confirms that anything recorded as agreed was actually agreed and owns the follow-up wording before sending. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A solution-selling plan is useful only if it changes pursuit execution. Focus on building a plan that can be worked.
keyTalkingPoints: Plan around customer outcome, solution play, stakeholders, proof needs, demo or workshop sequence, and next decision.
discussionQuestions: Which solution pursuit needs a clearer plan? What proof or stakeholder coverage is missing?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the solution-selling plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Solution-selling plans should expose who decides, what proof matters and where engagement is missing. preparationChecklist: Bring one solution pursuit, the customer outcome, known stakeholders and the proof or decision gap in its current plan. Use approved user-supplied evidence with source and date; review the prior commitment.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Pursuits stall at handoffs. Focus on making every role, partner, funding dependency, and checkpoint explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Name the objective, contributors, asks, owners, dates, dependencies, and escalation points.
discussionQuestions: Which handoff is currently assumed rather than owned? Where could partner or funding support change the path?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Bring funding into the pursuit orchestration plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from orchestration principles to one stalled handoff. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Make each ask specific enough to be accepted', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Cross-role orchestration should unblock the customer decision with the smallest necessary accepted contribution. Funding, partner capacity and technical help are not secured merely by requesting them. Make that evidence check part of recurring work; share a safe example of what changed so peers can adapt the habit.
preparationChecklist: Bring one pursuit handoff, current contributors, partner or funding dependencies and the owner or date still unconfirmed. Use approved user-supplied evidence with source and date; review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: Which specialist, technical, partner or funding dependency is stalled? What evidence and acceptance does the next owner need? How does a peer make that handoff executable without representing funding as approved?
listenFor: Unnamed owners, handoffs without dates, partner input treated as optional, and funding status overstated.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one specialist/technical/partner/funding handoff row: contribution needed, proposed owner, evidence, acceptance gap and next date. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which handoff is still assumed rather than accepted, and what owner, request, or date would make it actionable?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take the most consequential stalled handoff and personally send a reviewed, dated ask to its contributor. Do not request work from every role merely to complete the exercise. Ask the receiving owner to accept the work; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share an anonymized stalled handoff and whether a bounded ask clarified ownership or exposed a gap; no collection of every role request is needed. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Competitive response should be built on customer context and proof, not generic battlecards.
keyTalkingPoints: Use current approved competitive evidence, win/loss context, differentiators, objections, risks, and review flags.
discussionQuestions: Which competitor or alternative is shaping the decision? What proof is strongest and where is it weak?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the competitive differentiation brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from competitor context to one proof-backed response plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test the differentiator against the customer's real decision criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Competitive responses are credible when current approved proof addresses the customer decision criterion. Objection handlers are not permission for unsupported competitor claims. Use the next real case to test this habit, then compare what helped and what failed with the huddle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one competitive pursuit, the customer decision criteria and current approved competitive evidence; label gaps and assumptions. Use approved user-supplied evidence with source and date; review the prior commitment.
facilitatorQuestions: Which competitive claim changes the customer decision, and which dated source supports it? What would make it inapplicable here? How has a colleague tested differentiation against the customer's actual criteria?
listenFor: Stale battlecard claims, unsupported competitor statements, and differentiators not tied to customer priorities.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one competitive response row: customer criterion, proposed differentiator, dated source or unknown, applicability caveat and validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which customer criterion does approved competitive proof address, and what claim should you qualify or avoid?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, build one objection handler tied to approved proof, and use it in a live conversation. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a sanitized objection and whether approved proof answered it, required a caveat or showed a need for discovery. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle focuses on the next decision, not the whole deal.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect milestone readiness, stakeholder gaps, proof, blockers, dependencies, partner/funding needs, and owners.
discussionQuestions: What is the pursuit actually waiting on? What evidence or owner will clear the next decision?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect solution opportunity readiness'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from readiness inspection to a 14- to 30-day action plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Prepare the conversation that clears the next decision', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Opportunity progress means clearing an evidenced customer decision, not just advancing a record. Separate confirmed milestones from assumptions and validate the next conversation with its owner. Frontier Accelerator grows through repeated use and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Carry this judgment into the next work cycle.
preparationChecklist: Bring one live solution pursuit, its current milestone, decision evidence and next blocker. If selecting the customer-facing close-plan practice, bring an existing approved close plan for one opportunity, the customer decision process and outcome, and confirmed-versus-assumed dates. A portfolio action list is not that plan.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next customer decision, rather than the next internal task? Which evidence gap or missing owner prevents it? What would another specialist change in the next 14 to 30 days without promising a close?
listenFor: Close-date language instead of next decision, unowned blockers, missing proof, and unclear stakeholder gaps.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one solution-readiness card: next decision, proof gap, stakeholder gap, owner and bounded 14-to-30-day action. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal assumption changed when you inspected the evidence, and who owns the next decision or approval?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, draft or rehearse the conversation that could clear the next decision on a stalled opportunity, validate its ask with the owner, and use it when an appropriate meeting is available. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, use a sanitized manual example and identify the gap rather than inventing facts. For USPSI, use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with authorized supplied information; otherwise complete the same check manually. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access.
bringBackEvidence: Share a safe description of the next decision and whether preparing the conversation clarified a blocker; a closed decision is not required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, share the gap and next check.
